In the Year 1784* the Patent Officers at the Out Ports, and their Deputies (and some Offices were then vacant) amounted together to Three hundred and Sixty-five.

The Office of Customer suppressed, and those of Controller and Searcher vested only in acting Officers, the Number necessary to execute these Two last Offices, at the Seventy-two Ports, will be One hundred and Forty-four; and of those required at the Thirty-two Creeks, in lieu of the Deputies to the Patentees, Sixty-four; together, Two hundred and Eight The Diminution of Officers, therefore, as compared with those employed in fulfilling these Duties in the Year 1784, will be One hundred and Fifty-seven.

What we have hitherto suggested will, we trust, tend to perfect the Method of conducting this Revenue at the Out Ports: But there is a farther Regulation, in our Opinion, indispensibly essential to the Attainment of that Object. It regards the Collector, the supreme Officer at every Out Port. Enough has been stated to demonstrate the Importance of his Duty. In order to give at once a full Impression thereof, we subjoin a Copy of his Instructions.

It should seem that great Caution ought to precede the Delegation of this Trust; and yet, as we learn from the Examinations of William Stilts, Esquire, scarcely any is interposed. No Official Knowledge or Experience is required. Persons utter Strangers to the Office, and the Business of the Customs, have been frequently appointed to this Employment.

The Searcher, and many other Officers, are, upon being nominated, put under Instructions for a certain Time, and after the Expiration of that Period, not admitted to discharge the Duties of their Stations, until they produce a Certificate from the proper Officers, of their being duly qualified.

The Collector enters upon his Office without any such Preparation. There is, that we can find, but One Disqualification for this Appointment, the having been in the Service and dismissed; and but One Requisite, that of giving Security, by Bond, to a certain Amount. Here there seems to be urgent Need of some Reform; and that Reform ought, upon precisely the same Ground, to be extended to the Controller, the Officer next in Rank and Consequence.

We think that a Course of gradual Rise to the Office of Controller at an Out Port, and from that to the one of Collector, to be forfeited alone by Misconduct or Incapacity on the Part of the Officer who, upon a Vacancy, should stand entitled in the Order of Succession; commencing at, and passing through such intermediate Official Stations as might best suit the practical (Economy of the Department, is the obvious Remedy for the Defect adverted to, and would be a Regulation highly beneficial.

Such a System would secure to these Two important Offices, proved Ability and Fidelity: The Revenue would be fitly managed; and the subordinate Officer, having before his View a Reward certain, if merited, would have the strongest Motives to make himself Master of his Duty, and to execute it with Zeal for the Service.

WE have, in the preceding Part of this Report, stated the material Facts relative to the Fees taken by the Officers of the Customs at the Out Ports.

That Species of Payment appears, in very ancient

Times, to have been subject to Abuse, and to have required the Interposition of high Authority.

The Fourth of Henry the Fourth Chapter the 21st, ehaets, " That from henceforth they [the Searchersj " take of no Masters of Ships, for their Office of " Searching, any Silver, or Money, for their Welcome' " and parewel, nor any other Thing for the same, " as it hath been taken and received before this Time, " otherwise than shall be ordained to them for their " Office by our Lord the King."

Upon consulting the Journals of the House of Commons, we find, that at many Intervals between the Years 1557 and 1626, Bills were introduced into, or revived in, the Two Houses of Parliament, for the express Object of avoiding the Extortions and Exactions of Customers, Controllers, Searchers, and other Officers or Persons employed in the Customs. These several Bills none of them arrived at Completion, but were repeatedly lost in some Stage of their Progress towards being perfected into a Law.

At the /Era of the Restoration, the House of Commons seemed to have judged it requisite to institute a thorough Inquiry into the Fees received or demanded by the Officers of the Customs, and to have had it in Contemplation to correct or remove the Defects which then subsisted, and to provide against the like Evils in future, by establishing, upon delinite Footing, the Fees to be taken at the different Ports. This apparent Design of Parliament, commenced in Execution at that Period, and prosecuted at different Times, during some subsequent Years, was no farther matured that has been shewn; and the State in which the Subject remains, evinces that the Work has not since been resumed to Effect.

The System of Fees now existent is, in our judgment, fundamentally imperfect. — Such a System, if rightly constituted, should have Three Properties:

1st. It should conduce to the Ease and Accommodation of Commerce.

2d. It should offer a safe and equal Source of Reward to the Officer.

3d. It should be pure of all Tendency injurious to the Revenue.

The Observations which follow are intended to demonstrate that the Payment to the Officer by Fee does not accord with these Principles.

The Lists of Fees usually taken, returned to us by the Officers of the Out Ports, and of which we have annexed a Portion as Specimens, exhibit strongly the Defects under which the Subject labours in regard to the Merchant. Upon a general Examination of these Returns, we found them full of Perplexity, Disagreement, and Confusion. The Expressions used to describe the Business for which the Fee is payable to the Officer, arc frequently so dissimilar and irreconcilable at different Ports, as to render it a Matter of Difficulty, and in some Cases of Impossibility, to obtain a Ground for clear and certain Comparison. Where such Means were attainable, great Variety appeared both as to the Terms of the Description, the Amount of the Sum to be paid, and the Division thereof among the Officers entitled; and that for the same specific Service.

This Incongruity we did not find to be limited to One Class of Officers, to particular Ports, to local Circumstances and Transactions rarely occurring; nor did the Frequency and Degree of it seem to be regulated by die Proximity or Distance of the Ports. The Dissimilarity was general; as prevalent between the Head Ports and the respective Members and Creeks dependent thereupon, as between Ports separate and no Way connected; among Ports for which Tables had been appointed by the Authority of Parliament, as at those having no such Standard. It obtained not merely in the Transactions of Foreign

Commerce,

2y Geo. III. 26° Januariu

Commerce, but extended also to the Coasting Trade.

The most exact Inspection and Comparison of the Fees taken at the different Out Ports, which we were able to make, furnished numerous Examples of Discordance and Variation, few of Conformity or Agreement. And of this irregular System, how imperfect is the Information given to the Merchant, by any Notice publicly affixed in the Offices at the different Ports, has been detailed.

An Acquaintance with the Charge of Fees at one Port cannot impart a Knowledge, can scarcely warrant a Calculation, of the Expence which may be induced by them at another Port.

Amidst these Circumstances, the Merchant, in respect of the Payment by Fee at the Out Ports, dbes not, in the Course of his Transactions, appear to be guarded as he ought against Uncertainty, Trouble, and Imposition.

The Force of this Truth, as applied to the Port

N* 50. of London, is evident from the Examinations of N* 51,5'*‘ Mr. Thomas Hubbei't, Mr. William Walter , and

Mr. Thomas Coles.

N* 59. We also learn from the Examination of Arthur 'Hammond, Esquire, One of the General Surveyors resident in London, and who, in executing the Duties of his Office, has been sent upon Inspections to the Out Ports, that frequent References, by Order of the Board of Customs, are made to the General Surveyors, upon Complaints of the Merchants in regard to Fees, as either being excessive, or not warranted by Law; and that he has known the Fees to be represented in some Instances as uncertain and increasing in the Sum: And Complaints of a similar Kind have been made to him when upon the Inspecting Service at the Out Ports.

27. By the Examination of Mr. John Timothy

it appears that the same Evils are felt and complained of in the Plantations. In the Year 1785, a Memorial presented to the Treasury by the West India Merchants, and referred to the Board of Customs, states, among other Matters, " That Redress is necessary respecting the Island Customhouse Officers, who should " exact more than the established Fees, for Dispatch " Money, or on other Pretences; and that such as " shall by any Means require, take, or receive more " than the established Fees, or cause any unnecessary " Delay to Shipping, should be immediately proceeded " against."

Nor does the Officer of the Customs stand safely and well circumstanced touching his Emolument as derived from Fees — His situation is perilous. We have shewn how far the Parliamentary Authority for that Species of Payment extends. The larger Proportion of the Out Ports have it not; and in the Port of London, and at those Ports where there arc Tables so sanctioned, the Contents of them are very limited, and totally inapplicable to the Business and Officers of this Time.

All Fees are prohibited, except such as have been established by Parliament. Some of the Officers have no Salaries: Many have Salaries so small as not to afford common Support. Thus placed they must, by taking Fees forbidden by Law, offend against their Duty, and risque the Consequences; or endure an Official Situation whence the Means of Livelihood cannot be derived. Those Consequences are heavy: They go to Loss of Employment, Incapacity of being re-admitted into the Service, and other Penalties. Here the Officer seems to be placed in a hard and improper Alternative:

And the Danger is not the only Evil. The Fee, in various other Particulars, operates inexpediently by him. The Mode itself of receiving a Stipend by very small Sums is troublesome, and not always convenient for Business. Where one Officer (as often happens) collects the Fees due to another, that Transaction may Vol. 42.

beget Distrust; and, accordingly, Complaints are Fifteenth sometimes made by Officer against Officer, for Fees Report taken and withheld. on Pub*ic

The Income dependant upon Fees is precarious and Accounts< unequal: It may be greatly injured, and nearly lost, by the Diminution of particular Business, by new Regulations, or other Causes: A material Diversity in the Emoluments of Officers in the same Station and Trust may thereby be created. The Inconvenience we advert to extends farther. A Payment by Fee not only occasions (except where all the Fees received are carried to a common Stock, and equally divided) Disparity of Profit among the same Class of Officers, but it serves to break down the Uniformity of Emolument between Officers acting in Branches of the Department distinct from each other, yet equal in Official Rank, and those other Circumstances which form the Title to, and ought to fix the Standard of, Reward. Instances are not wanting, where, by Means of the same Operation, the Income of the Subordinate Officer is carried greatly beyond that of the Superior. These Effects are, we think, subversive of a just Equality in the Distribution of Recompence, and unfavourable to the proper Gradation of Office.

The Objections which we have in this general Way stated, are not built upon Hypothesis: They are founded upon Fact, and Illustrations of them contained in the Accounts of the Emoluments of the Officers of the Customs, annexed the one to our last, the other to this Report. *

We have hitherto, in considering the Subject of Fees, fixed our Attention upon the Merchant and the Officer; and it seems obvious that, for the Advantage of both, some material Change therein is requisite.

If the View extended no farther, it might become a Matter of Deliberation, whether a Revision and Amendment of the System might not be feasible and sufficient:

But a third Consideration, which must outweigh all others, does, in our Opinion, demand the total Abolition of this Mode of Payment to the Officers — we mean, the Good of the Revenue.

The Office of the Customs exists for the Purpose of a great and important Collection from the Subject.

The Officer holds his Employment by the immediate Appointment of, or through the Intervention of, some Authority originally flowing from the Crown.

The main Scope of his executive Duty is to secure the just Payment of the Sums due upon different Articles of Commerce, and to enforce a Compliance with the Requisites ordained by Law.

An Officer so appointed, and for such an End, ought, in Consistency and Prudence, to reap the Compensation for his Services solely from the Power whence his Authority is delegated, and to the Use of which the Produce of his Labours is applied. It is not, we think, proper or safe, that his Emoluments should proceed from any other Source than the Crown or National Treasure.

The Revenue of the Customs, however considerable in the Aggregate, rests, and must rest, in Origin, materially upon the Integrity and Diligence of Officers not high in the Official Scale. The vigilant Guard of the Ship, from her Arrival in Port until the legal Duties payable upon all her Cargo have been satisfied, and the ascertaining faithfully and accurately the Weight, Number, Quantity, Quality, or whatever may be the Rule for fixing the Amount of the Duty due upon the Article of Commerce, are the main Operations which secure and determine the Receipt.

The Officer, in discharging these Trusts, as well as those upon which the Diminution of the Receipt by Bounty or Drawback depends, is continually placed in a Situation where the Rights of the Public, and the Interests of the Individual, are opposed. In some

I Transactions

Fifteenth Report on Public Accounts.

3°

Transactions he has specially the Exercise of a discretionary Judgment, and in die general Course of the Business much is in his Po.wer.

With whatever Strictness a Line of Conduct under these Circumstances may be watched, it behoves, as a primary Precaution, to fix the Mode of Reward upon the purest Foundation. The Practice of allowing the Officer to be paid by the Merchant, for the Performance of Official Business, appears to be repugnant to that Maxim. It occasions an Intercourse unfit and dangerous, and brings them into a mutual Relation, in which they should never stand. Habits of pecuniary Obligation or Exchange of private Interest, ought not to mingle with the Execution of such Public Duty. The Subsistence of the Officer who collects Revenue, should in no wise depend upon the Person who contributes.

By these Observations, we would not be thought to convey Imputation upon any Officer or Class of Officers. We have no Instances of Misconduct in View. We reason upon general Truths.

It is not to be overlooked, that the Fee has in itself an inherent Defect. That Method of Payment cannot be so adjusted as to bear exact Proportion to the Value of the Subject which it affects. The Fee is a given Sum paid upon a certain Document, or for a certain Service: Whether it be upon an Entry, or by the Package, or Tale, or such like Measure, the different Value of the Goods does not produce any corresponding Variation in the Fee. And this is not barely a speculative Imperfection: It has hurtful Consequences. We have it in Evidence, that Orders, when but to small Amount, have been very frequently left unexecuted on Account of the Heaviness of the Fees which must have been paid upon them; and farther, that these Orders, there was great Reason to believe, were thereby diverted into the Channels of Foreign Trade.

The Principle which has determined our Judgment upon the Inexpediency of admitting the Payment by Fee to the Officer of the Customs, applies in equal Force to the Recompence or Gratuity. The Gratuity, as by Nature less definite than the Fee, is, where Usage has not corrected that Defect, more faulty. But this Kind of Discrimination matters little. Our Position, if solid, can allow of no Exception.

It is true that the Service for which the Gratuity is payable is special, and out of the ordinary Course. The Legislature has, however, authorized the Attendance of the Officer at Times and Places not required by Law, as a proper and necessary Accommodation for Trade; and it seems meet that the Execution of such Business should be made a Part of his regular Duty, and the Reward thereof be provided for in die Annual Stipend allotted to him.

We are accordingly of Opinion, that every Payment by Fee or Gratuity, or in any Shape whatsoever, by the Merchant or others to the Officer, for or on Account of Business done in the Discharge of his Official Duty, ought to be abolished throughout the whole Department of the Customs; and that the Reward of the Officer (except in what arises from Seizures) should be by Salary alone.

If this Regulation be adopted, a Provision for the Officer, in Lieu of the Emolument be now derives from Fees and Gratuities, must be made. That Charge must either be borne by the Revenue of the Customs, or, if to remain upon the Merchant, some equal and convenient Method must be devised, whereby Persons transacting Business with the Office may supply a Fund for that Purpose.

Whether, with the Load of Debt that presses upon the Country, the total Exoneration of Commerce from this Incumbrance might, by the many beneficial Effects to Foreign and Domestic Trade which must follow, sufficiently countervail and compensate for the Increase

1787.

of Public Expence thence induced, is one of those hmh Matters to be reserved for the Deliberation of the Legislature, and on which we do not presume to offer an Opinion.

If the Merchant is to have his Business in the Office* of the Customs transacted gratuitously, or if he is, by a Substitute for Fees, still to pay on Account of the Revenue what has hitherto been taken of him for the Benefit of the Officer, the Change introduced will in either Case be great. And it will no Doubt be an Object with the superintending Branches of the Department, to have the utmost Care that the Introduction of a System unsupported by former Habits, and placing the Officer and the Merchant in a new relative' Situation, may not obstruct or lessen any of the fair Official Accommodations to Trade now permitted.

We have proposed that a fixed Annual Salary should become the sole Reward to the Officer of the Customs for executing the Duty of his Office. That Salary ought, we think, in every Instance to be a Compensation fully adequate to the Employment. We do not thereby mean any Arrangement tending to the profuse Disposal of Public Money, or the Concession of unnecessary Advantage to the Officer — We mean such an Appointment as shall be judged reasonable and competent, due Regard being had to the Talents or Industry required, the Trust committed, the Responsibility annexed, and the Station in Office and Life of the Person employed. And this, we deem, is strictly consistent with sound (Economy, which manifests itself not by withholding from the efficient Servant of the Public a proper Return for his Service, and the fair Means of Support, but by suppressing useless Offices, reducing overgrown Emoluments, striking off unnecessary Expences, and modelling every Department upon such a Plan, that each Officer shall have a fit and sufficient Portion of Duty assigned to him, and all needless Superfluity in the Number of Officers maintained be rejected. A Salary estimated by this just and liberal Standard will, in our Opinion, be finally for the Safety and Welfare of the Revenue; whilst to admit the Pressure of Necessity, upon Situations exposed to frequent Temptation, and affording easy Opportunities of yielding thereto, can hardly be reconciled to Prudence or Humanity.

The Institution of One plain Salary to the Officer, will be attended with another good Effect: It will simplify the Mode of Reward in this Office. We found it complicate and perplexed, consisting often, in that Portion of it derived from the Crown, of various minute Payments by Salary, and of different Poundages or Allowances allotted to particular Services, and paid under special Authorities to the same Officer — Distinctions of no Use, and serving to multiply and subdivide Account. Nothing ought to be more clear, and speedily ascertainable, than the Charge upon the Public, and the Profit to the Officer, arising from any Employment. How little the System now obtaining in the Customs is suited to this Kind of Precision, is apparent from the Detail given at the Beginning of this Report. More than a Twelvemonth elapsed before tire Office could furnish us with a complete Account of the Emoluments of the Officers for One Year.

As the Stipend to the Officer should in the First Instance be in a simple Form, so it ought, we think, to be exempt from all subsequent Deductions upon Public Account. The Practice of issuing a Sum, to receive back a Portion thereof after that Portion has been subject to a Circuit, to Delay, and Diminution from Charges of Collection, seems to be inconsistent and unthrifty. In respect of the Payment for the Land Tax made by many of the Officers, this Incongruity goes farther. The Annual Contributions to that Tax, by Officers whose Salaries do not exceed Sixty Pounds 3 a Year,

Had Commerce been exhibited to the Understanding of our Ancestors, in the enlarged Form, and with the important Combinations, under which we behold that Subject, probably it would have been distinguished by a due Place, in this Spirit of provisionary Wisdom, against the Hindrance of Labour or Business useful to the State.

The Act of the 6th and 7th of William the Third, in some Measure supplied what was wanting in this ancient Law, by permitting the Officer of the Customs, upon urgent Occasions, to work at Times not legally required of him, in Consideration of a Recompence made by the Merchant for such Service. A farther Progress in the same Direction would be consonant with the ripened Policy and advanced State of Things at this Day. Since, therefore, on the one Hand, there does not appear to be any essential Necessity for continuing the Holidays in the Customs in their present Number; and, on the other Hand, their Observance may be productive of Evil to the Revenue, and is highly inconvenient and detrimental to Trade, with the Extension or Decrease of which the Custom Receipt must augment or diminish — we are of Opinion, that a Regulation rendering these Holidays less numerous would be to National Benefit.

The Restriction of the Annual Holidays in the Customs to the great Festivals, and a few memorable Anniversaries; or a Reduction of them, upon the Principle of preventing their happening near to each other ( Sunday being regarded as one) and of their being rejected at the Seasons when the Bulk of the Import or Export Trade is transacting, might either of them suffice, and the Mode judged most expedient be adopted.

We thought it to be our Duty thus to submit to the Wisdom of the Legislature what has occurred to U3 upon a Subject which arose in the Course of our Inquiries, and relates to Matters of high Public Concern.

In pursuing the Expenditure incurred in the Management of this Revenue for the Year 1784, the Plan upon which the Cruizing Vessels of the Customs are supported, came under our Observation. We found ' the Cruizers maintained either upon the Esablish-ment, or by Contract; and the Contract of Two Kinds. It is not for us to judge which of these different Modes of Maintenance, or whether a Plan like the present, mixed and comprehending each of them, is best adapted to the Nature and Exigencies of the Service, and most for the Public Advantage. To the ' Board of Customs, where the Aids of past Experience are united with continual practical Knowledge on the Subject (the true Means of determining) that Decision properly belongs. But observing one Part of the System which appears to us defective in Principle, upon that we consider ourselves bound to remark. It is this: The Contracts entered into for the Cruizers are, many of them, made with the Collectors and Controllers (together or separately) of the Ports at # which the Vessels are respectively stationed. Of Twenty-four Cruizers employed by Contract in the Year 1784, not less than Sixteen were thus circumstanced.

We apprehend it to be aq obvious Truth, that no Interest in the Performance of a Service ought to vest . in the Person whose Duty it is to controul the Execution thereof: The Union of these Two Trusts is not to be confided in; an Official Self-Controul seems to be practically a Contradiction, and a Thing impossible. The Application intended is plain.

The Cruizing Service in the Customs imports much to the Revenue and fair Trade of the Country: That

it may be conducted to the best Effect, depends upon, many Concurrences; as, the proper Outfit of the Vessel, the Repair and State in which she is kept, the Number and Condition of her Men, her plying her Station diligently, and other Particulars of a like Kind. The Superintendance and Check, at the Out Ports, over most if not the Whole of this Combination, reside with the Collectors and Controllers; these Officers are either to be informed of, inspect, examine, report, or certify upon the several Circumstances relative to the Performance of and Expenditure attending this Service.

It appears possible that the Crown and the Contractor, though the clear Produce of the Seizures made by the Cruizer is for their common Benefit, may in previous Instances have their Interests tending different Ways.

For Example, Savings in the Repairs of Victualling of the Vessel; a Complement of Men short of the Number allowed by and charged to the Crown; a Regard to the Safety of the Vesssl herself in hazardous Weather (and other Cases might be put) may, it should seem, in one or the other Species of Contract, be made to operate to the Prejudice of the Revenue, and the Advantage of the Contractor; and, what is not the least material Consideration, the Efficacy of a principal Instrument, used for the Repression of very pernicious Acts, thereby be diminished.

It is not on any supposed Prevalence of such ill Consequences that our Reasoning is built. We do not know that they exist. We look solely to these Positions — that every Check should stand upon Groond perfectly free from any interested Connection with the Subject to be checked; and, that all Official Arrangement ought to preclude the Opening for Injury to the Public Service. Therefore we think, that unless some very. powerful Cause obtains for adhering to the present Practice, no Collector, Controller, or Officer belonging to the Customs, should be admitted to contract for, or to have Share or Concern in, the C ontracts made for the Cruizing Vessels to be employed in the Service of this Revenue.

In our last Report we recommended the Suppression of several inferior Treasuries in the Customs; as also, of the Offices supported for the Purpose of controuling or passing the Accounts kept in those Treasuries.

These various Offices, we found, existed in order that the Produce arising out of Seizures and Fines might be kept distinct from the Custom Duties in all the Stages of Receipt, Payment, and Audit of Account. That Distinction, as repugnant to Uniformity, Perspicuity, and (Economy, we thought, ought to be discontinued; and, in Place thereof, One Treasury, and One Controul, to be established.

The Necessity of such Regulation has been farther confirmed to us. The Accounts in every Public Office ought to be so constructed, as to exhibit, if coming under the View of Parliament, a complete Statement of all Receipt and Expenditure within the Department. By the Practice of distinguishing these Two Sources of Revenue in the Customs, this End is counteracted.

An Account of the Gross and Net Produce of the Customs, we learn from the Examination of Mr. Jo- N° 13. shua Powell, is not presented regularly to Parliament, but only upon special Requisition. When an Order, pursuant to that Requisition, comes to the Board of Customs, they, by their Minute, direct the Controller General to make out and present the Account required: And no other Account is made out, by any Officer of the Customs, in consequence of the Requisition.

The Controller General includes in the Account, all he can include, the Gross Receipt of the Custom Duties, and the Payments therefrom. The Produce

arising

arising from Seizures and Fines, and the Payments out of that Fund, he cannot insert: They are not within his Cognizance or Controul.

N* *4. By the £xamination of Mr. John Bastin, First Clerk to the Accountant of Petty Receipts, in whose Office the Account of Seizures is passed, we find, that upon consulting the Books in his Office, it does not appear that any Account has ever been delivered to Parliament of the Produce of Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures, for London and the Out Ports, with the various Payments for Management made out of that Produce, and the Payments into the Exchequer. Thence it follows, that no perfect and entire State of the Produce and Expenditure of this Office is laid before Parliament, or can be, whilst the present Mode of forming and obtaining the Account is preserved.

In the Year 1784, the Payments into the Exchequer, out of the King’s Net Share of Seizures and Fines, by the Two Receivers of Fines and Forfeitures, and the Solicitors of the Customs, amounted together to Twenty-L * five thousand Nine hundred and Sixty-one Pounds, Sixteen Shillings, and Six Pence Three Farthings; their Payments for Charges of Management, together with those made by the Collectors at the Out Ports out of the King’s Net Share of Seizures, to Sixty-

t- Mf* 4- nine thousand Six hundred and Fifty-nine Pounds, Four Shillings — Sums which would not have appeared had the General Account of the Customs for the Year been called for.

And this Defect the more requires to be corrected, in as much as the System of directing the various Charges incident to this Revenue upon the Fund arising out of Seizures and Fines, has of late been gaining Ground.

N° 14. We are informed by Mr. John Mills, that a considerable Part of the Incidental Expences of the Customs, which used to be paid by the Receiver General, has for some Time past been paid by the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports.

Accounts laid before Parliament become the Subject for Deliberations and Proceedings of high National Concern: They should comprehend the full Means of Information. The Defect we are observing upon not only prevents that Information from being complete, but it may serve to mislead, and give Rise to erroneous Conclusions: For, whilst the Total Charges of Management stated in the Controller General’s Account may, comparatively with those of former Years, be decreasing, the real Expence of managing this Revenue, including the Payments made out of the King’s Net Share of Seizures and Fines, and which do not appear in the General Account, may augment

We are, therefore, of Opinion, that the Reform we suggested, of bringing all Receipt and Payment into the Office of the Receiver General, and of extending the Controul of the Controller General to the Produce of Seizures and Fines, in the same Way that it now operates upon the Custom Duties, is urgently wanted, and should, without Delay, be carried into Execution.

No Evil could arise from admitting them at any Period; for if they were afterwards found to be erroneous, the Collectors might lie surcharged in Cases where Sums were due to the Public, and have Credit where Balances were due to them.

It seetns therefore right, that proper Authority should be given to take these Balances at the Period most convenient for the Account. The Controller General will be enabled to include in the General Account of the Customs, when required by Parliament, the Gross Receipt and the Payments at the Plantations; whereas hitherto no more of that Receipt and Expenditure has been inserted than the Sum brought to Account by the Receiver General, and the Charges on the Head of the Plantations paid in England.

Thus Simplicity and Unity, Qualities essential to the apt and expedient Conduct of Business, peculiarly that of Account, and where the Transactions are of Magnitude, will be introduced into some of the most material Branches of this great Department.

We here conclude our Researches into the Customs — an Office which has employed much of our Time and Labourj and engaged us in Three successive Reports.

Various Matters of Moment have, in the Pursuit of that Object, been brought under our Consideration. Our Duty has called upon us for Opinions on Subjects extensive and intricate: Those Opinions have frequently terminated in Suggestions subversive of Forms long established; introductory of material Change in the System, wide and powerful in Effect.

In executing a Work thus arduous, we have not shrunk from the Pains of Inquiry: — We have attentively and perseveringly examined; cautiously and deliberately weighed: — We have used the best Lights of our Understanding to judge right, and endeavoured to render Service to the Public.

All the Returns from the Out Ports, and from the Patent Officers, as well as the Returns for the Port of London, were committed by the Secretary to tite Care of the Deputy Supervisor of the Receiver General’s Payments, to be arranged and digested into the Form required by this Board.

The Out Ports of the Customs are subject to a Distinction. They are either Head Ports or Members, and are so distinguished and constituted by Commissions issued at various Times from the Court of Exchequer, appointing Commissioners for assigning Ports, and settling the Limits and Boundaries thereof These Commissions were so issued, in pursuance of the Acts of the First of Elizabeth, and the Fourteenth of Charles the Second. There are likewise Places which are within the Limits of either the Head or Member Ports, as set out in these Commissions; and when Officers competent to transact Coast Business are by Order of the Board of Customs stationed at such Places, they are in the Department of the Customs distinguished by the Appellation of Creeks. The Circumstance which distinguishes the Head Port is, that the Three Patent Officers, that is, the Customer, the Controller, and Searcher, are by their Patents specially appointed to such Port: This Appointment gives to these Three Officers a Jurisdiction, as far as concerns their respective Offices, over all the Members, and the Creeks belonging to the Head or Member Port.

The Member Port is distinguished by a Dependance upon the Head Port, so far as regards the Three Patent Officers, who appoint and must have Deputies resident at the Member Ports, becatise all Foreign Commerce may be legally transacted at them, as well. as at the Head Port, there being at both Quays set out and described in the Commissions, where the Merchant has a Flight, at legal Hours to land or ship his Goods. This Dependence of the Member upon' the Head Port,' is wholly restricted to the Jurisdiction of the Patent Officers.

The Circumstance which characterizes a Creek is, that no Foreign Commerce can by Law be carried on there in atiy Instance, unless by virtue of a special Sufferance granted from the Head or Member Port; within the Limits of which such Creek is situate, and at which Head or Member Port the Duties, if any, must be previously paid or secured; but at a Creek

all Coast Business may be transacted, equally as at a Head or Member Port, and therefore the Customer and the Controller have Deputies at Creeks; the Searcher haying no Concern in the Coast Business, he has no Deputy at many of them; at some be has, for the Purpose of attending the shipping of Goods to Foreign Parts, in pursuance of the special Sufferances granted from the Head or Member Port: In Creeks where there is no Deputy Searcher, the Officer who transacts that Duty at the Head or Member Port must attend the Execution of such Sufferances. At several of the Creeks, Collectors, Controllers, and Meters, for the Purpose of carrying on the Receipt of the Coal Duties, are appointed by the Commissioners of the Customs, under whose Management the said Duties, as well as the Appointment of all Officers concerned therein, are by Act of Parliament specially placed: At these Creeks, the Coal Duties so received are, by Order of the Board of Customs, paid to the Collector of the Head or Member Port, of which such Creek is a Part, who includes the same in his Remittances of Duties to the Receiver General, and accounts for them with the Controller General, except at the Creek of Leigh, in the Port of Malden, where the Collector of those Duties remits them directly to the Receiver General, and accounts. for them with the Controller General; mad this Place, though a Creek, and consequently where no Import or Export Duties can be collected, is in the List of the Out Ports, which, including Leigh, are Seventy-two in Number.

The Three Patent Officers belonging to the Out Ports, that is, the Customer, Controller, and Searcher, are by Law to be resident upon their Offices. The Non-residence of these Officers at their proper Ports is attended with great Inconvenience: They appoint all their Deputies, as well at the Head Port, if they do not reside there, as ait the Members and Creeks thereunto belonging. Upon the Death, Resignation, or Removal of the Patent Officer, none of these Deputies are, as he apprehends, legally authorized to continue to act, unless re-appointed by the Successor' to such Patent Officer. Upon the Death, Resignation, or Removal of the Deputy, no Appointment of a Successor can regularly take Place but by Deputation from the Patentee. In the Year 1784, the Deputy Controller at the Port of Liverpool died; the Patent Controller of Chester, of which Liverpool is a Member Port, was in the East Indies, and consequently could appoint no Deputy in due Time. The Board of Customs represented this to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, who, in order to prevent so important ah Office from continuing vacant, and the Collector without Check, sent their Warrant to the Commissioners of the Customs, dated the 8th of January 1785, requiring them to issue their Deputation to a Person therein named, to be Deputy Controller there, upon his giving Security to the Crown in the like Sum as was given by the late Deputy to the Patentee. The Bond to the Patentee could not be found; no Entry of such Bond is ever made at the Custom House, and consequently the Penalty could not be ascertained; the Appointment therefore was delayed, and the Board of Customs at last was obliged to settle the Quantum of the Security, upon Information received from an Officer at the Port, of what had been the Security given by the late Deputy.

The Patentee has been always considered as responsible for his Deputy; but this Deputy is appointed without his Intervention.

A like Transaction has since happened, in Consequence of the Death of the Deputy Controller at a Lancaster, which is another Member of the Port of Chester.

The Collector is now the first or principal Officer at an Out Port, and has the whole Charge of collecting the Customs, as well on Goods Coastwise as on Goods imported or exported. The Controller is next in Rank to the Collector, and these Two Officers have jointly the Superintendance and Direction of all the Officers employed in the Service of this Revenue, at the Port to which they belong. This Jurisdiction extends over the Patent Officers and their Deputies, as well as over all the other Officers, and is delegated to the Collectors and Controllers by the Commissioners of the Customs, who derive such Authority from their

reconciled with the Sams stated to be received by those Deputies and Clerks in their Returns. This Disagreement, as he found upon Inquiry, frequently arose from this Circumstance, that die Deputy had blended Fees received for himself with those received for his Patentee.

To supply these Defects, and correct these Errors, Applications were made to the Patent Officers at all the Ports, to send up complete Returns; and he has been ever since, occasionally, and still is, applying by Letters to the Collectors and Controllers at the several Ports (being the Officers to whom the Board of Customs send their Directions, and on whom they rely for the Returns) in order to explain and correct them. Some of these Returns are still incorrect; and he is proceeding in his Applications to the Officers to rectify the Errors. The Board of Customs directed the Collectors and Controllers to call upon the Officers of their respective Ports, to make Returns to them of the State of their Offices. In some of the Ports they stated to the Board their Inability to make complete Returns, because of the Non-residence of the Patent Officers.

In order to accelerate the Returns necessary for the Formation of the Out Port Account required by this Board, he has himselfj where there has been Occasion, made Application to those Patent Officers whose Places of Residence he could discover, without applying for their Returns through the Intervention of the Collectors and Controllers of the Port He has found great Difficulty in making out the Account, from the different Mode of Payment between the Patentee and the Deputy in Practice at different Ports. In some Ports the Patentee, pursuant to Warrants of the Treasury, allows his Deputy a Salary of Twenty Pounds a Year, or the whole of the Fees, where they do not amount to that Sum. At other Ports he allows the Deputy no Salary, but the Whole or a Share of the Fees, according to the Terms of the Agreement between them; and those Agreements are different at different Ports.

Since the Receipt of the Out Port Returns by him from the Secretary’s Office, in last, he has continued to devote all the Time that could be spared from his Official Duty, and to make every Exertion in his Power, to render the Account complete; and in order that no Delay on his Part might arise in accomplishing this Object, he has procured Assistance at his own Expence. The Impediments to the Formation of the Account required, which have been various and great, are now so far surmounted, that he apprehends he shall soon be able to deliver it to this Board.

The Account on this Day (the 2 2d of February) delivered by him, is a complete Return to the Precept of this Board, dated December the 17th, 1784. It contains a List of all the Officers of the Customs employed at the Out Ports in that Year. The Employment, the Authority of Appointment, the different Sources and Gross Produce of the Emolument, the various Payments of each Officer, and the Net Produce to him, are kept under distinct Heads, in pursuance of tire Requisition of this Board.

This Account was made out by him from the Returns of the Officers themselves, from the General Account for each Port, transmitted by the Collector and Controller, and from Authorities which he had Recourse to in the Office of the Customs. The N umber of Ports included in this Account are Seventy-two; they are ranged in the following Order: The Head, sometimes also called Mother Ports, that is those Ports to which the Patent Officers are appointed, are placed in Alphabetical Order, and the Member Ports belonging to each Head Port are inserted in the same Order immediately after that Port Besides these Head and Member Ports, there are many Creeks included

in this Account; the Accounts for them are not distinguished, but blended with the Account of the Port to which they belong.

The Appointments of the Officers at the Out Ports are either by Patent from the Crown; by Constitution of the Board of Treasury; by Warrant of the Treasury, and Commission of the Board of Customs, pursuant to that Warrant; or, by the Commission of the Board of Customs; and in some Cases by the Order of that Board. The Appointment of the Deputies to the Patent Officers is by Deputation from the Patentee, subject to the Approbation of the Treasury, in those Cases where it is so expressed in the Patent. Some t>f the Officers at the Out Ports employ Persons as Clerks who have no Form of Appointment, and are paid by their Principals; Persons of that Description have not usually been considered as Officers of the Customs, and included in Accounts similar to this; such of them as appear to have received Fees or Gratuities are inserted in this Account, in Compliance with the Requisition of this Board. The Extra Officers at a Port, that is, Officers who are not constantly in the Service, are generally employed under the Authority of the Collector and Controller at the Port

The Collector and Controller at an Out Port, do not carry on the Collection of the Coal Duties under the Authority of their Appointments from the Treasury, but each by virtue solely of a Commission from the Board of Customs, for that special Service; all the Officers concerned in the Conduct of the Duties on Coals being, by the 9th and 1 oth of H'illiam the 3d, Chapter 13th, and the loth and 11th, Chapter 21st, directed to be appointed by the Commissioners of the Customs. Usually the Board appoint the Collector, and the Controller, if he executes his Employment himself, if not, the Deputy Controller at the Port, to that Duty. At Creeks, where there is no Collector, the Deputy Customer is generally appointed to collect the Coal Duties. Where the same Persons collect and controul the Coal, as well as other Duties, the Authority from the Board of Customs for their executing those Offices is not specified in this Account; where different Persons are appointed to the Coal Service by the Board, the Authority is inserted The Accounts of the Coal Duties collected at Creeks are passed with the Collector at the Port to which the Creek belongs, and by him with the Controller General, except in the Case of Leigh. The Commission of the Board of Customs for appointing Officers to conduct the Coal Service, does not impart to them those general Powers of seizing prohibited or uncustomed Goods, which are conveyed by other Commissions of the Board; it restricts the Rights of seizing to the Article of Coals, and the Ships or other Vesseles concerned in the Carriage thereof.

The Column of Salaries and Allowances from the Crown, includes all the Payments from the Crown to the Officer for himself, or for his Deputies and Clerks where the Allowance is made to him for them. The Quarantine Allowance, the Coinage, the Coal, and the enumerated Poundages, are likewise included in this Column, and, with the Metage and Commission, they comprehend all Payments made by the Crown to the Officers at the Out Ports, besides their Salaries; the Metage is an Allowance for measuring Coals, to Officers in the Customs appointed Meters by the Commission of the Board. The Rate of Poundage to the Collector and Controller of the Coal Duties, and of the Metage for the Measurement of Coals, are grounded upon the Warrant of the Treasury of the 19th of September 1699. Besides the Poundage and Metage, the Officers employed have sometimes Salaries for these Services, by Order of the Board of Customs.

Part of the Payments out of Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures at the Out Ports, consists of Allowances

to

2f Geo. IIL

2-6° Janu

to Officers as Commissioners For Superintending the Appraisement of seized Goods. The Writ of Appraisement issued from the Court of Exchequer for appraising Goods seized at an Out Port, i9 directed to the Collector, Controller, and Searcher at the Port; and in consequence of that Writ Two of them become Commissioners for calling in proper Persons to be the Appraisers of the Goods; for this Service the Two Commissioners are allowed, upon each Writ of Appraisement, Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence each, which is called Commission.

The Payments of every Species by the Crown to the Officers at the Out Ports, are made by the Collector at the Port, except the Salaries to the Patent Officers by virtue of their Patents, which are paid by the Receiver General of the Customs. Some of the Patent Officers have Salaries also upon the Establishment, and these are paid at the Port. All these Payments are made out of Custom Duties, except the Enumerated Poundage and Commission, which are made out of the Produce of Seizures, Fine3, and Forfeitures.

All the Officers at the Out Ports, whether established or incidental, are paid their Salaries and Allowances by the Collector at the Port, pursuant to an Authority transmitted to that Officer from the Board of Customs: If they are on the Establishment, this Authority is grounded upon, the Warrant issued Quarterly from the Treasury; if they are upon the Incidental List, the Authority originates with the Board of Customs. The Quarantine Allowance is paid by the Collector in consequence of an Annual Order sent from the Board, pursuant to the Warrant for that Purpose received by them from the Treasury. The Coinage Poundage is paid upon the Authority of the Treasury Warrant of the Year 1714; the Coal Poundage and the Metage, upon that of the Year 1699; both of course, without any Order from the Board of Customs. The Enumerated Poundage is paid pursuant to the original Minute of the Board of Customs of the 9th May 1728.

The Column of Fees, Allowances, and Gratuities, includes the Total Sum returned by each Officer at the Out Port, to have been by him received under those Heads of Emolument: The Particulars composing these Totals, or the respective Authorities, whether of Law or Usage, under which they were received, were in very few Instances stated in the Returns.

In the Column of Taxes are contained the Land Tax, the Shilling and Sixpenny Duties; being all

the Deductions to which the Emoluments of the Officers are liable on Account of Taxes. In this Column are also inserted, the Payments to the Superannuation Fund, by such Officers as are liable to that Deduction.

Where the Salary of the Officer does not exceed Sixty Pounds a Year, the Sum paid by him for the Land Tax is re-paid to him by the Collector, pursuant to an Annual Warrant of the Treasury authorizing such Re-payment.

The Payments to the Land Tax for Salaries which would have been on this Ground entitled to Re-payment, were not in general inserted in the Returns of the Officers, because, as he apprehends, they produced no Effect upon their Net Income; and they are none of them included in this Account: It appeared unnecessary to insert such Payments, as they are re-paid to the Officers by the Collector at the Port, and taken Credit for by him in his Account of Incidents for that Year.

The Articles which compose the Sums in the Column of Contingent Expences^ were not generally distinguished in the Returns; where they were so distinguished, the principal Articles were the Expence to Officers for Horses, kept by them for the Purpose of executing their Duty.

The Salary received by the Patent Officer, and all his Emoluments and Payments of every Kind, though belonging both to the Head Port and the Members and Creeks under it, if there are any, are in this Account collected into Totals, and placed under the distinct Heads to which they belong, in the Columns for the Head Port; and those Colums, as far as regards the Patent Officers, are left blank in the Member Ports: If it had been necessary, he could not have separated them, and placed to each Port the Proportion of tltese Totals which belonged to it, because the Patent Officers did not make such Distinctions, nor did the Returns from their Deputies supply him with the Information necessary for that Purpose.

None of the Officers or Mariners employed in the Cruizers belonging to the Customs, are included in this Account, nor were they in the Account returned for the Port of London. ‘

Memorial, 21st August 1699.

The Commissioners having had under Consideration the settling the Allowances for Payment of the Officers in the Out Ports, employed in the receiving and collecting the present Duty on Coals, upon looking into the Produce of the said Duty in the several Ports for a Year, from the Commencement thereof, which was the 15th May 1698, to the 15th May last, are humbly of Opinion, that there be allowed for the Yeceiving and accompting for the said Duty arising in the Out Ports for the said Time, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent, for the first One thousand Pounds, and One per Cent, for every Hundred Pounds afterwards; that is to say, where there has been received the Sum of One thousand Pounds, there be allowed the Sum of Thirty Pounds, Twenty Pounds whereof to be to the Collector, who has the Charge of receiving and accompting for the Money, and Ten Pounds to the Comptroller; and where the Sum of Two thousand Pounds has been received, there be allowed the Sum of Porty Pounds, Two Thirds whereof to be to the Collector, and One Third to the Comptroller — and so in Proportion; which the Commissioners conceive will prove a reasonable Allowance for the Service afore-mentioned, and be considerably less than was allowed for collecting the former Duty on Coals. And there having been Occasion, in some particular Ports, to employ some of the Officers to inspect the Meters in Places where the Coals are delivered, being at 'Distance from the ordinary Residence of the Officers, the Commissioners think it necessary to make them some Allowance for their Care, out of the said Duty, which they humbly hope their Lordships will approve.

And for Payment of the Meters, the Commissioners are of Opinion to pursue the former Method, and allow generally after the Rate of One Penny per Chal-der where the Meters are Corporation Meters, and where otherwise after the Rate of 2 per Chalder, except in some few Places where the Coals being delivered at a considerable Distance from the Ports, and common Place of Residence, it will be necessary to allow something towards the extraordinary Charge; Which however will be no considerable Increase thereof.

B.O. 11. H.

After our hearty Commendations. N* 8.

The Examination of Mr. Anthony Palmer Col-lings', taken upon Oath, November 15th, 16th, and 18th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Deputy Customer Outwards in the Port of Bristol; he has been in this Office upwards of Seven Years, and was appointed by a Deputation from Thomas White, Esquire, the Patent Customer Outwards.

There are in the Port of Bristol Eight Patent Officers; a Customer Inwards, a Customer Outwards, a Controller, a Searcher, and Four King’s Waiters. *

None of these Officers, except the Patent Searcher, executes any Part of the Business of his Office, that he knows of; nor does any other of them, except Mr. Greville, one of the King’s Waiters, reside at Bristol.

All Warrants Outwards are brought to the Deputy Customer Outwards, marked with the Initials of the Examiner, and signed by the Controller and Collector; the initials of the Examiner are Evidence; where the Goods are liable to Duties, that he has either computed or agreed to them; the Deputy Customer signs it, and a Copy is left with, or sent to him j he sees that the Computation is right; the Copy is entered in a Book, and compared with the like Entries of the Collector and Controller. The Daily Totals of the Duties in their several Cash Books are compared by the Collector, Controller, and Check Clerk; the Monthly Totals by the same Officers, and the Customer Outwards.

This Officer neither examines nor signs the Monthly Cash Account transmitted by the Collector to the Board of Customs, but every Quarter he sends to that Board a Duplicate of the Collectors Quarter Book Outwards. This Duplicate is made out from his own Entries, and compared with those of the Collector and Controller, and signed by himself; He sends up

likewise

Fifteenth Report on Public Accounts*

104 26° Januarii. 1787.

likewise all the Clearances, the Foreign Account, the -Coast Account, and the Account of Wool and Fuller’s Earth, all signed by the Collector, Controller, and himself.

Upon a Vacancy of the Office of Collector, the Receipt of the Duties, and all the other Business of that Office, does, as be apprehends, devolve of course upon the Customers; whilst there is a Collector, the Customers are Checks upon his Conduct respecting his Receipts, similar to that of the Controller. Certificates for Debentures for Bounties originate with the Customer Outwards, and pass through the Offices of the Controller, Searchers, Examiner, and Collector. Certificates for Debentures for Drawbacks originate with the Customer Inwards, and pass through the same Offices, together with the Office of the Customer Outwards.

The Whole of the Business Coastwise, Outwards, is transacted in this Office. All the Cockets and Transires, and some of the Sufferances, are made out there; all the Sufferances are examined and signed by that Officer. Special Sufferances are signed by the Collector, and Controller also. All these Transactions are entered in the Office. It is a Part of the Duty of this Officer to send Annually to the Exchequer Duplicates of the Quarter Books sent to the Board of Customs, and Accounts of all the Goods carried Coastwise, Part of which only are sent to the Customs.

The Patent Customer Outwards receives, as he is informed and believes, a Salary of Fifty-seven Pounds from the Crown, by a Dormant Warrant; and certain Fees for certain Instruments, grounded cither upon legal Authority, or Usage, and paid by the Merchant; they are collected either by the Deputy Customer, or Deputy Controller, upon the Delivery of the Instruments. The Amount of them last Year was Four hundred and Twenty-three Pounds One Shilling and Three Pence. He paid his Deputy a "Salary of Forty Pounds; for Taxes, Sixteen Pounds Pour Shillings and Six Pence; and for certain Stationary, One Pound Five Shillings; together Fifty-seven Pounds Nine Shillings and Six Pence; His Net Income was Four hundred and Twenty-two Pounds Eleven Shillings and Nine Pence.

The Deputy Customer Outwards received from the Patentee a Salary of Forty Pounds, and in customary Tees and Gratuities Three hundred and Ninety-two Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Seven Pence. His Payments to Clerks was One hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and One Penny, and for contingent Expences Three Pounds Seven Shillings and Four Pence. His Net Income was Three hundred and Two Pounds Eleven Shillings and Two Pence.

His Fees consist of very small Sums, the highest of them Five Shillings, and that but seldom, and the Half of it for extraordinary Attendance. It would be far more eligible and satisfactory to himself, and, as he believes, to many of the Officers at this Port, to be paid a certain fixed Annual Salary, in lieu of all i ces and Emoluments whatever.

Upon the Arrival of a Ship, whether from a Foreign Voyage or Coastwise, the Master delivers to the Customer Inwards his Manifest, from whence the Report is drawn, and, if Foreign, sworn to by the Master, before either the Collector, Controller, or Customer Inwards: This last Officer enters the Description of the Ship. The Transactions afterwards, relative to the Entry of the Goods; the Computation of the Duties, the Checks upon the Computation, and the Accounts kept of them, arc carried on by the Collector, Controller, Customer Inwards, Examiner, and Check Clerk. The Business Coastwise Inwards is transacted, and the Accounts kept and transmitted, by the Customer Inwards, in like Manner a--? the Business

Coastwise Outwards is conducted by the Customer Outwards.

A.

T. Anguish,

RichJ Neave,

Sam1 Beach croft,

Geo. Drummond,

WillmRoe.

N* 9.

The Examination of Thomas Craufurd, Esquire; taken upon Oath, November 18th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Patent Searcher in the Port of Bristol, and has been in that Office upwards of Ten Years.

This Office formerly consisted of the Patentee; One Deputy, nominated by the Treasury, but appointed by the Patentee, the other nominated by the Patentee: When he was appointed to this Office he found One Deputy, nominated by the Treasury; the Business of the other Deputy had been executed by his Predecessor himself. For the first Year he executed this Office himself, without appointing his own Deputy; lie then appointed One, and was absent for about Ten Months: He has ever since resided at Bristol, and retains his Deputy, but superintends the Business of the Office himself.

The Two Deputy Searchers take the Ships alternately, and each of them has his Deputed, that is, his Controlling Searcher, with whom lie constantly acts.

There is an ancient Table of Fees for the Patent Searcher hung up in his Office at Bristol: The I ces at present taken by hiip vary from that Table in some very trifling Articles only: The Fees taken by the Deputy and Controlling Searchers are either customary, or, where extra Service is required, grounded upon an Agreement with the Merchants.

The Patent Searcher receives a Salary under a Dormant Warrant, of Thirty-four Pounds a Year, and Twenty Pounds upon the Establishment: IIis Pees and Gratuities, exclusive of Seizures, amounted last Year to Nine hundred and Eighteen Pounds Seven Shillings and Four Pence. lie paid for Taxes Eight Pounds Four Shillings; to his Deputies Seventy Pounds; and to Clerks Thirty-six Pounds Four Shillings. His Net Income was Eight hundred and Fifty-seven Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence.

Thu' Craufurd.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neave,

Sam1 Bcachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will'*Roe.

N* 10.

The Examination of Thomas Barker, Esquire; taken upon Oath, November 22d and 23d, 1/85.

This Examinant saith, That about the Year 1762 he came into the Office of the Customs at Portsmouth; in the Year 1767 he was appointed Deputy Searcher, and Assistant Landing Waiter; in 1782 he w as appointed Deputy Controller; and in lust Collector — all at

the same Port; in this last Office he continued about Six Months, when he was appointed One of the Four General Surveyors.

Portsmouth is a Member of the Port of Southampton; it has One more Member, Cowes; and a Creek,

Lyminglou.

27 Geo. III. 26° J

Lymington.There are resident at Portsmouth a Collector, a Deputy Customer, Deputy Controller, and Deputy Searcher; there are the same Officers at

Southampton, Cowes, and Lymington, except that the Collector and Deputy Customer are, at the same Person; and at Lymington there is no Collector, and the Deputy Searcher is also Deputy Customer.

The Business of the Customs in every Office, at the Member Port, is, as he apprehends, conducted in a Manner similar to that at the Mother Port.

The only apparent Difference between the Mother Port and the Member is, as he apprehends, that the Duty of the Three Patent Officers extends over both the Mother Port and all its Members and Creeks, whereas all the other Officers at the Member Ports are separate from, and independent of, the Officers at the Mother Port; but the Officers at the Creek are dependent upon the Officers at the Mother Port, where the Creek is within the Mother Port, and upon the Officers of the Member Port, where the Creek is within the Member Port; and the Creek having no Collector, no Foreign Business, either Inwards or Outwards, can be transacted there; the Entries, both Inwards and Outwards, must be made at the Mother Port. There has always been an ancient Table of Fees hung up in the Office at Portsmouth, and he believes the Fees received by all the Officers were regulated by that Table, except for Business transacted at extra Hours, or extra Places. The Fees belonging to the Patent Officers are collected by the Deputy Customer, and the Share of each paid to the Deputies, and by them transmitted to the Collector at the Mother Port.

In the Year 1784 the Emoluments of his Office, as Deputy Controller at Portsmouth, consisted of, a Salary from his Principal, of Twenty Pounds; a Salary by Treasury Warrant, of Twenty-five Pounds; a Poundage on the Coal Duty, of Twenty-six Pounds Four Shillings and Tw’o Pence Three Farthings; the Enumerated Poundage, and from Indentures of Appraisement, Sixty-eight Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings; the Quarantine Allowance, Nine; Pounds; and Fees of Office, Thirty-seven Pounds Nine Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny: He paid the Civil List Duty, One Pound Five Shillings and Seven Pence Farthing; to a Clerk Fifteen Pounds; and for collecting his Fees Four Pounds Four Shillings. His Net Income was One hundred and Sixty-six Pounds Two Shillings and Three Pence Three Farthings.

Tho. Barker.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

RichdNeaxe,

Sam1 Bcachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will"Roe.

' N 11:

The Examination of Mr. John Philipps Adams; taken upon Oath, December 9th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Collector of the Customs at the Port of Milf ord, and has been in this Office about Eighteen Years.

The Port of Milford has dependent upon it, as far as relates to the Three Patent Officers, Three Member Ports, and Three Creeks. The Port, with its Members and Creeks, extends upwards of One hundred Miles upon the Coast. The Three Patent Officers, the Customer, Controller, and Searcher, all act by Deputy, none of them transact any Part of "the Business: As he believes, the Customer resides in Vox.. 42.

fanuarsi 105

Sussex, the Controller at Haverfordwest, and the Searcher in Carmarthenshire. .

The Customer and Controller have Deputies at alj the Member Ports, and at the Three Creeks; the Searcher at some of them: He believes the Patent Officers of this Port have never sent up any of the Exchequer Books to the Office of the Customs or the Exchequer.

The Three Member Ports transmit their Accounts to the Controller General, independent of the principal Port; the Coastwise Accounts, which are thd only Accounts of the Three Creeks, are passed by the Officers of the principal Port, annexed to their own, and sent up, with their Vouchers, by them to the Controller General.

There is, at the Custom House for the Port of Milford, a Table of Fees for the Collector and the Patent Officers, at the Bottom of which is wrote, to the best of his Recollection, " by Order of the Speaker " of the House of Commons," or some such Words: The Collector has a Fee of One Shilling, for a Certificate for the Carriage of Culm from the Port of Milford, by the Act of the 33d of George the Second; the other Fees taken by all the Officers there are according either to the Table or to the ancient Usagd of the Port.

The Collector has by his Warrant a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year; and, by Order of the Board, as an Allowance for a Clerk, Twenty Pounds; he received from the Poundage on the Coal Duty, and for Incidents, in the Year 1784, Fifty-two Pounds Four Shillings and Nine Pence: His Fees amounted to Sixty-six Pounds Twelve Shillings and Nine Pence; his Payment for Taxes was Nine Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence, and to a Clerk Twenty Pounds; his Net Income was Two hundred and Nine Pounds Fifteen Shillings.

The Office of Riding Surveyor is now abolished, by Order of the Board of Customs.

John Philipps Adams.

T. Anguish,

The Examination of Mr. Richard Butler; taken upon Oath, November.25th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That be is Deputy Controller of- the Port of Rye; he was appointed by William Higgins, Esquire, the Patent Controller, and has been in this Office about Five Years. Rye is a Member of the Port of Chichester; it has a Deputy Controller, a Deputy Searcher, and a Collector, who is also Deputy Customer.

Every Quarter he sends up to the Board of Customs his Quarter Book, containing an Account of the Imports, Exports, and Duties, during the Quarter: Before he sigus his Quarter Book he compares it with the Quarter Book of the Collector, to see that the Articles agree.

The Quarterly Establishment, and the Quarterly Preparatory List, are entered in the Books of the Collector and Controller. The Collector makes out his List of Salaries and Incidents; and after he has paid them he produces the List, with all the Vouchers annexed, to the Deputy Controller, who examines the Vouchers; the Collector sw ears to the Truth of it before him, and he signs the Jurat.

There is an old Table of Fees for the Patent Officers in the Office of the Customs at Rye, but he does E e not

N* 13.

The Examination of Mr. Joshua Powell', taken upon Oath, October 24th and 28th, 1785, January 31st, May 18th, and June 20th, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That in the Account of the Gross Receipts and Payments in London and the Out Ports for the Year 1784, in the Column of Salaries and Incidents, the Sums paid by the Receiver General in London to the Patent Officers at the several Ports are included in the Sum of Payments in London, and not in the Sums set opposite to those Ports to which the Patent Officers belong. The Sum of Payments exceeding the Receipts being paid out of the Net Produce, must be deducted from that Sum, in order to give the real Net Produce of the Year: The general Account cannot be made correct until the End of the succeeding Year, because the Accounts of the Receipts and Payments at the Out Ports for the last Quarter of the Year are not usually delivered to the Controller General, until after the next Midsummer; and such is the Multiplicity and Variety of the Accounts which compose that Account, that they cannot ' well be examined, and the Errors corrected, in a shorter Time than a Year.

The Customs in Scotland being managed by a distinct Hoard of Commissioners there, the Board of Customs in England are ignorant of the Expences attending that Collection, and know no more of the Receipt, than what appears, in the Weekly Certificate of the Receiver General, to have been remitted to him from the Receiver General of Scotland.

The Sum remitted to the Receiver General from . Scotland, is the Whole of the Produce of the Custom Duties in Scotland, which is paid into the Exchequer.

There are in England and Wales Twenty principal Out Ports, each of them has a Patent Customer, Controller, and Searcher. Bristol and Newcastle have each a Customer Inwards, and a Customer Outwards; and at Hull there are Two Customers. Most of them have inferior Ports contiguous to the principal Port, or to each other, Members of the principal Port, and dependent upon the Patent Officers of that Port; the Members pass a separate Account with the Controller General, and are thence, with the Principal, called the Accountant Ports; the Creeks, except Leigh, which is deemed an Accountant Port, pass their Accounts either with the Collector of the principal or the inferior Port, as they belong to one or the other; and he

incorporates these Accounts with his own, and transmits them to the Controller General; who passes them as the Accounts of the principal Collector.

All the Receipt and Expenditure, at these Creeks, are inserted in the Account made out by the Controller General, in the Columns set opposite to the Port with which they account. The Controller General Officially knows nothing of the Customer, except in those Instances where the Customer collects the Duties, there being now no separate Collector at those Ports; and except in Cases where, upon the Vacancy of the Office of Collector, the Collection devolves upon the Customer till a new Collector is appointed, if some Person i9 not directed by the Board of Customs to carry on the Business during the Vacancy. The Coast Business is the only Branch which is peculiarly under the Customer; but he has nothing to do with the Collection on Coals* which are the only Coast Duties.

The Account of the Gross Receipt of the Customs, and the several Payments at each Port, now delivered by him to this Board, is a complete Account for the Year 1784, he having received all the Materials necessary to render it correct. In the Column of Salaries and Incidents the Sums set opposite to each Port include all the Expences incurred at that Port, whether arising from the Payments to the Officers of the Customs, upon the Establishment, or Incidental List, or from other contingent Expences belonging to that Revenue; the Salaries paid by the Receiver General to the Plantation Officers, paid in London, are inserted in this Account

In the Column of Salaries and Incidents for the Out Ports, the Sums inserted are for the Charges incurred at the Port; except that at Whitehaven a List of Officers of the Customs at the Alan, though

not belonging to the Department under the Commissioners of the Customs, are regularly paid their Salaries, pursuant to Treasury Warrant, out of the Produce of the Duties collected at that Port.

This Account comprehends all the Payments made out of the Custom Duties at all the Ports, but only such as are made out of those Duties.

He kuows nothing Officially of the Charges of Management paid out of the Produce of Fines and Forfeitures in the Port of London, or at the Out Ports; nor in any Account called for by Parliament, of the Gross Receipt of the Customs, and the Payments out of it for any Year, are the Receipts and Payments belonging to this Branch of Revenue inserted; he cannot insert them, they not being within his Knowledge or Controul.

He does not regularly present to Parliament any Account of the Gross and Net Produce of the Customs, but only upon special Requisition; upon such Requisition, the Order comes to the Board of Customs, who by their Minute direct the Controller General to make out and present the Account to Parliament; and no other Account is made out by any Officer of the Customs in Consequence thereof.

Jos* Powell,

A. Piggott,

Ric/A Neave,

Samf Beachcrqft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will "Roe.

N* 14.

The Examination of Mr. John Mills', taken upon Oath, March 29th, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That the Account delivered by him to this Board comprehends all the Incidental Expences paid by the Receiver General out of the Custom Revenue in the Year 1784, except the Inci-7 dental

27 Geo. III. 26° Jamar toy

dental Salaries, and Day Pay to Officers. A considerable Part of the Incidental Expences of the Customs, which used formerly to be paid by the Receiver General, has for some Time been paid by the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports; and the Sums in hri Hands not having been sufficient for the Demands upon him, Imprests to a considerable Amount have, within the last Year, been made by the Receiver General to the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures, pursuant to the Orders of the Board of Customs. The Payments inserted in this Account are made pursuant to Warrants from the Treasury, or the Orders of the Board of Customs. The Land Tax repaid, though paid in the Year 1784, is the Allowance for the Year preceding, to Officers whose Salaries do not exceed Sixty Pounds a Year, and to the Five additional Deputy Under Searchers, who, though their Salaries do exceed Sixty Pounds a Year, are, by a Dormant Warrant of the Treasury, included in this Repayment of the Land Tax.

The Sum of Sixty Pounds, under the Title of Pension, is an Annual Allowance, by the special Order of the Board of Customs, for long and faithful Service, to an Officer who became insane. The Article of Payment to the principal Coal Meters in , is an

Allowance of One Halfpenny per Chaldron on all Coals imported into the Port of , which is made by virtue of the Order of the Board, grounded on the Certificate of the Collector of the Coal Duties.

The Accounts of the Customs are made up Annually to the 5th of January inclusive. On the last Day of the Year it has been usual for the Receiver General to take Credit for the Fees which would be paid to the Auditor of the Imprest, for auditing the Cash Account of the Customs for that Year, and to retain the Sum in his Hands until the Account was audited.

The Sum of Seven hundred and Twenty-six Pounds, subjoined to this Account, was in the Course of Office taken Credit for as a Payment by the Receiver General, on the 5th of January 1785. Before the Account of the Year 1784 could be delivered in, a Change . had taken Place in the Auditor’s Office, by which Alteration no Fees are to be received for auditing Accounts. The above Sum of Seven hundred and Twenty-six- Pounds, so taken Credit for by the Receiver

General, will in consequence thereof be carried back to the Account of the respective Branches of Duties from whence it was taken.

7. Mills.

Sami Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will* Roe.

N* 15.

The Examination of Mr. James Powell; taken upon Oath, February 8th, and March 24th, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That the Account delivered by him to this Board includes all the incidental Expences paid out of the Custom Duties* at all the Out Ports, for the Year 1784, except those paid to the Officers of the Customs on the Incidental List, the Quarantine Allowance, and Day Pay. The Sum paid at each Port is distinguished in this Account undet certain Heads, which include the whole incidental Expence at that Port, except the above-mentioned Payments to Officers. All Payments in this Account, amounting to above Forty Shillings, are made by the Collector at the Port, pursuant either to standing or special Orders of the Board. The Articles under the Head of Pettys, consist of sundry trifling Charges, not reduceable to any particular Head.

The Repayment of the Land Tax, made to Officers whose Salaries do not exceed Sixty Pounds a Year, is admitted in the Account, upon the Receipts being produced, of the several Collectors of the Land Tax for the respective Divisions, with a, List annexed of the Sum paid by the several Officers. Th|e Article of Civil List repaid is a Payment to Tradesmen, of the Sums charged to the Civil List upon their Bills. AH Payments out of this Revenue, but those made to the Officers upon the Establishment, are called incidental Expences.

The Suips of 410, and 316, have not been paid, but were taken Credit for, in the.

usual Manner, at Quarter Day, the Alteration in the Auditor's Office not being then expected; and although they are Fees -for passing the Account of the Year 1784, probably may not be taken: In that Case, they will be carried to the Account of the respective Branches as a Repayment.

N* 18.

The Examination of William , Esquire; taken upon Oath, December 23d, 1785.

This Examinant saith. That the Sum of Six hundred and Eight Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Six Pence, stated in the Account of the Incidental Expences of the Customs, to be paid to him by the Receiver General, every Quarter, consists of a Variety of Sums, subject to the Civil List and One Shilling Duties, paid to himself and several other Persons; Seven of them are Clerks in the Revenue Office of the Treasury, who are employed in making up Accounts of all the Branches of the Revenue, for the Use of the Board of Treasury, and some of them to be laid before Parliament; they have Annual Salaries, settled by a Minute of the Treasury, in the Year 1776, payable out of Customs, for the Business they transact, though that Business Relates to all the other Branches of the Revenue as well as that of the Customs.

IV. Speer.

T. Anguish,
