N* 21.

The Examination of Mr. John Bastin; taken upon Oath, October 25th and November 1st, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That in the Account of the Produce of Seizures and Fines transmitted to this Board, the Charges inserted in the Column under the Title of Charges of Condemnation, &c. paid out of the Gross Produce, comprehend the Payments to all the Officers employed in the Condemnation and Sale, and the Poundages payable to the several Officers of the Customs, except that to the Inspector of Prosecutions: After these Charges are deducted out of the Gross Produce, the Remainder is divided into certain Shares between the King and the Seizing Officers, according to the Directions of the Acts of Parliament relative to Seizures; the Shares of the Officers are paid at the Port, the Shares of the Crown are remitted by the Collectors to the Receiver for the Out Ports, but retaining in their Hands such Portions of those Shares as may be wanted for

I3S

maintaining the Custom House Cruizers, and to defray such other incidental Expences at the Port as the Commissioners may think proper to order. Such Part of the King’s Share as is remitted to the Receiver for the Out Ports, is applied to any of the incidental Charges of Management arising in London, pursuant to the Orders of the Board, and the Remainder paid into the Exchequer. The principal Heads of Expence defrayed out of the King’s Share, either arising in London or remitted from the Out Ports, are the Cutters, Tradesmen’s Bills, Stationary, Rewards to the Soldiers who assist in making Seizures, to the Officers for seizing Snuff and Tobacco, and the Poundage to the Inspector of Prosecutions.

Bastin*

T. Anguish,

N' 23.

The Examination of Mr. Samuel Brawn; taken upon Oath, March 27th, April 1st and 4th, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That there are Two Modes of Payment for the Cruisers employed in the Service of the Customs; one upon the Establishment, the other by Contract. Where a Cruiser is upon the Establishment, the Vessel herself is the Property of the Crown; and all Expences of Repairs, Wages, Victualling, and every other Article, is paid Quarterly by the Collector of the Port where she is stationed, except in one Instance of a Vessel stationed at , and paid in

London. There are two Ways of contracting for Vessels: In one Case, the Vessel herself is the Property of the Crown, and no Charge is made for the Hire; but the Outfit, and all future Repairs, Wages, Victualling, and every other Expence, are paid out of the Gross Produce of her Seizures; and after deducting those Expences, the Remainder is, according to the Terms of the Contract, to be divided between the Crown and the Contractor; but in case the Amount of her Seizures is not sufficient to defray such Expences, the Deficiency is made good jointly by the Crown and the Contractor. In the other Species of Contract, the Contractor provides the Vessel after the Rate of 4$. 6d. per Ton per Lunar Month, for which he finds the Outfit, and all Repairs of the Vessel: The Hire of the Vessel, the Wages, Victualling, and all other Expences, arc, in like Manner as in the former Contract, paid out of the Produce of the Seizures made by her, and the Remainder is divided; and the Deficiency, if any, made good between the Contracting Parties.

As Surveyor for Sloops, all Accounts of Expenditure relative to the Cruisers pass through his Office; and in the Account delivered to this Board, the Sum set opposite to each Vessel is the Expence incurred for her during the Year, so far as appears by the Accounts transmitted to him, and by Computation, in Cases where the Bills have not yet been transmitted,

but where he can form a Computation, by knowing the Complement of Men, and those other Circumstances which will ascertain the Expence: The Contracts for these Vessels are formed by Minute of the Board of Customs. When a Contract is made, a Letter is sent by the Board to the Collector and Controller of the Port where the Vessel is to be stationed, specifying the Name of the Contractor, and informing them of the Terras of the Contract, that is, the Hire of the Vessel, if she is upon Hire, the Number of Men, and their Allowance for Wages, Victualling, and other Charges; and it is the Duty of those Two Officers to see that the Vessel is constantly Cruising, and that the full Complement of Mariners allowed by the Crown are actually on Board, which they are ordered to certify on the Back of the Journals of the Commanders and Mates of Vessels returned to his Office Quarterly. If any Deficiency in the Complement of the Crew is stated, they certify that the Wages and Victualling have been dedocted accordingly. At several of the Out Ports the Collectors and Controllers of the Port arc the Contractors for these Cruisers; at some of them both these Officers arc jointly Contractors; at others, One of them only. In the Year 1784, of 24 Cruisers which were upon Contract, 16 were contracted for with the Collectors and Controllers, or One of them, at the Port where the Cruiser was stationed.

The Vessels are directed to Cruise between Two certain Places, which are their Stations: These Stations frequently take in many Ports, and the Vessel is considered as stationed at that Port where she is paid.

When a Cruiser goes into any Port, the Master or other Person having the Command is instructed to attend the Collector and Controller, and acquaint them with his Reasons for coining in, and the Time when he intends to sail again. The Commander, the Chief Mate, and Second Mate, are Officers of the Customs in all the Cruisers; and in the larger ones, generally One of the Mariners is also an Officer, in Consequence of a Commission from the Board of Customs, and is called a Deputed Mariner. The Officers of the Cruisers upon the Establishment are in general appointed by the Board of Customs, pursuant to Warrants

27 Geo. III. 26° Janu 127

from the Treasury for that Purpose. The Officers in the Vessels upon Contract are recommended by the Contractor, and in Consequence thereof appointed by the Board of Customs.

The Pay of the Master is Fifty Pounds a Year; that of the Mate, in some Cases, Thirty-live Pounds a Year, and in others Thirty Pounds. The rest of the Crew have Fifteen Pounds a Year each. The Allowance for Victualling is Nine Pence a Day for each of the Crew, and One Shilling pe Lunar Month for each Person for Fire and Candle.

Brown.

A. Piggott,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will" Roe.

N' 24.

The Examination of Mr. John; taken upon Oath, April 5th, 8th, and 15th, and May loth, 1786.

This Examinant saith. That in the Account of the Produce of Seizures, and from Fines delivered to this Board, the Sum stated as remitted to the Receiver for London is the King’s Net Share arising from the Seizures in London, and paid into the Receiver’s Hands by the Warehouse-keeper.

The Payments out of the King’s Net Share in London, for Charges of Management, whether made by the Receiver for London, or the Out Ports, are for various Heads of Service, of which that for the Maintenance of the Cruisers is one; most of these Payments are, pursuant to the Orders of the Board, made by the Receiver for the Out Ports, and if the Fund in his Hands is insufficient to answer the Charges directed upon him, an Order is issued l»y the Board for his receiving Sums for that Purpose from the Receiver lor London: If the Receiver for London has not a sufficient Fund in his Hands, a like Order is made upon the Receiver General, for him to imprest such Sums as are wanted by the Receiver for the Out Ports. Since the Year 1781, the Charges of Management paid by the Two Receivers for Fines and Forfeitures in London ltave increased considerably. In the Year 1785, the Funds in the Hands of the Two Receivers having proved deficient, owing, as he apprehends, to the Act whereby the condemned Spirits were directed to be spilt, and to the other Acts whereby Smuggling has been checked, Sums to a very considerable Amount were imprested by the Receiver General to the Receiver for the Out Ports.

The Two Articles under the Heads of Allowances to Officers of the Customs, the one in the Account of Payments by the Receiver for London, the other in that of those by the Receiver for the Out Ports, consist of Salaries and Allowances to Officers in the Port of London, and should be included in the Returns of

those Officers to the Precept of this Board, for their Emoluments in that Year.

The Articles under the Title of Charges of Ma- Fifteenth nagement at the Out Ports consist principally of Payments made for the Maintenance of the Cruisers and ^"count^ Boats in the Service of the Customs: Regularly all the Charges of every Kind relative to that Service are paid out of the Fund arising from the King’s Net Share of Seizures. The Sums inserted in this Account include all the Payments made at each Port in the Year 1784, but they do not comprehend all the Expences incurred in that Year for the Maintenance of the Cruisers. The Expence of the established Cruisers is a regular Annual Charge, and the Accounts of the Expenditure relative to them are transmitted to his Office from the Out Ports Quarterly; but that of those upon Contract only takes Place from the Commencement of the Contract, and the Accounts in regard to them are not transmitted to his Office at regular Periods; and thence the Whole of the Expence incurred for the Service of these Cruisers for that Year is not comprehended in the Account.

In the Cruisers upon Contract, after the Gross Produce of the Seizure made by each Vessel has been legally divided, where the Share of the Seizing Officer amounts only to a Third, the Difference between that Third and a Moiety is, according to the Terms of that Species of Contract, made good to the Contractor, in order that the Amount of the Seizing Officer’s Share may be equal with the King’s Share; and such Payment, when the Account for the Contract Vessel is liquidated, is made by the Collector at the Out Port, under a Special Order of the Board, and is included in the Articles in the Column of Charges of Management, paid out of the King’s Net Share.

This Allowance to the Contractor is made in Consequence of his agreeing to defray Half the Charges incurred for the Maintenance of the Vessel; and if the Produce of the Seizures by her is insufficient to defray her Expences, be is bound to pay Half the Deficiency, which Payment is made to the Collector at the Port where she is stationed, and carried to the Account of the King’s Net Share.

The Sums paid into the Solicitor’s Hands, as Fines or Compositions upon Seizures, are, as he apprehends, scarcely ever subject to the Charges of Condemnation; and therefore in this Account, except in Two Articles, there is no Deduction from them under that Head.

Out of the King’s Share of Fines there are regularly paid Allowances to Officers of the Customs, which, with some trifling Charges, make the Sums inserted in that Column.

Upon examining the Books in his Office, he does not find that any Account has ever been delivered to Parliament of the Produce of Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures, for London and the Out Ports, with the various Payments for Charges of Management made out of that Produce, and the Payments into the Exchequer.

The Examination of Mr. John Timothy;

taken upon Oath, July 3d, 5th, 7th, and 10th, 1786.

The Examination of Mr. Potvell; taken

upon Oath, June 27th, July 7th, 10th, and 22d, 1786.

This Examinant faith, That the Account delivered by him to this Board contains all the Officers of the Customs in the Plantations for the Year 1784, both in the Islands and at the American Ports. The Officers belonging to the 4$ per Cent. I Hands, are distinguished in this Account, because the Salaries and Allowances

This Examinant faith, That in the Account of the Gross Amount of the Duties arising in the Plantations, and of the Charges of Management, the Grols Receipt in the Plantations includes not only the Produce of the Duties collected, but also what ariles from the King’s Net Share of Seizures and Fines: This Share, and the

received by them, whether in England, of the Husband of the 4% per Cent, or at the Ports, of the Collectors, are not paid out of the Produce of the Customs, but out of that of the 4! per Cent. Duty. The Incidental Allowances in this Account are Annual, and fixed by the Board of Customs, in order to enable the Officers to provide themselves with the Articles set opposite the Sums in that Column: These Incidental Allowances, except in the same of the Custom House Rent at Bermuda, were paid at the Port; by a Regulation of the Year 1785, they are to be paid there, if the growing Receipt of Duties is sufficient; and if not, a Certificate thereof is to be transmitted to the Board by the Collector and Controller of the Port, and an Order is to be made to the Receiver General to pay them. In the Year 1784 all the Officers upon the Establishment at those Islands not subject to the Cent. Duty, as well as the Collectors and Controllers, were paid their Salaries by the Receiver General: By the Regulation of the above-mentioned Date, the Collectors and Controllers only are to receive their Salaries in England', but if the Produce of the Duties at the Port be not sufficient to pay the Salaries of the inferior Officers, a Certificate thereof is, in like Manner, to be transmitted from the Port, and their Salaries to be paid by the Receiver General.

The Salaries to the Officers in this Account are paid out of the Custom Revenue, though the Annual Sums due to them have not all been received within the Year: The Payment of the Salaries to some of the Officers has been flopped by Order of the Board, for Non-transmission of their Accounts, or other Causes; and in some Cafes, their Attornies in England have neglected to apply for them. Some of the Allowances are made in Sterling, others in the Currency of the respective Islands.

The Officers of the Customs in the Plantations are authorized to take Fees by several Acts of Parliament. In a Memorial of the West India Merchants, in the Year 1785, made to the Treasury, and referred to the Board of Customs, it is, among other Matters, stated, That Redrefe is necessary, respecting the Island Custom House Officers who should exact more than the Amount of the established Fees, for Dispatch Money, or on other Pretences; and that such as shall by any Means require, take, or receive, more than the established Fees, or cause any unnecessary Delay to Shipping, should be immediately proceeded against. The above Memorial was, by an Order of the Board, of the 2ift of January last, referred to the Collector and Controller at every Port in the West India Islands, to report thereupon.

The Salaries to the Officers in the Plantations are not subject to any Payment brought to public Account, except that the Officers in the 4f per Cent. Islands pay the Civil List Duty.

There are at present Three American Ports not included in this Account, New Port Roseway,

and Cape Breton; these Ports were established in the Year 1785, and the Incidental Allowances for them are not yet adjusted.

J Timothy Swainson.

The Sums inserted in the Column of Charges paid at the Port consist of Salaries and Allowances to the inferior Officers, and all other Contingent Expences incurred at the Port: Some of these Allowances are in Sterling, and feme in the Currency of the Island; those in Currency are in this Account reduced into Sterling Money, from the Certificate of the Governor upon the Account, ascertaining the Value of the Currency for each Quarter.

The Collectors and Controllers, and all Officers at the Plantations upon the Establishment, in the Islands not subject to the 4-{- per Cent. Duty, in the Year 17S4 received their Salaries in England from the Receiver General; and all the Collectors and Controllers in the Plantations are, by a late Regulation, not entitled to receive their Salaries, which are paid Half Yearly, until the Accounts of the Receipts and Ditburfcments at their respective Ports, for the Two Quarto's in that Half Year, are transmitted to the Commissioners of the Customs.

In those Ports where the Receipt falls ffiort of the Expenditure at the Port, the Collector niuft either advance himself the Money necessary to defray the Expences, or he must transmit a Certificate to the Board, in order that the Payments may be made in;

and he cannot receive the Balance due to him until he has produced proper Vouchers and Receipts for all the Sums charged in this Account

In the Islands subject to the 4f per Cent. Duty, all the Payments to the Officers of the Customs, and for Contingent Charges, are made out of the Produce of that Duty, except that at the Island of Montserrat Three Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, a Proportion of the Fee to the Governor, upon the Collector’s swearing to his Account, is regularly paid out of the Customs.

The Article inserted as a Payment at St. Johns, Antigua (likewise one of the 4l per Cent. Islands) is an accidental Charge paid out of Seizures.

The Account of the Grols Amount of the Duties arising in the Plantations, and of the Charges of Management, and of the Net Produce, includes the Sums actually received and paid in the Year 1784. The Sum paid by the Receiver General into the Exchequer, on Account of the Plantation Duties in that Year, arose from the Collection of former Years, which had either not been remitted to him, or, if remitted, not converted into Calli till that Year; and from the Duties transmitted from the Plantations in that Year, but not applied by the Receiver General to the Charges of Management on Account of the Plantations, most of those Charges in England not been paid out of the Produce of the Plantation Duties, but out of that of the Customs collected in England.

The Accounts of the Duties received, and the Payments out of them in the Plantations, have never been passed in the Exchequer, but by the Controller General, under the Authority of the Board of Customs: They were not made out in such a Manner as to be admissible, according to the Forms of the Exchequer. The Accounts have within these Two or Three Years been put upon such a Footing that they might go through the Exchequer, if the Balances depending

N° 31.

The Examination of Mr. George Litchfield; taken upon Oath, November zd 1785.

This Examinant saith, That as Solicitor for carrying on Criminal Prosecutions in the Customs, and to recover Debts due on Bonds, and to prosecute Appeals, he receives from Time to Time, by Imprests either upon the Receiver General or the Receivers for Fines and Forfeitures, Sums of Money to defray the Expences of the Prosecutions, of which he passes his Account with the Auditor of the Solicitor’s Accounts; he receives for these Purposes no other Money out of the Revenue of the Customs. The Penalties recovered he pays by Order of the Board of Customs, either into the Exchequer, or into the Hands of the Receivers for Vox.. 42.

Fines and Forfeitures; the Debts he recovers he pays, either by the Orders of the Board, or of the Court of Exchequer, into the Exchequer, or into the Hands of the Receiver General, or of the Receivers for Fines and Forfeitures: Sometimes, where Sums are recovered in consequence of Proceedings carried on by him, the Court of Exchequer direct the Officers, or Persons in whose Hands those Sums are, to pay them into the Exchequer, without passing through the

Hands of the Solicitor. G. Litchfield.

T. Anguish, A. Piggott, Richd Weave,

Sam1 Beachcrof Geo. Drummond

N" 33-

The Excmination of Mr. George Litchfield; takeri upon Oath, May 9th, and August 3d, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That the only Authorities* by Act of Parliament that he knows of, under which die Officers of the Customs at the Out Ports take Fees, are the Tables made out pursuant to the Order of the House of Commons of the Year 1662, and particular Acts, whereby Fees are allowed to be taken by certain. Officers specified therein for particular Services, at particular Ports; these last are very few in Number: The rest of the Fees taken by the Officers at the Out Ports are, as he apprehends, grounded solely upon Usage.

By a printed Order of the Board of Customs, of August the loth, 1716, founded upon an Address of the House of Commons to the Crown, respecting Fees, and enforced by an Order of that Board, of April 12th, 1776, it is enjoined, That in every Office of the Customs, where ancient, just, and legal Fees are taken, an exact Table thereof, signed by the proper Officers, shall be hung up, and that no other Fees shall be taken; and that in every Office where no Fee is taken, a Paper, containing a Declaration thereof, shall be set up for public View.

Under the Act of William the Third, the Officers are empowered to take Compensations for extra Service; and he knows of no other legal Authority for that Species of Reward.

G> Litchfield.

A. Piggott,

MichdNeave,

Gto. Drummond,

Will« Roe.

N. B. Since the Year 1752, the Deputy Customer has allowed the Patentee, by mutual Agreement, 14 Annually, the Deputy having received all Fees, &c\

----- The Deputy Comptroller pays his Patentee Ten Pounds per Annum, in lieu of all Fees, notwithstanding

the Patent Fees do not amount Annually to £. 20.

----- The Deputy Searcher always paid the Patentee £. 11 per Annum from his Appointment until the

Year 1783, but receiving Orders from the Honourable Board, " That Deputies were to be allowed Twenty Pounds per Annum on the whole Fees," nothing has been paid to the Patentee from that Time, as the Fees did not amount to £. 20.

N. B. The Bushellage of Com is usually received by the Patent Officers in its Kind, viz. One Bushel each out of every Ship or Vessel.

N. B. From the above Fees, received by the Patent Searcher, he allows One Third to his Deputy.

N. B. Exclusive of the foregoing Fees, the Officers receive Gratuities from the Merchants, under the Act of 6th and 7th William the Third, for attending at Times as well as Places not required by Law, on sundry urgent Occasions, at the landing Goods out of Ships wrecked or stranded on the Coast, and at the landing and re-shipping Goods out of and into Ship putting into the Port in Distress to refit; which Gratuities are more or less, as the Merchants and Officers agree, and are generally regulated by the Difficulty attending such Services, and the Nature of the Attendance required, and according as the Merchant is accommodated, viz.

N. B. Every Foreigner, not a Freeman, pays Double Fees.

N* 42.

The Examination of Esquire; taken

upon Oath, May 22d and 27th, August 10th, October 2d and 4th, and November 1 ith, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That the Recompences or Gratuities received by the Officers of the Customs, are taken under- the Authority of the Act of the 6th and 7th of William the Third, and he knows of no other legal Authority for this Species of Gratuity. These Recompences are for Business done by the Officer at Times or Places not required by Law.

The Times not required by Law, are either out bf Office Hours, as settled by the Rules annexed to the Book of Rates, or on Holidays. The Places not required by Law, are all those not being legal Quays; The legal Hours of Business at present remain as fixed by the Rules above mentioned. The Hours of Attendance by the Officers who sit in the Custom House at the Gut Ports, are different from those who sit in the Custom House in the Port of London; but the Hours of Attendance of the Waterside Officers are in Practice the same in and at the Out

Ports.

The Holidays Annually kept in the Department of the Customs, are Forty-five in Number; Thirty-one of them are founded upon the Authority of the following Acts of Parliament,. the 5th and 6th of 'the 6th, Chap. 3; the Third of James 1st, Chap, l; the 12th of Charles 2d, Chap, the 14th ajid 30th; and the 19th of Charles 2d, Chap. 3: The remaining Fourteen are customary, but he does not know the original Authority for them; they are not founded, as he is informed by the proper Law Officer, upon any specific. Acts of Parliament Most of the Holidays, if they fall upon a Sunday, are not kept, some are.

The Board of Customs do not meet on Holidays. Five Commissioners attend on Days of Business (subject to the following Exception) although Four of them constitute a Board, and are competent to every Official Transaction whatever. The excepted Days are Mondays and Saturdays in the Summer Half Year, which is from the 15th of April to the 15th of November; and Mondays only in the Winter FJalf Year. One Commissioner always attends upon the excepted Days, unless they are Holidays.

If the Merchants make previous Application to the Board, for Leave to work on a Holiday, that Permission is constantly granted.

To all Orders for the Payment of Money, the Signature of Four Commissioners is essential. To almost all the other ordinary Business of the Customs for the Port of London, in which the Merchants are concerned, the Signature of One Commissioner is sufficient.

All Orders respecting the Out Ports, which require to be signed by the Commissioners, are signed by Four of them. A great Part of the common and regular Bqsiness, in regard to the Out Ports, goes on bf course by Means of the Secretary, the Western and Northern Clerks, under the Authority of the Board; but in those Cases where a final Order from the Board is necessary, the same is signed by Four Commissioners.

The legal Quays are such as have been appointed and described in Commissions issued out of the Court of Exchequer. The Business not transacted upon the legal Quays is done by Special Sufferance, this Sufferance is made out by the proper Officers in the Long Room, and there must be the Signature of One Commissioner to every such Sufferance 1 The Execution of it is principally committed to the Landing Surveyors, Landing and Deputy King’s Waiters.

At an Out Port the same Kind of Sufferance is granted, and signed by the Collector and Controller and executed by the Waterside Officers.

The Coast Bonds taken by the Customer are required to bq taken with the Approbation of the Collector and Controller, which is to be signified by their being Witnesses thereto. All the Coast Bonds, either certified or uncertified, are to be transmitted at certain Periods to the Remembrancer of the Exchequer; together with a List thereof, which is to be examined and signed, as well by the Collector as the Patent Officers. A like Schedule is at the same Time required to be seut to the Commissioners of the Customs, and another to the Solicitor for Coast Bonds. All these Schedules are to be signed as aforesaid.

W. Stiles.

A Piggott,

SamI Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond

Wilt11 Jloe.

A Table of Fees lent in August 1785 contains, to the heft of my Knowledge and Belief, every Fee received in my Office. Most of the Patent ones come under One Head or other in the within Table; where they differ, it seems to be in consequence ot a Variation in the Modes of packing, and a Change of Names; and, from the best Information I have been able to procure, must have taken Place from an Opinion of Sir Edward Nor I hey, dated 19th of May T720, in consequence of some Hesitation about Payment of Fees for Goods, where the Packages were altered, or where they were flowed loose, a Trade, as to Glass Bottles, &V. taken up about that Time. The Answer to the Query is as follows: I am of Opinion that, no Rate being settled, the " Officer may take such Fee as was anciently received; and if Fees would be due if packed, the Officer may take such Fee for the like Quantity unpacked " as he might take if they were packed." 1 am the more inclined to think this was the Cale, as I cannot find there ever has been any Alteration or Complaint, by viva Voce Evidence of above Thirty Years. The Deputies and Clerks are from their own Declaration, and, I believe, are all the Fees received.

Bristol, Sept' 21st 1786.

That Craufurd.-

An Order of the Comons in Parlyment assembled, establishing and confirming Fees and Allowances to the Officers of His Majesties Customes and Subsidies.

Whereas in and by an Act of this present Parlyment, intituled, An Act for confirming of Publique Acts, an Act therein, intituled, Subsidy granted to His Majesty, of Tonnage and Poundage, and other Sumes of Money, payable upon Merchandizes exported and imported, and confirmed j by which Act, so confirmed, it is amongst other Things enacted and ordained, That during the Continuance of this Grant, where the Goods exported or imported amount to the Value of Five Pounds, or more, the Customers and Collectors, and all other His Majesty’s Officers in the several Ports, shall take and receive such Fees, and none other, as were taken in the Fowerth Yeare of late King James, until such Time as the said Fees should be otherwise settled by Authority of Parlyment.

And whereas also, among the Rules, Orders, and Directions, annexed to the Booke of Rates, ratified and confirmed by the aforesaid Act, it is ordered and directed, that, for the avoiding of all Oppressions by any of the Officers of the Customes in any Port of this Kingdom, in exacting unreasonable Fees from the Merchants, by Reason of any Entry or otherwise, touching the Shipping or Unshipping of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes, it is ordered, That no Officer, Clerk, or other, belonging to any Custom House whatsoever, shall ask, require, or receive any other or greater Fee of any Merchant or other whatsoever,

\ 1787.

then such as are or shall be established by the Comons assembled in Parlyment: And if any Officer or other shall offend, contrary to this Order, he shall forfeit his Office and Place, and be for ever after incapable of any Office in the Custom House.

In Prosecution of which said severall Clauses in the Act and Book of Rates before mentd, and for Settlement and Certainty of all the aforesaid Fees, in Satisfaction as w ell of the Merchant and others, as of the Officers, what Fees are to be paid or received for any Matter or Thing whatsoever, for or concerning the Importation or Exportation, shipping, landing, or entering of any Shipps Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes, of what Nature or in what Kind soever; it is ordered and declared by the Comons assembled in Parlyment, That the severall and respective Fees and Allowances mentioned in a Schedule or Table of Fees relating to the Port of Kingston upon Hull, and the Members and Creekes thereunto belonging, and none other, shall be paid to the Officers and others imployed and to be imployed in and about his Majesties Customs in the Port aforesaid, and are by the Authority aforesaid settled and confirmed.

And bee itt further ordered and declared by the Authority aforesaid, That the Allowances hereby intended to be sett down, menconed, and expressed in a Schedule or Table of Fees and Allowances to be paid to the Officers of His Majesties Customs and Subsidies in the Port of Kingston upon Hull, and the Members and Creekes thereunto belonging, and subscribed with the Hand of S' Edu ard Turner, Kn', now Speaker of the House of Comons, in Parliament assembled, and every particular Clause therein menconed and conteyned, shall be and remain as effectual, to all Intents and Purposes, as if the same were included and particularly expressed within the Body of this Order.

And in case any Merchant, Master of Colliers, or other Person or Persons whatsoever, shall refuse to pay all or any the Fees hereby ordered or intended, That in such Case it shall and may be lawful for any Officer or Officers to make Stay of every Bill of Entry, Cocquet, or other Warrant that shall be tendred or given in for passing of any Shipps Goods or Merchandizes whatsoever, exceeding the Value of Five Pounds in the Booke of Rates, for which the Fees shall be claymed, and denyed to be payed as aforesaid.

And be it further ordered and ordeyned, That Copies or Transcripts of this Order and Table of Fees shall be made and sett up in Publick View in the Custom House of Kingston upon Hull, and in all other Offices and Places where the said, or any of them, are to be payed or received.

An ORDER of the Coraons assembled in Parliament, establishing and confirming Fees and Allowances to the Officers of his Majesties Cus-tomes and Subsidies.

Whereas, And by an Act of this p'sent Parliament, entituled An Act for confirming of other Acts, An Act theirin entituled A Subsidy granted the King of Tonnage and Poundage, and other Sumes of Money payable upon Merchandize exported and imported, was confirmed; by wcfc Act soe confirmed it is (amongst other Things) enacted and ordained, that during the Continuance of that Grant, where the Goods exported or imported amounteth unto the Value of Five Pounds or more, the Customers and Collectors, and all other of all his Majesties Officers, within the said several Ports, shall take and receive such Fees, and none other, as where taken in y* Fourth Year of the late King , untill such Time as the said Fees should be otherwayes setled.

And whereas also, Amongst the Rules, Orders, and Directions anexed to the Book of Rates, ratified and confirmed by the aforesaid Act, It is ordered and directed, that for avoiding of all Oppression by any of the Officers of the Customes in any Port of this Kingdome, in exacting unreasonable Fees from the Merchants, by reason of any Entryes or Wayes touching the shipping and unshipping of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, It is ordered. That no Officer, Clerke, or other, belonging to any Customhouse whatsoever, shall exact or require, or receive any other or greater Fee, of any Merchant or other whatsoever, then such as are or shall be established by y* Comons in Parliament; and if any Officer or other shall offend contrary to this Orders, he shall forfeit his Office and Place, and be for ever incapable of any Office in the Customhouse.

In Prosecution of which said severall Clauses in the Act and Booke of Rates beforementioned, and for the

Settlement and Certainty of all the aforesaid Fees, concerning the Exportation and Importation, Shipping, Landing, or Entering of any Ships, Goods or Merchandizes, of what Nature and in what Kind soever, It is ordered and declared by the Comons in Parliament assembled, that the severall and respective Fees and Allowances mentioned in a Sedule or Table of Fees relating to the Port of Yarmout, and Members and Creekes thereunto belonging, and none other, shall be paid to the Officers and others imployed in and about his Majesties Customes in the Port aforesaid settled and confirmed.

And be it further ordered, and declared by Authority aforesaid, that the Fees and Allowances hereby intended and sett down, mentioned and expressed in a Sedule or Table of Fees, entituled, Fee’s and Allowances due and payable to the Officers of his Majesties Customes and Subsidies in the Port of Yarmouth, and the Members and Creeks thereunto belonging, and subscribed with y* Hand of S' , Kn',

now Speaker of the House of Comons in Parliament assembled, and every perticular Clause therein mentioned and contained, shall be and remain as effectuall to all Intents and Purposes, as if the same were particularly expressed and included within the Body of the said Order.

And in case any Merchant, Master of a Ship, or other Person or Persons w'soever, shall refuse to pay all or any of the Fees hereby ordered and intended, that in such Case it shall and may be lawfull for all and every Officer and Officers to make Stay of every Bill of Entry, Cocquett, or other Warr" that shall be finished'or given in for passing of any Ships, Goods, or Merchandize whatsoever, exceeding the Value of Five Pounds in the Book of Rates; for which the Fees shall be detained and denied to be paid as aforesaid.

N° 50.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas; taken

upon Oath, June 9th, and July 21st, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That he is a Ship Broker, and Owner of Ships, and as such he has for many Years transacted Business for Merchants, and on his own Account, at the Custom House in London.

The Payment to the Officer of the Customs by Fee, for Business done at Times and Places warranted by Law, is in some Cases fixed as to the Sum, in others not. Within his Memory the Fee for the same Business has in various Instances increased. It is hardly practicable to apportion the Fee to the Value of the Article on which it is taken, the Fee being by the Package er Tale of Goods, and the Goods themselves frequently very different in Value. In some Instances, the Fee is paid in One Sum, in others to the different Officers who are to have a Share of it.

Where the Fee is a certain and reasonable Sum, and Notice of it publicly affixed, he does not apprehend that Species of Payment to be very inconvenient to the Merchant.

The Compensation to the Officer for Business done at Times or Places not required by Law, where there is not some customary Agreement between the Merchant and the Officer, fixing the Sum, is a Source of great Inconvenience.

The Hours of Business at the Long Room, as settled at present by Law, that is from Nine to Twelve, do not appear sufficient. He apprehends that Four Hours would suffice, and that the Attendance of the Officers from Ten to Two in the Long Room would be the Arrangement the most convenient for Trade.

The Number of Holidays now observed in the Customs is injurious to Commerce. In the Long Room, where the Ship is reported, the Entry of the Goods Inwards and Outwards made, the Duties paid, and all Ships cleared Outwards, no Business whatever can be transacted on a Holiday.

The Business at the Water Side and on Ship Board may be carried on upon Holidays, previous Permission being had from the Commissioners of the Customs, and a Recompence made to the Officers appointed, for their Attendance. These Permissions are mostly granted upon perishable Articles, or in particular Cases.

In Time of Peace the Trade from many Parts of the World, owing to various Circumstances, affecting the Commerce, commences and continues to arrive at certain Periods of the Year. In Time of War the greatest Part of the Commerce of the Country is carried on by Fleets. In both Cases the frequent Intervention of Holidays is particularly detrimental.

The greatest and most regular Arrival of the Trade, and the chief Part of the Export Business, is from the Month of June to the Month of February, both inclusive.

Tho, Hubbert.

Sard Beackcroft,

Geo. Drummond, lViUmRoe.

N* 51.

The Examination of Mr. Walter;

taken upon Oath, October 5th and 9th, 1786.

This Examinant saith, That he is in Partnership with Mr. Kennett Dixon, and that they are Agents for Merchants.

It is common for the Merchants to employ Agents in

transacting the Business they have to do at the Custom House. His House has been in that Line of Business for upwards of Thirty Years; they carry on the Transactions at the Custom House for Merchants in general, and in every Line.

The Fee to the Officer for the Inward Business, at Times and Places warranted by Law, he has found in most Instances to be a fixed Sum.

The Fee in the Outward Business, particularly in the Searcher’s Office, is very uncertain; upon some Articles it has increased much within his Knowledge. There being no Table or Rule to appeal to for the Sum to be paid the Officer, frequent Disputes between tho Merchant and the Officer thence arise, and the shipping the Goods is thereby delayed, and the Fee taken by different Officers of the same Description, for the same Business, varies.

He does not apprehend that the forwarding of Debentures, either for Bounty or Drawback, or any other of the regular Course of Business, is impeded by the Non-payment of Fee; but he appreliends that greater Dispatch than could be had in the common Course, is often obtained by that Mode of Reward.

The Recompence to the Officer, by the Merchant, for Business done at Times and Places not required by Law, is in some Instances fixed, in others not. Where the Sum to be paid for this Service is uncertain (as it frequently is) great Inconvenience may arise; the Merchant must either pay the Sum demanded, or submit to let his Goods remain unshipped, or not landed, until he has made Application to the Board of Customs, and their Decision is known; which creates much Trouble, great Loss of Time, and is often attended with other considerable Loss. Disputes on this Head very frequently arise.

The Hours of Attendance in Practice by the Long Room Officers, are from Ten to One in the Inward Department, and from Ten to Two in the Outward. If both these Sets of Officers attended from Ten to Two, it would be very convenient for Trade, and he apprehends sufficient.

The Holidays observed in the Customs are very prejudicial to Commerce. In the Long Room no Business whatever can be transacted on a Holiday. The Report of the Ship, the Entry, the Payment of the Duty, the Entry of the Ship Outwards, the Entry of the Goods for Export, the Clearance of the Ship, and most of the essential Formalities to the making out or passing Debentures for Drawbacks and Bounties, in order to complete them for Payment, are carried on in the Long Room. Interruption or Delay, in the Course of any of the Particulars above enumerated, are attended with much Detriment to the Merchant.

Every Day a Book, containing the Names of all Ships reported that Day, goes in to the Board; this Book is sent in at One o’Clock. No Ship after she has reported, can have her Cargo unladen until the Board have appointed the Landing Waiters to that Ship.

All the Officers at the Waterside whatever, except the Searchers and the Officers under them, will work upon a Holiday, previous Permission of the Board being had, and Compensation to them being made. The Searchers and the Officers under them will not. Thence, as far as regards the Waterside Officers, the Inward Business can go on upon a Holiday; the Outward cannot.

In Ships, whether arriving or Outward bound, the Cargo itself, and the Object of the Voyage, may be very materially affected by the Delay arising from Holidays: When they happen together, or at those Periods of the Year when, from the Nature of the Commerce, or from other Circumstances, the Ships arrive in Fleets, or mostly about the same Time, these inconveniencies are much increased. „

The greatest1 Proportion of the Inward and Outward Trade does, as he apprehends, ordinarily occur from the Month of June to the Month of January.

The Delay in loading or unloading Ships, occasioned by Holidays, must afford greater Time and Opportunity for Practices injurious to the Revenue of the Customs.

Wm Walter

N«52.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas Coles; taken upon Oath, October 12th and 14th 1786.

This Examinant saith, That he is in Partnership with Mr. George Godtvin, and their House is employed by Merchants in general, and in the different Lines of Commerce, as Brokers; and as such, they conduct the Business which the Merchant has to transact at the Custom House. They have been extensively engaged in that Line of Business for Twenty Years, and are conversant with the various Branches of the Custom House Business.

The Fee, that is, the Sum paid by the Merchant to upon the Long Room, is on Holidays wholly stopped; the Officer for Business transacted at Times and Places from thence great Delay and much Loss to the Mer-required by Law, is, according to his Observation, in chant does frequently arise. These Evils are greatly some Cases a settled customary Sum, in others not so. increased when Holidays happen to fall together, or He is so conversant in the Business, that it would not at those Periods of the Year when the Bulk of the

He has very frequently known, that Orders, to Fifteenth small Amount, have been left unexecuted, on Ac- Report count of the Heaviness of the Fees which must have on *'U,^1C been paid upon them; and these Orders, he has great Account"-Reason to believe, have thereby been diverted to other Countries.

The Recompence to the Officers, for Business done at Times and Places not required by Law, he has in general found to be reduced to a fixed Sum.

Four Hours would, he apprehends, be very sufficient for the Business done in the Long Room: He thinks the most expedient Hours would be from Nine to One, in order to give the more Time for the Dispatch of the Export Business, and to prevent the Confusion arising from late Shipping. Much Inconvenience arises at present from the iate Attendance of the Long Room Officers, who are not all of them regularly in their respective Seats, so that the Business may be carried on, till near Fleven o’Clock; and also from this Circumstance, that the Searchers absent themselves from their Offices (as he is informed, for Dinner) from One till Half after Three, during which Time all the Export Business is at a Stand.

The Number of Holidays observed in the Office of the Customs interferes much with the general Dispatch of Business, and is very injurious to Commerce.

The Inward and Outward Business, as far as depends

be practicable, in any Case, to make him pay more than the usual Fee, though Attempts of that Rind have been made; but Strangers, or Persons, less acquainted therewith, are liable to Imposition, and he has known many Instances thereof. No Table, except of the Fees taken by the Patent Officers, is hung up in the Long Room; nor does he know of any other Tables of Fees being hung up in the different Offices. There are certain Parts of the Custom Business which are left much to the Discretion of the

Trade is arriving or exporting.

With many Parts of the Transactions of the Customs the Excise is connected, and the Presence of the Excise Officers necessary; the Holidays observsd in the Excise Office occur more frequently than those in the Customs; and thence the Custom Business is, in those Cases, much interrupted.

The Occurrence of Holidays in the Customs may be attended with material Detriment to the Revenue^ by extending the Time limited by Law for reporting Officer, and where the Uncertainty and Difference of of Ships after their passing Gravesend. This Extension

the Fee paid may be attended with Consequences injurious to the Revenue.

The Fee is not a Species of Payment which can bear any Proportion to the Value of the Article on which it is paid; the same Fee being paid upon the Entry, whether great or small, or by Tale or Package, whatever may be the Value of the Contents.

N* 55-

The Examination of Mr. Edward Dew; taken upon Oath, November 22d, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Deputy Surveyor of the Out Ports. It appears from the Books in his Office, that in the Year 1784 Two Patent Customers and Six Patent Controllers only at the Out Ports made Returns to this Office , the Returns for all the rest of the Ports were made by the Deputy Controllers, except Poulton, where there is no Deputy Controller. There are several Ports from whence no Returns were made, either by the Patent or Deputy Customer; and it appears from the Quarter Books seot up by the

Vol. 42.

Collectors, and delivered to the Examiners, and compared with the Quarter Books of the Controllers, by the Surveyor, that several of the Collectors are also Deputy Customers, some of which send up Duplicates of their Quarter Books to the Surveyor. The Quarter Books sent up to this Office, either by the Patent or Deputy Customers, are never examined; they are considered of no Consequence, tied up together, and deposited in the Office.

EdwJ Dew.

T. Anguish,

RiclANeave,

Sand Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond, mil. Roe.

After our hearty Commendations. Whereas by letters Patent bearing Date the 9th Day of May 1770, the Office of Comptroller of His Majesty’s Customs in the Port of Chestei', together with the Ports, Places, and Creeks thereunto belonging, was granted to John goyne, Esquire, (now Sir John ); and whereas the Office of Deputy Comptroller of the Customs at the Port of Liverpool is lately become vacant by the Death of Richard Atkis, and that you have represented unto us that the said Sir John Burgoyne is out of the Kingdom: We, in consideration of the particular

Circumstances of the Case, and in order to prevent any Detriment which may arise to His Majesty’s Revenue of Customs by the Absence of the Patentee, think fit that some proper Person should be appointed to act as Deputy Comptroller of the Customs there; and Edmund Rigby being recommended unto us as a fit Person for this Purpose, these are therefore to authorise and require you to issue forth your Deputation to the said Edmund Rigby to be Deputy Comptroller of the Customs there accordingly, upon his giving Security to the Crown for the faithful Discharge of the said Office, in the like Sum, at least, as was given by the late Deputy Comptroller to the Patentee.; And for so doing this shall be your Warrant.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers,. the 8th Day of January 1785.

To our very loving Friends W. Pitt.1 2 3 4

the Commissioners of His Graham.

Majesty’s Customs. Ed J. Eliot.

A true Copy.;

Custom House, London. IV. Stiles, Secretary.

INSTRUCTIONS for Collector of

His Majesty’s Customs in the Port of !

1. You shall from Time to Time, so long as you

shall continue and be employed in the said Office, well and truly collect and receive all and every; Sum and Sums of Money arising and growing due and payable to our Sovereign Lord the King, within the said Port of and the Members and Creeks

thereunto belonging, for or in respect of any Goods, Wares, Wines, or other Merchandizes, imported into, or exported out of, the same.

2. You shall, during the Time aforesaid, make up

for the Comptroller -General of the Accounts of the Customs for the Time being, a true and just Account of all such Duties, Dues, and Monies, so by you, the said to be received at the Four usual

Feasts of the Year; that is to Say, at the Feast of the Birth of our Lord Christ, the Annunciation of the Virgin Mary, the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, and

St. Michael the Archangel, or within Fourteen Days next after every of the said Feasts in every Year, or oftener if thereunto required.

3. You shall, from Time to Time, well and truly

pay, or cause to be paid, unto Re-

ceiver General and Cashier of the Customs, or to the Receiver General and Cashier thereof for the Time being, at the Custom House within the Port of

don, all and every Sum and Sums of Money to be by you collected and received as aforesaid, as you shall receive the same, making Distinction in your Payments, whether by Bill of Exchange or otherwise, betwixt the Monies payable for Customs, Subsidy, Additional Duty and Impositions, or other Duties payable to His Majesty.

4. You shall, at the Feast of Christmas in every

Year, or within Thirty Days after, fully pay in, discharge, and clear your Accounts of all the Monies due, and by you collected, for the Year ending at the Feast aforesaid; and also shall well and truly perform and execute the said Office or Place in all Things thereunto appertaining.

5. You shall not, directly or indirectly, either in your own Name, or in the Name or Names of any other Person or Persons, or in Company or Partner* ship with any other, trade as a Merchant for yourself, or as a Factor or Agent for any other, in or for any Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes.

6. You shall do your best Endeavour, with tha Privity and Approbation of the Comptroller, in taking good Security by Bond or Bonds, for the Additional Duty, Impositions, or other Duties, in such Manner as the Law directs; and you shall duly answer and pay all such Sum and Sums of Money as you shall receive upon any such Bonds, unto tire said Receiver General and Cashier, with the Interest due thereon.

7. You shall, upon Demand to be mode by the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, or any Four or more of them, or by any Person or Persons to be by them appointed in that Behalf, deliver up to the said Commissioners, or such Person or Persons so appointed, all such of the said Bonds as shall at the Time of such Demand remain unsatisfied or undischarged, whole, safe, and uncancelled.

8. You shall not pay or allow any Salaries, otherwise than as you shall from Time to Time be directed by us, or the Commissioners of the Customs for the Time being, nor any Monies by Way of Incident Charges, but in the usual Cases of Tidesmen’s and Boatmen’s Daily Pay, with the Rent for His Majesty’s Custom House in your Port, unless you receive our Directions in Writing for so doing; and before you shall pay any Tidesman or Boatman his Daily ray, you shall have the Surveyor’s Certificate of such Tidesman’s and Boatman’s Service, and Money due unto him.

9. You shall grant no Bill of Sight or Sufferance for the landing of any Merchandize, but only to such Persons who shall make Gath before you, that they have neither Invoice, Letter, or other Advice, whereby to make known the true Contents of such Goods for which they desire such Bill of Sight or Sufferance; and when Goods are landed by such Bill, you are to take Care that a sufficient Deposit be made with the Privity of the Comptroller, to answer the Duties due on those Goods.

10. You shall cause all Warrants and Entries for Goods and Merchandizes, both Inwards or Outwards, to be entered, dc Die in Diem, in the open Custom House, in the Books which we have or shall transmit unto you, and shall write and adjust your Quarter Books to be sent unto us in the Method and Form prescribed; and every Quarter Book is to be signed by yourself, and by the Surveyor, expressing, that you and the Surveyor have examined the whole Book, and find that the Quality and Quantity of all Merchandizes, imported and exported within your Port during such Quarter, is truly entered therein.

11. Besides the Quarterly Account as aforesaid, vou shall also send to us a Monthly Abstract of the Receipts and Payments within Six Days after the End of each Month, except those Months where the respective Quarters end; and then for the Months of March and September, the next Post after each Quarter Day; and, for the other Quarters, within Six Days after each Quarter Day; and such other Accounts as we from Time to Time shall direct.

12. You are to take Notice, that you and the Comptroller are to have separate Locks on the Money and Bonds, and every Day to lock up the Receipts of that Day; and, in making up all Accounts, you are to call

Mooring, kc. A Petition of Joseph , of Christchurch, in the

Vessels in the County of Surrey, and of the Parish of

aou.1 ° °n" Saint Peters, Paul’s in the City of London,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Number of Ships and Vessels of all Descriptions, frequenting the Port of Iffndon, is exceedingly great, and the Value thereof, and of their Cargoes, is computed to amount, at all Times, to near Four Millions of Money; and that the Navigation of the Itiver Thames, between London Bridge and Cuckold's Point, is much impeded by the Practice of Ships and Vessels lying at their Anchors in the Middle of the River (which, from the Insufficiency of proper Moorings, is in some Degree unavoidable) where every Captain or Master chusing his own Station, and the Tiers or Moorings being extended to an improper Length, great Obstructions, Delay, and Danger, arc thereby occasioned, many Accidents happen, and heavy Losses are sustained, by the sinking or damaging of Ships, Vessels, and small Craft, navigating the said River within the abovementioned Limits; and that the irregular and improper Manner in which Ships and Vessels lie at the W harfs and Landing Places, within the Limits aforesaid, occasions them to project so far into the Itiver, as to make the Navigation thereof laborious, inconvenient, and dangerous, particularly for Lighters and small Boats; besides which, great Inconvenience and Danger are thereby occasioned to the Vessels themselves, in changing their Situations, and in getting up to the Wharfs, or quitting them, and, by Means of the Circumstances before mentioned, frequent Losses and Inconveniencies are occasioned by Lighters, Barges, and other small Craft, being delayed in getting to their Places of Destination to receive or discharge their Cargoes; and that Robberies, Piracies, and various Outrages and Misdemeanors, are frequently committed within the said Limits in the Night-time, and, although the Lives and Properties of the Inhabitants of the Me-tropolis are protected by an ample and well-regulated "Watch and Police, no such Safety is provided for the Ships and Vessels frequenting the Port of where Thieves and Robbers form themselves into such large Gangs, as to render it impossible for single Vessels to protect themselves from iheir Attacks and Depredations; and the above Evils are particularly alarming to Foreigners, and it is apprehended are, on many Accounts, extremely detrimental to the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London; and that the Petitioners apprehend that, in order to provide an effectual and permanent Remedy for the Evils and Inconveniencies hereinbefore enumerated, it is necessary that proper Rules and Orders, for the stationing and regulating of Ships and Vessels frequenting the said Port, should be framed, and that the same should be carried into Effect by Persons to be appointed and authorized to act therein as Harbour Masters; and that, for the Protection of the Lives and Properties of all Persons resorting to, or continuing in, the said Port, within the Limits aforesaid, the Petitioners also apprehend it is necessary that a good and sufficient Nightly Watch should be established, consisting of able-bodied Men, and divided into proper Stations, and, as the Number of Men required for such Watch would be very considerable, they would be found exceedingly useful, and would always be at Hand to assist and direct Ships and Vessels coming into the Port in the Night-time, whereby Accidents might be

prevented,

Mi Great Britain, Jl iUiam Eden, Esq; Privy Councillor in Great Britain and Ireland, Member of the British Parliament, and His Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to His Most Christian Majesty; and the Most Christian King, the Sieur Joseph Mathias Gerard de liayneval, Knight, Councillor of State, Knight of the Royal Order of Charles 3d. who, after having exchanged their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

Article I.

It is agreed and concluded between the Most Serene and Most Potent King of Great Britain, and the Most Serene and Most Potent the Most Christian King, that there shall be a reciprocal and entirely perfect Liberty of Navigation and Commerce between the Subjects of each Party, in all and every the Kingdoms, States, Provinces and Territories subject to their Majesties in Europe, for all and singular Kinds of Goods, in those Places, upon the Conditions, and in such Manner and Form as is settled and adjusted in the following Articles.

Article II.

For the future Security of Commerce and Friendship between the Subjects of their said Majesties, and to the End that this good Correspondence may be preserved from all Interruption and Disturbance, it is concluded and agreed, that if, at any Time, there should arise any Misunderstanding, Breach of Friendship, or Rupture between the Crowns of their Majesties, which God forbid! (which Rupture shall not be deemed to exist until the re-calling or sending Home of the respective Ambassadors and Ministers) the Subjects of each of the Two Parties residing in the Dominions of the other, shall have the Privilege of remaining and continuing their Trade therein, without any Manner of Disturbance, so long as they behave peaceably, and commit no Offence against the Laws and Ordinances: And in case their Conduct should render them suspected, and the respective Governments should be obliged to order them to remove, the Term of Twelve Months shall be allowed them for that Purpose, in order that they may remove, with their Effects and Property, whether entrusted to Individuals or to the State. At the same Time it is to be understood that this Favour is not to be extended to those whose Conduct shall be contrary to the public Peace.

Article III.

It is likewise agreed and concluded, that the Subjects and Inhabitants of the Kingdoms, Provinces, and Dominions of their Majesties, shall exercise no Acts of Hostility or Violence against each other, either by Sea or by Land, or in Rivers, Streams, Ports, for Havens, under any Colour or Pretence whatsoever; so that the Subjects of either Party shall receive no Patent, Commission, or Instruction for arming and acting at Sea as Privateers, nor Letters of Reprisal, a3 they are called, from any Princes or States, Enemies to the other Party; nor by virtue or under Colour of such Patents, Commissions or Reprisals, shall they disturb, infest, or any Way prejudice or damage the aforesaid Subjects anil Inhabitants of the King of Great Britain, or of the Most Christian King; neither shall they arm Ships in such Manner as is abovesaid, or go out to Sea therewith. To which End, as often as it is required by cither Party, strict and express Prohibitions shall be renewed and published in all the Territories, Countries, and Dominions of each Party wheresoever, that no one shall in anywise use such Commissions or Letters of Reprisal, under the severest Punishment that can be indicted on the Transgressors, besides being liable to make full Restitution and Satisfaction to those to w horn they have done any Damage: Neither shall any Letters of Reprisal lie hereafter granted by either of the said High Contracting Parties, to the Prejudice or Detriment of the Subjects of the other, except only in

Vox.. 42.

such Case wherein Justice is denied or delayed; which Treaty with Denial or Delay of Justice shall not be regarded as France, tu-. verified, unless the Petition of the Person, who desires the said Letters of Reprisal, be communicated to the Minister residing the re on the Part of the Prince against w hose Subjects they are to be granted, that within the Space of Four Months, or sooner, if it be possible, he may manifest the contrary, or procure the Satisfaction which may be justly due.

Article IV.

The Subjects and Inhabitants of the respective Dominions of the Two Sovereigns shall have Liberty, freely and securely, w ithout Licence or Passport, general or special, by Land or by Sea, or any other Way, to enter into the Kingdoms, Dominions, Provinces,

Countries, Islands, Cities, Villages, Towns, walled or unwalled, fortified or unfortified, Ports, or Territories whatsoever, of either Sovereign, situated in Europe, and to return from thence, to remain there, or to pass through the same, and therein to buy and purchase, as they please, all Things necessary for their Subsistence and Use, and they shall mutually be treated with all Kindness and Favour. Provided, however, that, in all these Matters, they behave and conduct themselves conformably to the Laws and Statutes, and live with each other in a friendly and peaceable Manner, and promote reciprocal Concord by maintaining a mutual good Understanding.

Article V.

The Subjects of each of their said Majesties may have Leave and Licence to come with their Ships, as also with the Merchandizes and Goods on board the same, the Trade and Importation whereof are not prohibited by the Laws of either Kingdom, and to enter into the Countries, Dominions, Cities, Ports, Places, and Rivers of either Party, situated in Europe, to resort thereto, and to remain and reside there, without any Limitation of Time; also to hire Houses, or to lodge with other Persons, and to buy all lawful Kinds of Merchandizes, where they think fit, either from the First Maker or the Seller, or in any other Manner, whether in the Publick Market for the Sale of Merchandizes, or in Fairs, or wherever such Merchandizes are manufactured or sold. They may likewise deposit and keep in their Magazines and Warehouses, the Merchandizes brought from other Parts, and afterwards expose the same to Sale, without being in anywise obliged, unless willingly and of their own Accord, to bring the said Merchandizes to the Marts and Fairs. Neither are they to be burthened with any Impositions or Duties on Account of the said Freedom of Trade, or for any other Cause whatsoever, except those which are to be paid for their Ships and Merchandizes conformably to the Regulations of the present Treaty, or those to which the Subjects of the Two Contracting Parties shall themselves be liable. And they shall have free Leave to remove themselves, as also their Wives, Children, and Servants, together with their Merchandizes, Property, Goods, or Effects, whether bought or imported, wherever they shall think fit, out of either Kingdom, by Land and by Sea, on the Rivers and Fresh Waters, after discharging the usual Duties, any Law, Privilege, Grant, Immunities, or Customs, to the contrary thereof in anywise notwithstanding. In Matters of Religion, the Subjects of the Two Crowns shall enjoy perfect Liberty: They shall not be compelled to attend Divine Service, whether in the Churches or elsewhere; but, on the contrary, they shall be permitted, without any Molestation, to perform the Exercises of their Religion privately in their own Houses, and in their own Way. Liberty shall not be refused to bury the Subjects of either Kingdom who die in the Territories of the other, in convenient Places to be appointed for that Purpose; nor shall the Funerals or Sepulchres of the Deceased be in anywise disturbed.

Article VIII.

No Merchandize exported from the Countries respectively under the Dominion of their Majesties shall hereafter be subject to be inspected or confiscated, under any Pretence of Fraud or Defect in making or working them, or of any other Imperfection whatsoever; but absolute Freedom shall be allowed to the Buyer and Seller to bargain and fix the Price for the same, as they shall see good; any Law, Statute, Edict, Proclamation, Privilege, Grant, or Custom to the contrary notwithstanding.

Article IX.

Whereas several Kinds of Merchandizes, which arc Usually contained in Casks, Chests, or other Cases, and for which the Duties are paid by Weight, will be exported from and imported into France by British Subjects; it is agreed that, in such Case, the aforesaid Duties shall be demanded only according to the real Weight of the Merchandizes; and the Weight of the Casks, Chests, and other Cases whatever, shall be deducted, in the same Manner as has been and is now practised in England.

Article X.

It is further agreed, that if any Mistake or Error shall be committed by any Master of a Ship, his Interpreter or Factor, or by others employed by him, in making the Entry or Declaration of her Cargo, neither the Ship nor the Cargo, for such Defect, shall be subject to Confiscation; but it shall be lawful for the Proprietors to take back again such Goods as were omitted in the Entry or Declaration of the Master of the Ship, paying only the accustomed Duties according to the Pancart; provided always that there be no manifest Appearance of Fraud. Neither shall the Merchants, or the Masters of Ships, or the Merchandize, be subject to any Penalties by Reason of such Omis-.sion, in case the Goods omitted in the Declaration shall not have been landed before the Declaration has been made.

Article XI.

In case either of the Two High Contracting Parties shall think proper to establish Prohibitions, or to augment the Import Duties upon any Goods or Merchandize of the Growth or Manufacture of the other, which are not specified in the Tariff such Prohibitions or Augmentations shall be general, and shall comprehend the like Goods and Merchandizes of the other most favoured European Nations, as well as those of either State: And in case either of the Two Contracting Parties shall revoke the Prohibitions, or diminish the Duties, in Favour of any other European Nation, upon any Goods or Merchandize of its Growth or Manufacture, whether on Importation or Exportation, such Revocations or Diminutions shall be extended to the Subjects of the other Party, on Condition that the latter shall grant to the Subjects of the former the Importation and Exportation of the like Goods and Merchandizes under the same Duties; the Cases reserved in the 7th Article of the present Treaty always excepted.

Article XII.

And forasmuch as a certain Usage, not authorized by any Law, has formerly obtained in divers Parts of Great Britain and France, by which French Subjects have paid in England a Kind of Capitation Tax, called in the Language of that Country Head Money; and English Subjects a like Duty in called Argent

Du Chef: it is agreed that the said Impost shall not be demanded for the future, on either Side, neither under the ancient Name, nor under any other Name whatsoever.

Article XIII.

If either of the High Contracting Parties has granted, Trontv with or shall grant, any Bounties for encouraging the *f*

Exportation of any Articles, being of the Growth,

Produce, or Manufacture of His Dominions, the other Party shall be allowed to add to the Duties already imposed, by virtue of the present Treaty, 011 the said Goods and Merchandizes, imported into his Dominions, such an Import Duty as shall be equivalent to the said Bounty. But this Stipulation is not to extend to the Cases of Restitutions of Duties and Imposts,

(called Drawbacks) which are allowed upon Exportation.

Article XIV.

The Advantages granted by the present Treaty to the Subjects of His Brit amuck Majesty shall take Effect, as far as relates to the Kingdom of Great Britain, as Soon as Laws shall be passed there for securing to the Subjects of His Most Christian Majesty the reciprocal Enjoyment of the Advantages which are granted to them by the present Treaty.

And the Advantages granted by all these Articles, except the Tariff, shall take Effect, with regard to the Kingdom of Ireland, as soon as Laws shall be passed there, for securing to the Subjects of His Most Christian Majesty the reciprocal Enjoyment of the Advantages which are granted to them by. this Treaty; and, in like Manner, the Advantages granted by the Tariff shall take Effect, in what relates to the said Kingdom, as soon as Laws shall be passed there for giving Effect to the said Tariff'.

Article XV.

It is agreed, that Ships belonging to His Majesty’s Subjects, arriving in the Dominions of His Most Christian Majesty from the Ports of Great Britain or Ireland, or from any other Foreign Port, shall not pay Freight Duty, of any other like Duty. In the same Manner, French Ships shall be exempted, in the Dominions of His Britannick Majesty, from the Duty of Five Shillings, and from every other similar Duty or Charge.

Article XVI.

It shall not be lawful for any Foreign Privateers, not being Subjects of either Crown, who have Commissions from any other Prince or State, in Enmity with either Nation, to arm their Ships in the Ports of either of the said Two Kingdoms, to sell what they have taken, or in any other Manner whatever to exchange the same; neither shall they be allowed even to purchase Victuals, except such as shall be necessary for their going to the nearest Port of that Prince from whom they have obtained Commissions.

Article XVII;

When any Dispute -shall arise between any Commander of a Ship and his Seamen, in the Ports of either Kingdom, concerning Wages due to the said Seamen, or other Civil Causes whatever, the Magistrate . of the Place shall require no more from the Person accused, than that he give to the Accuser a Declaration in Writing, witnessed by the Magistrate, whereby lie shall be bound to answer that Matter before a competent Judge in his own Country; which being done, it shall not be lawful either for the Seamen to desert their Ship, or to hinder the Commander from prosecuting his Voyage. It shall moreover be lawful for the Merchants in the Places of their Abode, or elsewhere, to keep Books of their Accounts and Affairs, as they shall think fit, and to have an Intercourse of Letters, in such Language or Idiom as they shall chuse, without any Molestation or Search whatsoever. But if it should happen to be necessary for them to produce their BooJ<s of Accounts for deciding any Dispute or Controversy, in such Case they shall be obliged to

concerning Ships and Goods, that every Thing shall be deemed to be free, which shall be found on board the Ships belonging to the Subjects of the respective Kingdoms, although the whole Lading, or Part thereof, should belong to the Enemies of their Majesties, Contraband Goods being always excepted, on the stopping of which such Proceedings shall be had as are conformable to die Spirit of the following Articles; it is likewise agreed, that the same Liberty be extended to Persons who are on board a free Ship, to the End that, although they be Enemies to both or to either Party, they may not be taken out of such free Ship, unless they are Soldiers, actually in the Service of the Enemies, and on their Voyage for the Purpose of being employed in a Military Capacity, in their Elects or Armies.

Article XVIII.

It is further agreed and concluded, that all Merchants, Commanders of Ships, and others the Subjects of the King of Great Britain, in all the Dominions of His Most Christian Majesty in Europe, shall have full Liberty to manage their own Affairs themselves, or to commit them to the Management of whomsoever they please; nor shall they be obliged to employ any Interpreter or Broker, nor to pay them any Salary, unless they shall chuse to employ them. Moreover, Masters of Ships shall not be obliged, in loading or unloading their Ships, to make Use of those Persons who may be appointed by publick Authority for that Purpose, either at Bourdtaux or elsewhere, but it shall be en-

tirely free for them to load or unload their Ships by themselves, or to make Use of such Persons in loading or unloading the same, as they shall think lit, w ithout the Payment of any Reward to any other whomsoever; neither shall they be forced to unload into other Ships, or to receive into their own, any Merchandize whatever, or to wait for their Lading any longer than they please. And all the Subjects of the Most Christian King shall reciprocally have and enjoy the same Privileges and Liberties, in all the Dominions of His Britannick Majesty in Europe.

Article XIX.

The Ships of either Party being laden, sailing along the Coasts of the other, and being forced by Storm into the Havens or Ports, or making Land there in any other Manner whatever, shall not be obliged to unlade their Goods, or any Part thereof, or to pay any Duty, unless they, of their own Accord, unlade their Goods there, and sell some Part thereof. But it shall be lawful, Permission having been first obtained from those who have the Direction of Maritime Affairs, to unlade and sell a small Part of their Cargo, merely for the End of purchasing Necessaries, either for victualling or refitting the Ship; and in that Case the whole Lading shall not be subject to pay the Duties, but that small Part only which shall have been taken out and sold.

Article XX.

It shall be lawful for all the Subjects of the King of Great Britain, and of the Most Christian King, to sail with their Ships, with perfect Security and Liberty, no Distinction being made who are the Proprietors of the Merchandizes laden thereon, from any Port whatever, to the Countries which are now or shall be hereafter at War with the King of Great Britain, or the Most Christian King. It shall likewise be lawful for the aforesaid Subjects to sail and traffick with their Ships and Merchandizes, with the same Liberty and Security, from the Countries, Ports, and Places of those who are Enemies of both, or of either Party, without any Opposition or Disturbance whatsoever, and to pass directly not only from the Places of the Enemy aforementioned to Neutral Places, but also from one Place belonging to an Enemy to another Place belonging to an Enemy, whether they be under the Jurisdiction of the 6ame or of several Princes. And as it has been stipulated,

Article XXI.

This Liberty of Navigation and Commerce shall extend to all Kinds of Merchandizes, excepting those only which are specified in the following Article, and which are described under the Name of Contraband.

Article XXII.

Under this Name of Contraband, or prohibited Goods, shall be comprehended Arms, Cannon, Har-quebusses. Mortars, Petards, Bombs, Grenades, Sau-cisscs, Carcasses, Carriages for Cannon, Musket-Rests, Bandoleers, Gunpowder, Match, Saltpetre, Ball, Pikes, Swords, Head-Pieces, Helmets, Cuirasses, Halberds, Javelins, Holsters, Belts, Horses and Harness, and all other like Kinds of Arms and warlike Implements fit for the Use of Troops.

Article XXIII.

These Merchandizes which follow shall not be reckoned among contraband Goods, that is to say, all Sorts of Cloth, and all other Manufactures of Wool, Flax, Silk, Cotton, or any other Materials, all Kinds of Wearing Apparel, together with the Articles of which they are usually made, Gold, Silver, coined or uncoined, 'Tin, Iron, Lead, Copper, Brass, Coals, as also Wheat and Barley, and any other Kind of Com and Pulse, Tobacco, and all Kinds of Spices, salted and smoaked Flesh, salted Fish, Cheese and Butter, Beer, Oil, Wines, Sugar, all Sorts of Salt, and of Provisions which serve for Sustenance and Food to Mankind; also all Kinds of Cotton, Cordage, Cables, Sails, Sailcloth, Hemp, Tallow, Pitch, Tar, and Rosin, Anchors, and any Parts of Anchors, Ship-Masts, Planks, Timber of all Kinds of Trees, and all other Things proper either for building or repairing Ships. Nor shall any other Goods whatever, which have not been worked into the Form of any Instrument, or Furniture for warlike Use, by Land or by Sea, be reputed Contraband, much less such as have been already wrought and made up for any other Purpose. All which Things shall be deemed Goods not contraband, as likewise all others which are not comprehended and particularly described in the preceding Article; so that they may be freely carried by the Subjects of both Kingdoms, even to Places belonging to an Enemy, excepting only such Places as are besieged, blocked up, or invested.

Article XXIV.

To the End that all Manner of Dissensions and Quarrels may be avoided and prevented, on both Sides, it is agreed, that in case either of their Majesties should be engaged in War, the Ship3 and Vessels belonging to the Subjects of the other shall be furnished with Sea-Letters or Passports, expressing the Name, Property, and Bulk of the Ship, as also the Name and Place of Abode of the Master or Commander of the said Ship, that it may appear thereby that the Ship really and truly belongs to the Subjects of One of the Princes; which Passports shall be made out and granted, according to the Form annexed to
