Mr. Beaufoy, according to Order, reported from the Report on Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- Treaty with ferred to consider of so much of His Majesty’s Most France-Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 23d Day of January last, as relates to the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce between His Majesty and the Most Christian King, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the (Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient. That all Articles of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, which are not specified in the Sixth Article of the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce between His Britannick Majesty and the Most Chris-

tian King, signed at Versailles the afith of September 1786, shall be imported into this Kingdom on Payment of Duties as low as any which shall be payable

on

&7 Geo. Ill* rp° Febru385

on the Importation of the like Articles from any other European Nation.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be ex-

Eidient, That Wines, of the Produce of the European ominions of the French King, imported directly into this Kingdom, shall, in no Case, pay any higher Duties than the Wines of Portugal now pay.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient,. That the Duty hereafter to be paid upon Vinegar, of the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Thirty-two Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Ten Pence upon every Ton, containing Two hundred and Fifty-two Gallons.

Resohced, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty hereafter to be paid upon Brandy, of the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall be at a Rate not exceeding Seven Shillings for every Gallon.

Resolved That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That Oil of Olives, coming directly from the European Dominions of the French King, shall, for the future, pay rto higher Duties on the Importation thereof into this Kingdom, than are now paid for the same from the most favoured Nation.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon Beer, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Thirty Pounds pci' Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty hereafter to be paid for all CabinetWork, and Turnery, and for all Instruments of Music, being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom* shall be at the Rate of Ten Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resoloed, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty hereafter to be paid for all Articles composed of Iron and Steel, separately, or mixed, or worked, or mounted with other Substances, such Articles being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King and not exceeding in their Value Fifty Shillings by the Hundredweight, imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty hereafter to be paid for all Articles composed of Iron or Steel, separately, or mixed, or worked, or mounted with other Substances, and exceeding in their Value Fifty Shillings by the Hundred Weight; and for all Buttons, Buckles, Knives, or Scissars, and for all other Articles of Hardware of* Cutlery, and for all Articles composed of Copper and Brass, separately, or mixed, or worked, or mounted with other Substances,. such Articles being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Ten Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon all Sorts of Cottons and Woollens, whether knit or woven, including Hosiery, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported jinto this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Twelve Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon all Linens made of Flax or Hemp, of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported into this Kingdom, shall be no higher than the Duty which Linens of the Manufacture of . Vo 1. 49.

Holland or Flanders, imported into this Kingdom, now Report pay. . Treal>M

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient* That the Duty hereafter to be paid for Cambricks and Law'ns, being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall be, for every Demi-piece of Cambrick, and for every Demi-piece of Lawn, not exceeding Seven Yards and Three Quarters of a Yard English Measure in Length, and not being above the Value of Fifty Shillings respectively, Five Shillings, and so in Proportion for any greater Length; and that the Duty for any Cambrick, imported in Pieces exceeding Seven Eighths of a Yard, English Measure, in Breadth* and for any Lawn imported in Pieces exceeding One Yard and a Quarter, English Measure, in Breadth, and being above the Value of Fifty Shillings respectively, shall be Ten Pounds per Centum ai Valorem.

Resolved, That. it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon all Saddlery, of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Fifteen Pounds per Centum ad Valorem. t

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon Gauzes of all Sorts, of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Ten Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon the Importation into this Kingdom of Millinery made up of Muslin, Lawn, Cambrick, or Gauze, of any Kind, or of any other Article specified in the Sixth Article of the said Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King shall be at the Rate of Twelve Pounds per Centum hdValorem; and that, if any Articles not so specified, and which may be legally imported into this Kingdom, shall be used in such Millinery, such Articles shall pay Duties as if separately imported into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon all Porcelain, Earthen Ware, and Pottery, of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Twelve Pounds per Centum ad Valorem.

Resolved, That it appears td this Committee to be expedient, That the Duty of Customs hereafter to be paid upon all Plate Glass and Glass Ware of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall be at the Rate of Tw elve Pounds per Centum ad Valoi'em.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That all Cottons and Linens stained or printed, being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall pay, over and above the Duty of Customs to be paid on the Importation thereof, a further Duty sufficient to countervail the Internal Duty actually payable on the like Goods manufactured in Great Britain.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee to be expedient, That all Plate Glass and Glass Ware, being of the Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, imported into this Kingdom, shall pay, over and above the Duty of Customs to be paid on the Importation thereof, a further Duty sufficient to countervail the Internal Duties actually payable on the like Goods manufactured in Great Britain, and also the Import Duties charged on the Raw Materials used therein.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro* That the said Resolutions be now read a Second Time;

The Amendments following were proposed to be made to the Question; viz.

To leave out the Word " now," and at the End of the Question to add the Words " upon this Day Sevennight"

And the Question being put, That the Word " now " stand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

Mr. John James -milton,

Mr. Rose:

Mr. St. John,

Mr. Minchin: J

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Ordered, That the said Resolutions be now read a Second Time.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said Resolution be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Third Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

And the Question being proposed. That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

The House was moved, That an Act made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of King Eduard the Third, intituled, M The Warranty of Packing of " Wooll shall be put out An Inquest shall be " Medietate Lingua where an Alien is Party," might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, That an Act made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of King Rickard the Second, intituled, " A Confirmation of Part of the Stat. u of 28 Edw. III. C. 13. touching Merchant Strangers," might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, That certain Rules, Orders, Directions, and Allowances, for the Advancement of Trade and Encouragement of the Merchant, as also for the regulating as well of the Merchants in making of due Entries and just Payments of their Customs, as of the Officers in all the Ports of this Kingdom, in the faithful Discharge of their Duty, annexed to an Act made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, " A Subsidy granted to the King " of Tonnage and Poundage, and other Sums of Money, payable upon Merchandize exported and " imported," might be read.

And the same were read accordingly.

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the unfortunate Debtors in the King's Debton Bench Prison, in Behalf of themselves, and several P«htwnj. Thousands Prisoners and Fugitives for Debt, either pining in Gaols at Home, or wandering in Exile Abroad: And also,

A Petition of the Prisoners confined in Hull Gaol;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Complaining of their Distress, and praying Relief.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table;

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Kymston reported from the Committee, to Shrewsbury whom the Petition of several Trustees appointed by Roads Ped* an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-ninth don reported. Y^ar of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for repairing and " widening the Roads from the Town of Shrewsbury " to Preston Brockhurst, to Shawbury, and to Shrey " Hill, in the County of Salop," and also, of several Persons who have advanced considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the Tolls thereof, and also, of several Gentlemen, Traders, and Farmers, residing near and frequently Travelling the said Roads, and the several other Roads herein after mentioned, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read:

Then an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending an Act of the Sixth of His said Majesty, for repairing and widening the Stone Bridge in the Town of Shrewsbury, and for other Purposes, was also read; by which it appeared, that an Addition of Twenty-one Years was added to the Term of the said Act of the Twenty-ninth Year of His late Majesty, upon certain Conditions therein mentioned: And

William Smith, Esquire, being examined, said, That great Progress has been made in the Execution of the said first-mentioned Act, for which Purpose several considerable Sums of Money have been borrowed, and the Sum of 1.2,900 now remains due, which . 51 cannot

Trecastle A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders Itoad tv of the County of Carmarthen, and also of the several tition. Trustees and Creditors of the several Turnpike Roads in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing and widening several Roads in the County of Brecon, a certain Road leading from the Village of Trecastle, in the County of Brecon, to the Confines of the County of Carmarthen, leading to the Village of Talsarn, in the said County of Carmarthen, is the First Road mentioned in the said Act as necessary to be widened and repaired; and that by another Act, passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for continuing the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Road from the Fourteen Mile Stone, in the Parish of to Taoarn Spite,

in the County of Carmarthen, and for repairing, amending, and keeping in Repair, several other Roads in the said County, the Road leading from the Village of Talsarn, in the County of Carmarthen, to the Borders of the County of Brecon, is the Road lead-- ing to the Village of Trecastle, in the said County of

Brecon, as mentioned and described; and that, in Consequence of the stud Two Acts, the Petitioners were induced to borrow large Sums of Money, for the Purpose of widening and repairing the Road above described, and have, at a very considerable Expence, made, and nearly compleated, the said Road, from the Borders of the County of Brecon, through the Village of Talsarn, to the Town of Llandilo, in the County of Carmarthen, which Road will be altogether useless, and the whole Expence and Trouble the Petitioners have been put to entirely thrown away, unless the Road described in the first-mentioned Act from the Village of Trecastle, in the County of Brecon, to the Confines of the County of Carmarthen, on the Roild leading to Talsarn, in the said County, be

amended, widened, and repaired, agreeable to the Intention of the said Act; and representing to the House, That the said last mentioned Road is not only founderous, ruinous, and out of Repair, and left in the Situation it was before the said Act passed, and the Trustees of the said Act have not only neglected and refused to repair the same, but still refuse, and do not mean to do it: And the Petitioners observing Advertisements in the Hereford and Gloucester Journals in the Month of August last, that Application would be made to enlarge the Terms and Powers of an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening several Roads in the County of Brecon, the Petitioners therefore pray,

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, assuring His Majesty that we have taken into our most serious Consideration the Provisions contained in the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, concluded between His Majesty and the Most Christian King; and that we beg Leave to approach

sincere and grateful Acknowledgments for this additional Proof of His Majesty’s constant Attention to the Welfare and Happiness of His Subjects:

That we shall proceed with all proper Expedition in taking such Steps as may be necessary for giving Effect to a System so well calculated to promote a beneficial Intercourse between Great Britain and France, and to give additional Permanence to the Blessings of Peace:

That it is our firm Persuasion, that we cannot more effectually consult the General Interests of our Country, and the Glory of His Majesty’s Reign, than by concurring in a Measure which tends to the Extension of Trade and the Encouragement of Industry and Manufacture, the genuine Sources of National Wealth, and the surest Foundation of the Prosperity and Happiness of His Majesty’s Dominions.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty, upon the said Resolution.

A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Royal Assent Usher of the Black Rod: to Bills.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed' upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to'hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore mentioned, had been, at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several public Bills and One private Bill therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Cantei'bury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: And that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Osborne, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as follow eth; viz.

An Act to render more effectual the Laws now in being for suppressing unlawful Lotteries.

An Act for the Regulation of His Majesty’s Marine Forces while on Shore.

An Act to enable His Majesty to establish a Court of Criminal Judicature on the Eastern Coast of New South Wales, and the Parts adjacent.

An Act for naturalizing George Wackerbarth.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,-

Dumfries A Petition of the Provost, Baillies, Dean of Guild, Two Pennies Treasurer, and Common Council of the Borough of ScotsPetition. Dumfries, for themselves, and as representing the Community of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting an Act passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for continuing and rendering more " effectual an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of his " late Majesty King George the Second, intituled,

" An Act for continuing an Act passed in the Third " Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George " the First, for laying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots,

" or One-sixth Part of a Penny Sterling on every " Pint of Ale or Beer that shall be vended or sold " within the Town of Dumfries, and Privileges " thereof, for paying the Debts of the said Town,

" and for building a Church, and making a Harbour " there; and for laying a Duty on the Tonnage of " Shipping, and a Duty on Goods imported arid u exported into and out of the Port of the said Town,

" for tire better repairing of the said Harbourand Setting forth, That the Yearly Amount of the said Duty upon Ale, Beer, and Porter, has considerably diminished for some Years past, and, though managed with the greatest Frugality, has been found inadequate to pay off the Debts for which it was granted, and although the Duties arising from Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes imported and exported from the said Port of Dumfries, and the Duties upon Tonnage granted to the said Town by the Act of the Tenth of George the Second, and continued by the Act of the Second Year of His present Majesty, have been solely applied for the Purposes of improving the said Harbour, and the Navigation of the River, and for preserving and maintaining the same, the said Duties have been insufficient for discharging the Debt incurred by the Town in making such Improvements and Repairs, and which must continue to be incurred in the Preservation thereof, and making other Improvements still necessary; and that by sundry useful and necessary Improvements in the public Schools of the said Town, and in building a new English School House, and purchasing Property for, and making sundry new Streets, and in building a new Flesh Market and Slaughtering Houses, and in purchasing Ground

for a House of Correction, and other public Works, the Debts of the said Town are considerably increased, and which the present Revenues of the Town are not sufficient to discharge: and that the Streets of the said Town arc ill paved, cleansed, and not sufficiently lighted, nor a proper M atch kept for preventing Disorders in the Night Time, and the Streets in some Places want widening for the more easy Passage of Carriages, and are often incumbered with Nuisances, which ought to be removed and prevented, but tha paving, cleansing, lighting, and widening the Streets, and removing and preventing Nuisances, and keeping Watchmen in the Town, will be attended with considerable Expence, which the ordinary Revenue of the Town cannot defray: And therefore praying.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing, for such further Period as to the House shall, seem proper, the Duty on Ale, Beer, and Porter, and the Duty on Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, and also the Duty on Tonnage granted by the Acts before-recited, and for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Streets, and widening the same where necessary, and keeping Watchmen in the Town; and for levying such a Tax upon the Inhabitants of the Town, by such Ways and Means as may be judged by the House to be reasonable and necessary for these Purposes.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it. shall appear to them, to the House:

Ancl it is referred to Sir James Johnstone, Sir Archibald Edmonstone, Scc.: And they are to meet To-

morrow Morning, ,at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of several Freeholders, Justices of the Peace, and Heritors of the County of Berwick, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the great Post Road between London and Edinburgh, leading from the Extremity of the Liberties of the Borough of Berzoick upon Tweed, by Ayton Bridge, and the new Bridge, over the Pees or Pass of Cock-burnspath, to Dunglas Bridge, on the Coniines of East Lothian, and also the Branches leading from Causeway and Preston Bridge to join the said Post Road at or near Cockburnspalh Tower, are, in many

Places, so deep and ruinous that Travellers cannot pass without great Inconvenience, and are in Danger of becoming altogether impassable; and that the Aids which already have been obtained from the public Bounty, and from private Contributions, have been found insufficient for the Purpose of making the said Road, and the same cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair by the Funds arising from the Laws now in Force, that Part of the Country being but thinly inhabited: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for erecting Turnpike Gates and Toll Houses on the said Road, and levying Tolls thereat, in order to establish a Fund to maintain and keep in Repair the said Road, and Bridges built and to be built thereon.

Mr. Secretary at War, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters, was committed; the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take into further Consideration so much of His Majesty’s Most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 23d Day of January last, as relates to simplifying the Public Accounts in the various Branches of the Revenue;

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Steele took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Steele reported from the Committee, That they had made a further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and that he was directed by the Committee to more, that they may have Leave to sit again.

A Petition of John Raban, of Hatton Street, in the Petition to Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, in the County of prevent Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That several Acts have been passed to ment of prevent Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals.

Coals sold by Wharf Measure within the Cities of London and Westminster, and County of Surrey, which

have given great Security to the Consumers thereof, but such Security is not given to those Consumers of Coals who buy the same by Ship or Pool Measure; and that the Petitioner has every Reason to believe, and much to offer in Proof, that Frauds of an enormous Magnitude have been, and still continue to be, committed in the Sale of Coals by Ship or Pool Measure, greatly to the Injury of the Consumers thereof, and particularly to the fair Trader, the unfair Practices complained of being committed after the Public Meters have discharged their Duty, and the Coals taken away from the Ships; and the Petitioner, flattering himself that such Frauds (if Provision was made) might be completely prevented in future, and conceiving the great Utility which the Inhabitants of this Metropolis would derive therefrom, is willing to promote and establish an Office, at his own Expence, for the Inspection of all Coals, Culm, Cinders, or Coke, sold as and for Pool Measure, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Counties of Middlesex, Surrey, and Kent, upon having an Allowance granted upon all Coals, Culm, Cinders, or Coke, sold in Manner aforesaid, to enable him to support the said Office and a sufficient Number of Persons under him; and Representing to the House,

That, as no Land Coal Meter is appointed for the several Wharfs extending along the River Thames, from the Parish of Saint Mary Rotherhithe to the farthest Limits of the Parish of Sain Mary Woolwich, the Inhabitants of that, and the adjacent Part of the County of Kent, are not so secured in the fair Admeasurement of their Coals as those of the Cities of London and Westminster, and County of Surrey are, the Want of which not only affords an Opportunity of committing Frauds and Abuses, upon the said Inhabitants, but will also tend to frustrate, if not defeat,

Petition A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses

gainst Port- of the Borough of Portsmouth, in the County of hfbtsPeti- amPtoni >n Common Hall assembled, the 19th Day of lion. February, in the Year of our Lord 1787, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application for Leave to bring in a Bill to establish a Court of Requests in the Island of Portsea, for the Recovery of Small Debts; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners Conceive, the Acts for establishing such Courts in general are of the most dangerous and alarming Tendency, being founded on Principles directly opposite to those of our happy Constitution, and not only deprive the Subject of the Benefit of the Common Law, but vest discretionary and arbitrary Powers in Persons too often interested in the Abuse of them; and the Petitioners are particularly apprehensive, that a Court of Requests in the Island of Portsea will be prejudicial to the Interests of the Inhabitants, will tend greatly to corrupt the Morals of the lower Order of People, introduce much Distress, Vexation, and Oppression, increase the Poors Rates, countenance improper Credit, and be liable to manifold Inconveniencies and Abuses; and that the Petitioners conceive, the Island of Portsea is locally unfit for the Introduction of a Court of Requests, on Account of the great Number of Artificers, Workmen, Labourers, Seamen, and others, employed in the public Service in the said Island, and of the Credit necessarily given by them to Government for their Wages, on the Receipt of which the Current Cash of the Island in a great Degree depends; for which Reasons, the Petitioners conceive, a Court of Requests cannot be established in the said Island

Vol. 42.

without the most alarming Inconvenience to the public Service of the Kingdom, and manifest Injustice and Distress to Individuals; and that the Petitioners apprehend there is the less Reason for introducing a Court of Requests into the said Island, because, a Court of Record is holden Weekly, before the Mayor and Aldermen of the said Borough of Ports, for the Recovery of all Debts within the said Borough, even from the highest down to the lowest Denomination, and the said Borough includes the Whole of the Town of Portsmouth, Portsmouth Common, Portsmouth Harbour,

His Majesty’s Dock Yard, Gun Wharf, Victualling Office, Custom House, Excise Office, and the Bulk of the Trading Part of the said Island: And therefore praying, That no such Bill may pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion was made, and a Question was proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to represent to His Majesty, That David Esquire, a Captain in His Majesty’s Navy, has not been included in the late Promotions to the Flag, on the Ground of his not having served in the War before such Promotions took Place.

That it appears however to this House, That the said Captain Brodie had, both in Person and by Letter, applied to the Board of Admiralty to be employed, but which Offers of Service were not accepted.

That this House cannot but consider such Offers to serve as equivalent to actual Service, inasmuch as it is not in the Power of any Officer to serve but under the Appointment of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty; and it would be contrary to Justice, that an Officer should suffer, owing to his not having served, when the Power of serving does not depend upon himself.

That it likewise appears to this House, That the said Captain David Brodie had, during the Time he was employed, distinguished himself as an active, zealous, and gallant Officer.

That in particular Captain David Brodie has been Sixty Years in the Royal Navy, was One of the Admiral’s Lieutenants at the taking of Porto Bello; bombarding Carthagena; taking of Chagre; taking of Boc-cachica; and in most of the Actions that happened in the West Indies during that War with the combined

Arms of France and Spain.

That Captain David Brodie was promoted to the Command of the Merlin, a Sloop of Ten Guns, and One hundred and Ten Men, in the Indies, and rendered the following Services to his Country:

1st. He sustained an Attack from a Fifty Gun Ship a considerable Time, in which he lost many Men. — Two other Ships coming in Sight, the Enemy left him — They afterwards proved to be Tw’o of our own.

2d. He took the Union, a French Privateer of superior Force.

3d. He took the Vainqueur, a French Privateer of superior Force.

4th. He took the Bacchus, a French Privateer of superior Force.

5th. He took the Saint Antonio, a Spanish Privateer.

6th. He took the Petit Guava, a French Privateer of equal Force.

7th. He took the Ferdinand, a French Privateer of superior Force, which he boarded. — She had Forty-two Men killed and wounded.

8th. He attacked Two Spanish Xebecks, that had taken the Blast and Achilles, Two of our Sloops of War, and after a desperate Engagement, they were obliged to retire, and never appeared more on those Seas. — Captain David Brodie derived peculiar Satisfaction from this Success, as he afterwards found they had been fitted out expressly to take him.

qth. He took Two French Ships of much superior Force, in which Action he was wounded in the Side, and lost his right Arm.

That, for these Services Captain Brodie was honoured with a Letter from the then Lords of the Admiralty.

Captain Brodie was made a Post Captain in March 1747, and commanded the Canterbury at. the taking of Port Louis, and the Attack of S' Jago-da Cuba. — He commanded the Stretford in the Engagement off the

That this House is therefore induced humbly tq beseech His Majesty, That His Majesty will be graciously pleased to confer some Mark of His Majesty’s Favour on the said David Brodie, Esquire, this House being convinced that such a Measure must be highly conducive to the Advantage of His Majesty’s Navy, by encouraging that Zeal and Gallantry of which there tire so many, Instances herein contained; whereas so honourable a Series of Services and Sufferings not meeting with regular Promotion, may tend to extinguish that Spirit of Emulation and Enterprize which has hitherto animated the British Navy, and characterized it in every Part of the Globe.

Note. — As the Order requires in the First Account " the Number of American Loyalists who receive " Allowances for Services performed, although they have lost no Property" — And in the Second " the Number of Persons who receive Annual Allowances in Consequence of the Loss of Professions " and Offices " — it is proper to observe that the Allowances w'ere not granted singly " on Account " of Services performed," or " of Offices or Professions lost," but were intended as Provisions for temporary Subsistence, having Reference to the general past and present Circumstances of the Party.

Mr. Rose accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read ini his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all and singular the Subsidies, Customs, Impositions, or Duties whatever (respecting the Revenues of Customs) payable to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, by virtue of any Act or Acts of Parliament now in Force, upon the Importation of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, into Great Britain, or upon the Exportation of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, from Great Britain, or upon any Goods,

Wares, or Merchandize, being brought or earned Coastwise, or from Port to Port within the same, and the several and respective Drawbacks allowed upon the Exportation of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, from Great Britain, or on any other Account whatever, respecting the Duties of Customs, and all and singular the Duties and Drawbacks of Excise, and other Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise . in England and Scotland, respectively, granted by any Act or Acts of Parliament now in Force, and also, thp additional Imposts or Duties charged upon the Product and Amount of the said several Duties of Customs and Excise, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid or allowed, except in all Cases relating to the recovering or allowing any Arrears thereof, which may remain unpaid, or to any Penalty or Forfeiture relating thereto respectively, and except the Duties upon Malt,

Mum, Cyder, or Perry, granted by an Act made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and also except the Rates or Duties payable for any Licence or Licences which the Commissioners of Excise in England and Scotland, or any or either of them, or the Collectors, Supervisors, or Officers of Excise, or any of them, are, by any Act or Acts of Parliament now in Force, authorized or impowered to grant; and that new Duties of Customs and Excise be granted in lieu of the said Duties which shall so cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Sixteen Shillings and One Penny Farthing be charged upon every One hundred Weight of Materials, or Metal, or other Preparations whatsoever, by what Name soever the same are, or may be, called or known, that shall be made Use of in Great Britain in the making of all other Window Glass (not being Spread Glass) whether flashed or otherwise manufactured, and commonly called or known either by the Name of Crown Glass, or of German Sheet Glass, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2358. Resolved, That It is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Four Shillings and One Farthing be charged upon every One hundred Weight of Materials, or Metal, or other Preparations whatsoever, by what Name soever the same are, or may be, called or known, that shall be made Use of in Great Britain in the making of Common Bottles (the same not being Phials) and of Vessels made Use of in Chymical Laboratories, and of Garden Glasses, and of all other Vessels, or Utensils, made of Common Bottle Metal, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2359* Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several Rates and Duties upon the Materials, or Metal, or other Preparations for making Glass, be paid by the Maker or Makers thereof respectively.

2360. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Penny Half-penny be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of Hides of what Kind soever, and of Calf Skins, Kips, Hog Skins, Dog Skins, and Seal Skins, which shall be tanned in Great Britain, and of Sheep Skins, and Lamb Skins,

which shall be tanned in Great Britain for Gloves and Bazils, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2361. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Four Pence be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of Goat Skins, which shall be tanned with Shotnack, or otherwise, in Great Britain, to resemble Spanish Leather, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2362. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of Sheep Skius, which shall be tanned for Roans (being after the Nature of Spanish Leather) within Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2363. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Thirty Pounds be charged upon every One hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all other Skins, and Parts and Pieces of Skins, which shall be tanned in Great Britain, not hereinbefore particularly charged, and so in Proportion for greater or lesser Numbers or Quantities.

2364. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several Rates and Duties for and upon all such Hides and Skins, and Parts and Pieces of Skins, tanned in Great Britain, be paid by the Tanners thereof respectively.

2365. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Shilling and Six Pence be charged upon all Hides of Horses, Mares, and Geldings, which shall be dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, for every such Hide, and so in Proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity or Number of such Hides.

2366. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Shillings be charged upon all Hides of Steers, Cows, or any other Hides, of what Kind soever (those of Horses, Mares, and Geldings excepted) which shall be so dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Britain, for every such Hide, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Number or Quantity.

2367. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Penny Half-penny be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of all Calf Skins, Kips, and Seal Skins, which shall be so dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2368. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Shillings be charged upon every Dozen of Slink Calf Skins, which shall be so dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, with the Hair on, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Number or Quantity.

2369. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Shilling be charged upon every Dozen of Slink Calf Skins, which shall be so dressed or tawed without Hair, and every Dozen of Dog Skins which shall be tawed as aforesaid, in Great Britain, and for every Dozen of Kid Skins which shall be tawed in Great Britain (except such Kid Skins as paid the full Duty on the Importation thereof) and so in Proportion for any- greater or lesser Number or Quantity.

2370. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of Buck and Doe Skins (except such as paid the full Duty on the Importation thereof) which shall be dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or be otherwise tawed as aforesaid, in Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2371. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings be charged upon every Dozen of Goat Skins and of Beaver Skins, which shall be so dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or be otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Number or Quantity.

2372. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Penny Farthing be charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of Sheep Skins and Lamb Skins, which shall be dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2373* Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Thirty Pounds be charged upon every One hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all other Skins, and Parts and Pieces of Skins, which shall be tawed in Great Britain (not hereinbefore particularly charged) and so in Proportion for greater or lesser Numbers or Quantities.

2374. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several Rates and Duties for, and upon, all Hides and Skins, and Parts and Pieces of Hides and Skins, which shall be dressed in Alum and Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, in Great Britain, be paid by such Persons who shall be the Tawers or Makers thereof into Leather respectively.

2373. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence bo charged upon every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise of all Hides and Skins, and of all Deer Skins, Goat Skins, and Beaver Skins, which shall be dressed in Oil, in Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of the Whole of the Duties be allowed upon all Linens, Stuffs, Fustians, Velvets, Velverets, Dimities, Figured Stuffs, Stuffs wholly made of Cotton Wool, wove in Great Britain, commonly called British Manufactory, Callicoes, and Muslins, which shall be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts.

2527. Resohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of the present Duties be allowed upon all Silks and Silk Handkerchiefs, which shall be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts.

2528. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Two Pence Farthing be allowed upon every Pound Weight, Avoirdupoise, of hard Cake Soap, or Ball Soap, which shall be made in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts.

2529. Resolved, That it is. the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of One Penny Three Farthings be allowed upon every Pound Weight, Avoirdupoise, of Soft Soap, which shall be made in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts.

2530. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Coni-i mittee, That a Drawback of Three Pence Farthing be allowed upon every Pound Weight, Avoirdupoise, of Starch, which shall be made in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts.

2531. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of all the present Duties be allowed upon all Tea which shall be exported to Ireland, or His Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in America.

2532. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Fourteen Pounds Seven Shillings be allowed upon every Ton of Foreign Wine, which shall be exported from Great Britain to any British Settlement in the East Indies, or to any British Colony or Plantation in America, as Merchandize, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2533. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Five Pounds Thirteen Shillings be allowed upon every Ton of Foreign Wine, which shall be exported from Great Britain, as Merchandize to any other Part or Place beyond the Seas, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2534. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Seven Shillings and Eight Pence be allowed upon every Pound Weight, Avoirdupoise, of Gold Thread, Gold Lace, or Gold Fringe, made of Plate Wire spun upon Silk, such Plate Wire being made of Gilt Wire, which shall be made in Great Britain, and exported as Merchandize to Foreign Parts, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

2536. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several and respective Duties of Customs and Excise, together with the several other Duties composing the Public Revenue, be consolidated and constituted into a Fund, to be issued and applied to such and the same Uses and Purposes as all and every the Duties and Revenues now composing the Sinking Fund, or all or any other of the said Duties or Revenues, are or may be issued and applied, in pursuance of the several and respective Acts of Parliament for granting and appropriating the same.

2537. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all such Sum and Sums of Money, as-shall remain in the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, which hath been reserved for the Payment of any Annuity or Annuities for Life or Lives, and which hath or have not been claimed for a certain Space of Time, be paid to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, to be placed to the Account of the Commissioners, appointed by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, for vesting certain Sums in Commissioners at the End of every Quarter of a Year, to be by them applied to the Reduction of the National Debt.

and Claims whatever against the and that

the Traders having agreed to accept the proposed Cession, the Indians, by some of their Head Men authorized for that Purpose, at a Meeting in February 1771, formally executed the necessary Deeds; and that Sir James Wright, Governor of the Province of Georgia, in which Province the Lands so ceded were situated, and the late John Stuart, Esquire, then Superintendent of Indian Affairs for the Southern District of America, disapproved of the Conduct of the said Traders, in accepting the said Cession, as being contrary not only to His Majesty’s Instructions, but to the several Provincial Laws, which strictly prohibit private Persons from making any Purchase of Lands from Indians; and that, in consequence of such Disapprobation, the Indiatu, persisting in their Resolution of ceding the Lands in Question, and being thereby released from their Debts, offered to make the Cession to Governor Wrightfor that Purpose, and named the Day for running the Lines, but be, declining the Offer, desired they would defer their Intentions, until His Majesty's Pleasure should be known thereupon; and that the ensuing Year Sir James , being

then in England, stated the several Matters above mentioned, in a Memorial to the Earl of Hillsborough, and proposed certain Measures, by which the Cession of the said Lands, if approved by His Majesty, might be the Means, not only of answering the proposed End of the Indians and the Traders, but of bringing in a Number of valuable Settlers, to the great Advantage of the Province, and, consequently, of the Mother Country; and that the said Memorial having been referred to the Consideration of the Lords of Trade, their Lordships, in a Representation, dated the 9th of November 1772, advised His Majesty to accept of the proposed Cession, for the intended Purpose of paying the Debts due to the Traders from the Indians, by the Sale of the Lands ceded, at the same Time proposing, that the Crown should not stand pledged, either to the Indians or the Traders, for the Payment of any Part of the Debts, that the Debts should be fairly liquidated, and confined to those contracted within certain Periods, and that all Monies arising from the Sale of the Lands 80 ceded should be placed in the Hands of a Receiver, to be appointed by the Governor, and, after Payment of the Debts so to be liquidated, together with the Expences of Survey, and Means of Protection to the Persons settling the same, be subject to such Payments, upon Warrants of the Governor, for the Service of the Province, as His Majesty should approve of and direct; and that, in Consequence of the above Representation, His Majesty was graciously pleased to give conformable Instructions to Sir Janies Wright, who arrived in Georgia, for the Purpose of putting them in Execution, in March 1773; and that it appearing the Creek Indians had a Claim upon the Lands proposed to be ceded by the Cherokees as aforesaid, alledging, that their Ancestors had heretofore conquered those Lands from that Nation, that the Cherokees had acknowledged that Right of Conquest, by abandoning the Possession to them, and which Possession they had uniformly held, and it also appearing that the Creeks, being considerably indebted to their Traders, were inclinable to join in the Cession, upon being released from their Debts, a Congress was appointed to be held at Augusta with both Nations,' in the Month of May following, for finally adjusting the Terms, and formally accepting the Cession, for the express Purpose upon which it was to be made, namely, the Discharge of the Debts due from the Cherokees and Creeks, to their respective Traders; and that a Congress was accordingly held at Augusta, in May 1773,. by Sir James Wright and the late Super-intendant on the Part of the Crown, at which a very considerable Number of the Head Men of both Nar tions attended, who, after having previously delibe-Vol. 42.

rated apon the Matter between themselves, joined iri a solemn and formal Cession of the Lands in Question to His Majesty, for the sole Purpose of paying the Debts due from their respective Nations to their Traders; and the Traders, or their Attornies, did, at the same Time, release and discharge their several Debtors of both Nations from all Debts, Claims, and Demands whatever: That it must be supposed, such considerable Debts being due from the Indians to their Traders, the latter must have been proportionably indebted to the Merchants who supplied them with Goods; this, in Fact, was the Case, and the Merchants were obliged to take Assignments from those Traders of their Claims and Demands, to be liquidated m Payment of their several Demands, and to give them full Discharges for their respective Debts; and that, after the Lands had been ceded as aforesaid, Steps were taken by Sir James Wright for surveying the said Lands, selling them in distinct Allotments, for protecting the Purchasers, settling the same, and, particularly, for adjusting and liquidating the Debts claimed as owing from the within certain

fixed Periods, agreeable to His Majesty’s lastructioits, and, in consequence of these necessary Measures, a Progress was made in the Liquidation of the Debts, and Certificates of the Sums allowed were given to the Claimants, when the-Disturbances and

particularly in Georgia, prevented any further Proceedings therein, and the Petitioners were, on their own Accounts, and those of their Correspondents, in-interested in those Claims, either liquidated, or to be liquidated, to a very' considerable Amount, and without any Dependence for Reimbursement, but on the Produce of the Lands so ceded; and that, prior to the unhappy Disputes in America, several Allotments of the said ceded Lands were sold, but, as they are given to understand, that the Charge of surveying, the raising and maintaining a Troop of Rangers, and other Expences (whether necessary or not the Petitioners will not take upon themselves to determine) have amounted to more than the Sums received, no Part of the Sums due to die Petitioners, or their Correspondents, upon such of their Claims as have been settled, liquidated, and certified as aforesaid, has ever been paid; and that, in the Month of May 1780, the Petitioners having Reason to presume that some Accommodation would soon take Place with the re* volted Colonies, did, on the 3d of that Month, by a Memorial to the Marquis of Lansdown, then Earl of Shelburne, one of His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, fully state their Situation, and the Manner in which the Lands in Question wrere bound to the Payment of the Debts for which Purpose they were ceded, and their Reliance that, in every Event of Ne-gociation which might happen, those Lands should be deemed as charged with, and made liable to, the Payment of those Debts, or that some other Mode of Payment might be adopted, to the Satisfaction of the Petitioners and the Parties interested; and that the Petitioners finding that, by the Articles of Peace concluded between the Commissioners, named by His Majesty and the United States of America, no Stipulation was made in Favour of the Petitioners, and that the Lands vested in Trust in the Crown, as before stated, were ceded to, and acknowledged to belong to, the said United States, without any Condition

whatever respecting them, did, on the 11th of February 1783, in a Memorial to the Right honourable Charles James For, then one of His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, briefly represent the Facts as they stood, and prayed, that, as it appeared

no Satisfaction had been obtained, or Attention

paid to their former Application, some Mode of

Payment might be adopted, or other Expedient proposed for their Relief, and that, taking die Merits of their Case into Consideration, he would be pleased to

lay

/I. 17 87 .

lay their humble Representation beifore His Majesty, for His gracious Pleasure thereon; and that the Definitive Treaty with the United States of America being signed, and, to the Petitioners Surprize, and great Disappointment, no Regard being paid therein to their repeated Representations, they, in the Month of May 1784, presented a Memorial to His Majesty in Council, stating the aforegoing Transactions, and praying, that, as they stood precluded from every Possibility of Satisfaction from the Produce of the Lands, His Majesty would be graciously pleased to direct some Mode of Satisfaction, or other Relief, adequate to the Discharge of their respective Claims upon the said Lands; which Memorial having been referred to the Lords of the Privy Council, when, after waiting near Twelve Months in a State of the most anxious Suspense, the Lord President, and other Lords present, were pleased to advise them to apply to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, the Petitioners did accordingly apply to the Commissioners of the Treasury, by . a Memorial, dated April last, stating the foregoing Facts, and praying for Relief; and that, after so many Months ineffectual Application to the Lords of the Treasury, the Petitioners have now no Resource left, but to throw themselves upon the Justice, Equity, and Humanity of the House, for Redress — Should it be urged that the Application they now make ought to have been brought forward at an earlier Period, considering the Time that hath elapsed since the Conclusion of the Peace of Paris, they hope it will appear, that as they gave timely Information to His Majesty’s Ministers of the Condition on which the Lands ceded were vested in the Crown, they might have had their Claims satisfied out of the same, had it been thought expedient to make that a Stipulation when the Cession was made to the United States of; and they have also, since they found that their former Representations were not attended with that Success they had so much Reason to hope for and expect, lost no Time in making what they deemed the proper Application to obtain Redress in some other Mode, but those Applications having all failed, their only Hope is, that the House, taking the Hardships of their Case, and the singular unhappy and helpless Situation in which they stand, into Consideration, will, with their accustomed Liberality and Justice, afford them that Relief, which they,' in their great Distress, pray for, and to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

... toe

27 Geo. III.

the Bill for confirming the Purchase of a House situate in Little Chelsen, to be used as an additional Workhouse for the Poor of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, within the Liberty of the City of Westminster; and Setting forth, That the Inhabitants of the said Parish have, for some Time past, been much dissatisfied with the Conduct of the Select Vestry, conceiving themselves to be materially aggrieved by Expences unnecessarily incurred iu Buildings, new Purchases, and fresh Establishments, relative to the Ilegulation and Support of the Poor of the said Parish; and that, at a General Meeting of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, held by Public Advertisement, it was unanimously resolved, that the Rate assessed for the Relief of the Poor was oppressive, and that proper Measures should be taken to prevent any unnecessary Expenditure in the Money raised for the Poor of the said Parish; and that at such General Meeting a Committee of the Inhabitants was appointed, and the Petitioners compose that Committee, and, by virtue of such Appointment, have caused an Appeal to be preferred, agreeable to the Directions of an Act of the Twenty-sixth of the late King, to the General Quarter Sessions for the City and liberty of -minster, against the Accounts of the Poor of the said Parish, which Appeal will be heard before the Magistrates in Sessions assembled in the Beginning of April next, and the Purchase Money of the said House and Premisses at Little Chelsea is a material Objection in the said Appeal, the same being, in the Conception of tire Petitioners, an unnecessary and imprudent Expenditure of the Money raised for the Poor; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will not only prove an ex post facto Law, but will frustrate the judicial Proceedings of the Courts below; and, the Petitioners are satisfied that an additional Workhouse is quite unnecessary, and that the Appointment of one so remote from the Parish will prove greatly expensive, burthensome, Oppressive, and injurious, to the said Parishioners, as a new Household, with additional Masters, Agents, and Servants, of every Denomination, must be appointed, whereas, for a much less Sum than the Money laid out in the Purchase of the said Premisses, and the altering and repairing the same, the old Workhouse in Mount Street might have been made sufficiently commodious for the Reception of all the Poor of the said Parish; and that the Petitioners conceive that the said Bill is irregular, the same having l>een brought in upon the Petition of some of the Vestrymen only, without the Concurrence and joint Approbation of the Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, without whose Consent and Approbation no Money raised for the Poor should be expended, and that the said Bill is defective, for, if any Purchases were really necessary, the Conveyances thereof should have been to the Rector, Churchwardens, and Overseers of the Poor, of the said Parish for the Time being, and not to the Rector and Churchwardens only, in their private Capacities: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, inasmuch as it tends to stay the Proceedings of an inferior Court (pendente Lite) and to indemnify Persons who have acted without Authority, and in direct Violation of the Rights and Interests of the said Parish; and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves or Counsel against the said Bill, and have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

That, notwithstanding the partial and erroneous Statement in the said Petition, and also the Foundation and Grounds of establishing the Dock Company, as a Corporate Body, in Manner as in the Act of the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty is mentioned, which arc artfully suppressed, the Petitioners apprehend, and are advised, that the Rights and Interests of the Dock Company, as a Corporate Body, given and granted to them by the said Act, which were intended to be permanent, cannot be altered or taken away in Manner as prayed by the above-mentioned Petition, without annulling the Faith of Parliament, and totally destroying the Property of the Subscribers to the Undertaking, injuring the Revenue, and entirely defeating the original Designs of the Legislature, in promoting and compleating the expensive Works of the said Company; and that the making of a Dock or Quay at the said Port of Kingston upon Hull had been in the Contemplation' of Government many Years before the Establishment of the Dock Company as a Corporate Body, and the Inhabitants of the said Town of Hull, during such Time, were adverse to the Establishment of a legal Quay, and divers Disagreements took Place, between the Commissioners of the Customs and the said Town, concerning the same, which continued from Time to Time, down to the Year 1772, owing to the irregular Manner of conducting the Business relating to the Revenues, for Want of a legal Quay, contrary to the Practice of every other Port; and that, in the Year 1772, the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs being determined to have a legal Quay at the said Port of Hull (the same being of great Importance to His Majesty’s Revenues) or at some other Place adjoining the River Humber, signified to the then Collector and Comptroller of the Customs there, that, unless the said Town of Hull would co-operate with the said Board of Customs in the Establishment of a legal. Quay, the said Commissioners would carry their Resolutions into Execution, and establish a legal Quay at sotne other Place connected with the River Humber; and that the Merchants of Gainsborough having applied for the Establishment of a legal Quay at Gainsborough, and the Memorial then presented for that Purpose being very strongly supported by Persons interested therein, in order to prevent such a Step as threatened by the said Commissioners being taken, so prejudicial to the Port of Hull, and to the Trade thereof, and to

Yol. 42.

1773, and which w’ere communicated to the said'

Mr. Hills being examined, said, That several of the Regulations established by the Two first-mentioned Acts have been found very beneficial; and that it will be for the Convenience and Good of the Public, if the said Act of King George the Second, so far as the same relates to the Trade and Business of Pawnbrokers, and the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty, are repealed, and the necessary Powers, Provisions, and Regulations contained therein, together with such Alterations, Amendments, and Additions, as shall be deemed necessary or expedient, are comprized in One Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Trade and Business of Pawnbrokers:

And that Mr. Alderman Newnham and Mr. Alderman Watson do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Baker’s Com- A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants

p«iy Peti- of the Company of Bakers, of the City of London, was ,on‘ presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That

the Petitioners, with their Brethren of the Commonalty, are an ancient Corporation, instituted by Royal Charter, for the Purposes of supervising and teaching, by Ap-. prenticeships, and according to the Custom of the City of London, the Art and Trade of making and baking Bread for public Sale, and for regulating the Makers and Sellers thereof, within the City and Liberties of London, and certain Districts adjoining thereto; and that, by the late Extension of the Streets and Buildings of the said Metropolis, and by some Alterations in the Trade itself, Doubts have arisen whether the Powers and Provisions contained in their Charters, and their Bye Laws founded thereon, are now adequate to the Occasions of the Trade, or compatible with certain Regulations contained in an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the due making of " Bread, and to regulate the Price and Assize thereof,

" and to punish Persons who shall adulterate Meal,

" Flour, or BreadAnd therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaining the Powers and Limits of the Petitioners Jurisdiction, for preventing any undue Exercise of the Trade or Business of a Baker, and to amend so much of the said Act as relates to the Charters and Bye Laws of the said Company, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

louder Road Mr. George Douglas reported from the Committee Petition re- to whom the Petition of the several Persons thereunto ported. subscribing, Owners of Lands adjoining or near to the Road thereunder mentioned, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for repairing the Road from " the Burgh of Lauder, in the Shire of Berwick, to and " through Kelso, in the Shire of Roxburgh, to the " Marchburn," was read; whereby it appeared, That certain Trustees were appointed for carrying the said Act into Execution.

Then a Member present informed your Committee,

That the said Trustees have, in making and repairing the said Road, incurred a Debt of £. 3,900 Sterling, which was borrowed upon the- Personal Credit of the said Trustees, and, together with the Produce of the Tolls, has been expended in the Execution of the said Act — That the said Money cannot be repaid, and the said Road effectually made and kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act be enlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Road from the Burgh of Lauder, in the Shire of Berwick to and through Kelso, in the Shire of Roxburgh, to the Marchburn: And that Mr. George Douglas and Sir Robert Lawrie do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Calicoe Printers, Artists, Designers of Drawings, Engravers, and other Proprietors of original Patterns for printing Linens, Cottons, Callicoes, and Muslins, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners and others have, with great Industry and Expence, severally invented, designed, or engraved, divers Sets of new and original Patterns for printing Linens, Callicoes, and Muslins, in Hopes to have reaped the Benefit of such their own Labours, and the Credit thereof; but divers Callicoe Printers, and other Persons, to save themselves the Expence of original Designs, have of late too frequently taken the Liberty of copying, printing, and publishing, great Quantities of base and mean Copies and Imitations thereof, to the great Detriment of the Petitioners and other Artists, and to the Discouragement of the said Arts and Manufacture: And therefore praying, That I^eave may be given to bring in a Bill for preventing such Frauds and Abuses for the future, and for securing the Properties of the Petitioners for a limited Time, in the same Manner, as the Laws now in being have preserved the Properties of Authors of Books, and the Inventors and Engravers of Historical and other Prints, or in such other Manner as by the House shall be thought fit.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Peirce being examined, said, That the Town of Margate hath, for Time immemorial, had a Pier and Harbour, very convenient for the exporting and importing of Corn and other Merchandize, and for the Preservation of Shipping; and that the Safety of the Town very much depends upon the Maintenance of the said Pier, which in its present State requires either an immediate and thorough Repair of the present Pier Head, which from the Nature of its

Construction

540 16° Martii. . 1787*

Construction (being Timber-built) would be liable to frequent Accidents and Expences, or the Erection of a new Stone Head; and that it is conceived the latter, although attended with a greater Expence in the First Instance, will be the most eligible.

Then an Act passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act to enable the Pier Wardens of the Town of Margate, in the County of Kent, more effectually to recover the ancient and accustomed Droits, for the " Support and Maintenance of the said Pier," was read: And,

The Witness informed your Committee, That the said Act does not contain Powers sufficient for ascertaining and recovering the Harbour Droits.

And he further said, That the Town of Margate, by Reason of the great Resort of Persons for the Benefit of Sea Bathing, hath of late Years very much increased in the Extent of Buildings and Number of Inhabitants, and that the Trade thereof hath proportionally increased; by Means whereof the Streets, Lanes, and other Passages, which are very ill-paved and incommodious, are frequently very difficult of Passage; and that it would be very convenient to the Inhabitants, and to all Persons resorting to the said Town, if the said Streets, Lanes, and other Places, were properly paved, cleansed, lighted, and watched.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend and render more effectual an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty King George the First, for the Support and Maintenance of the Pier of Margate, in the County of Kent; for building a new Stone Pier; and, for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the said Town, and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein: And that Mr. Charles Robinson, Mr. Marsham, Mr. Hollywood, and Mr. Parry, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Thomas Beach, Nash, George Attnrni««f

Rhodes, and William Windale, the Four Attornies of l-ord Mayor* the Lord Mayor’s Court of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That by an Act passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Certificates to be taken out by Solicitors, Attornies, and others practising in certain Courts of Justice in Great Britain, and certain other Duties with respect to Warrants, Mandates, and Authorities, to be entered or filed of Record, as therein mentioned, the Petitioners are charged with a Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence, for a Retainer on every Action entered, and every Bail filed, in the said Court, over and above all former Duties payable thereon, which Duties they are, by the said Act, restrained from charging to their Clients; and that the Petitioners Charge for every Action is no more than Five Shillings and Four Pence, whereout they pay Duty, by former Acts of Parliament, Two Shillings and Six Pence, and the Duty imposed by this Act, Two Shillings and Six Penc^, which leaves a Profit of only Four Pence; and that the Petitioners are entitled to charge, for every Appearance and Common Bail, Six Shillings only, and they pay to the Clerk of the Bails, for every Common Bail, Three Shillings and Six Pence, and the new Duty being Two Shillings and Six Pence, the Petitioners receive no Profit whatsoever from the Appearance and Bail; and that the Causes in the said Court, in which further Proceedings are had, are very few, in Proportion to the Number of Actions and Appearances entered, and the Petitioners being obliged to be admitted Attornies of the Superior Courts, are subject to the Payment of all other Duties imposed on them by the said Act, and are admitted in the Lord Mayor's Court by Purchase for a very large Consideration: And therefore praying, That so much of the said Act as respects the Duties thereby imposed on the Practisers in the said Lord Mayor’s Court, may be repealed, or such other Relief granted, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Milford Road A Petition of several Persons, who lately acted* Pet‘tWD' as Trustees for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for " amending and widening the Road from a Place " near the Village of Mijfrrd, through Haslemere, to " the Portstnouth Road, between Lippock and Rake, " in the several Counties of Surrey, Sussex, and ampton," and of other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That during the Continuance of the said Act the Trustees appointed under the same proceeded in the Execution thereof, and large Sums of Money were borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls, which still remain unpaid; and that the Money ao owing, together with the Tolls collected upon the said Road, have been applied according to the Directions of the said Act, and great Progress hath been made in repairing and widening the said Road; and that the Term of the said Act hath been suffered to elapse without any Application being made to Parliament for enlarging thereof, by Reason that the Whole of the Monies borrowed, and all the Monies which from Time to Time, during the Continuance of the said Act, arose from the Tolls of the said Road, were applied towards, and totally exhausted in, the Reparation of the Road, and in the Salaries of the Treasurer, and Clerk, Surveyor, and Gate-keeper, appointed by the said Trust, and no Subscription could at that Time be raised for defraying the Expences of a fresh Act; and that several of the Petitioners have agreed to subscribe divers Sums of Money, for the Purpose of obtaining an Act for repairing so much of the said Road as leads from the said Place, near the Village of Milford, through Haslemere, to a Place within a Mile from Haslemere aforesaid, towards the South, where now stands the Forty-third Mile Stone from London, near Famhurst Lane, in the said County of Surrey, to the End that such Part of the said Road may be effectually repaired, and that the Money borrowed under the said former Act may (after paying the present Subscription, and the Interest thereof) be liquidated; and that those Parts of the said Road which lie between the Forty-third Mile Stone, near Famhurst Lane aforesaid, and the said Place between Lippock and Rake, are wholly destitute of Traffic, and afforded, during the Continuance of the said Act, no Benefit, by Tolls Vo l. 42.
