A Petition of the Planters, Merchants, Public Of- West Florid* fleers, and other late Proprietors of the Province of Planters P«-West Florida, being offered to be presented to the tmon-House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer^ by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That, in consequence of His Majesty’s Proclamation of 1763, the Petitioners emigrated to the Province of West Florida, and, after incurring every Danger, Difficulty, and Expence incident to first Settlers, cultivated Plantations, and formed Commercial Arrangements, which, in a few Years, arrived at a Degree of Prosperity beyond their Expectations, and

55$ i 6° Martii../f. 1787.

such as had never been experienced, in so short a Period, by any American Colony and that, at the Commencement of the late unfortunate American War, the Petitioners were solicited by Congress to join in their Confederacy, and declare the Province of West Florida an independent State, but this Solicitation was treated with Contempt, and the Province steadily persevered in Loyalty to His Majesty and Attachment to the Mother Country; and that, in consequence of this Refusal, the Congress fitted out a Squadron, under the Command of Commodore Hfor the Purpose of attacking Pensacola, but, despairing of Success from the Information he received of the Loyalty and Unanimity of the Province, he altered his Destination, and took and plundered the Island of New Providence; and that a Detachment of the Rebel Army, by the River Ohio, made a Descent on West Florida, and plundered and burnt several Rlantations, and seized Ships and other valuable Property on the River Mississippi, but were soon after attacked and driven into the Dominions of Spain by the loyal Inhabitants, who kept Possession of the Western Parts of the Province till they were relieved by a Detachment of His Majesty's Troops; and that the Inhabitants of Pensacola raised a considerable Sum of Money, by voluntary Subscriptions, for erecting Redoubts, and formed themselves into Volunteer Companies for their Defence, and the Inhabitants of Mobile made a sudden Expedition to Sea, attacked and defeated some Rebel Privateers, recovered a valuable Property, and restored it to the Owners, without any Expence; and that many loyal Inhabitants joined and did Duty with His Majesty’s Troops, while others formed themselves into Provincial Corps, and were employed upon the most dangerous Services, till the Reduction of the Province; and that, in order to make a Diversion when Pensacola was attacked, the Inhabitants of the District of Natchez laid Siege to Fort Pand obliged the Spanish Garrison to surrender as Prisoners of War; and that some of the Petitioners, Refugees from the States, who, in Obedience to His Majesty’s Proclamation, took Protection in West Florida, and contributed to its Defence, now find themselves excluded from that temporary Support and Compensation for Losses which was granted to many of their Fellow-sufferers who retired to Great Britain, and enjoyed comfortable Pensions in Peace and Security during the Whole of the War; and that some of the Petitioners had their Plantations plundered and burnt by the Rebels when they invaded the Province in the Year 1778, others had their Properties laid Waste, and large Stocks of Cattle destroyed, by the Rebel Indians and Spaniards, during the Operations of the War, and some of the Petitioners had their Houses burnt by Order of the Officers commanding in Forts, to prevent their being used by the Enemy as Covers for erecting Batteries, and others had their Property taken in the Forts, and condemned by the Spaniards, for having contributed to the public Defence, and some of the Petitioners lost valuable Tracts of Land acquired by Purchase, Mandamus, and other 'Pities, upon which they had laid out considerable Sums of Money in Expences necessary towards the forming of Plantations; and that Three-fourths of I Vest Florida has been ceded to the States of America, and no Stipulation made in Favour of the Property of its loyal Inhabitants, and the Remainder of the Province has been ceded to Spain, but under Stipulations which have proved totally ineffectual; and that the Spaniards considered the Time allowed by the Treaty for the Disposal of Property as a Period of Prescription, at the Expiration of which the Inhabitants must either remain Subjects of Spain, or suffer their Properties to become forfeited and extinct; the Petitioners are therefore returned to Great Britain, the Spaniards and Americans are in Possession of their Property, and not 7

a single Plantation has been sold in the Province; and that Commissioners have been appointed to enquire into the Losses sustained by the Proprietors of East Florida, whose Possessions were cedetl as a Price of Peace to the Kingdom of Spain, and the Property of the Petitioners was also ceded to and America, to purchase Peace and Security for the Empire at large, whereby many are reduced from affluent to indigent Circumstances, and some are in Want of immediate Support; and that the Petitioners conceive there is not the smallest Difference between their Case and that of the Inhabitants of East Florida, which should induce the House to compensate the Losses of the one, and refuse Compensation to the other; both Provinces have been ceded to the Enemy, to procure Peace for the rest of the Empire; both remained equally attached to the British Government during the War; it was indeed the Fate of the Petitioners to experience greater Calamities, on Account of their Attachment to the Mother Country, and also to make greater Exertions for their own Defence, and to be exposed to more Hardships and Dangers in the common Cause, than their neighbouring Province; but these Circumstances, which they conceive to form a Plea for greater Favour, never can he the Reason that they are treated less favourably; yet the Petitioners are at a Loss to assign any other Cause for the Distinction made oh this Occasion between East and W estFlorida: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Situation into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordavd, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act made in the Sixteenth Year of His Majesty’s Reign, ail Trade and Intercourse with the Colonies therein mentioned (of which New York was one) was prohibited, during the Continuance of the Rebellion within the said Colonies respectively; and that in Septembe 1776 His Majesty’s Troops obtained Possession of New York, Long Island, and Staten Island, and continued in Possession thereof until the Peace, in the Year 1783; New York, being fortified and garrisoned, became a Place of Refuge for the Loyalists from all Parts of the Continent, and Numbers of Persons also, who availed themselves of the Benefit of the Proclamations of His Majesty’s Commissioners, repaired thither, made their Submission to Government, and received Pardon and Protection, in consequence of which there were at Times within the British Lines not less than 80,000 Persons, who could not have subsisted without receiving from Great Britain various Articles of Manufacture and Merchandize, besides Provisions, imported under the Licence of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, as permitted and directed by the said Act; and that, to remedy this Inconvenience, and supply those Wants, such Vessels as-brought Provisions under Licence from the Lords of the Admiralty, and cleared out at the Custom Flouses in Great Britain for New York, brought other Goods and Merchandize of the Manufacture of Great Britain, cleared out by Cocket for Halifax, and these Cargoes were openly and publicly shipped, were duly and regularly cleared out,

July 1777, issued a Proclamation, appointing Andrew Elliot, Esquire, Superintendant of all imports and Exports to and from New York, and in virtue of the said Proclamation all Vessels arriving at that Port were admitted to a regular Entry, and fully protected; and that the Mayor of New certifying, under the

Seal of Mayoralty, the landing of the Goods so cleared out for Halifax, the Bonds so as aforesaid entered into at the Custom Houses in Great Britain were cancelled, and the Duty of Draw back immediately paid; and that, from the Commander in Chief in America thus inviting and authorizing such Importations, and the Custom Houses in Great Britain giving their Sanction to a Trade so openly and fairly carried on as that to New York, the Merchant could have no Doubt but that he was justifiable and safe in trading thither, without the smallest Imputation of Fraud, or Violation of the Spirit of an Act of Parliament, intended solely to prevent Supplies being carried to the People of America then in Rebellion, because the Port of New York was, to all Intents and Purposes, as fully opened as though it had been declared at the King’s Peace; and, that such was the Case must be evident, from the following Consideration, many Hundred Sail of Vessels, taken from the Rebels and their Allies, were carried into New York, where they were libelled and condemned in the Court of Vice Admiralty, exercising its judicial and executive Powers, as fully and amply as the Courts of Vice Admiralty in other Parts of His Majesty’s Dominions, and which could not have been done, had that Port not have been open, and at the King’s Peace, because, by the Act aforesaid, it is provided that no Captures which shall be taken in virtue of the said Act should be carried into any of the Colonies or Plantations in America, thereinbefore particularly mentioned, during so long Time as such Colonies or Plantations should continue in a State of Rebellion; and that, by the Trade thus carried on, not only the Navy, Army, and Loyal Inhabitants at New York were supplied with the Comforts and Necessaries of Life, but the Manufacturers of this Country were also greatly benefited by the increased Demand for, and Consumption of, Goods so imported there; and that the Petitioners, from the Reasons aforesaid, conceiving the Trade to New York fully authorized, protected, and encouraged, and that other Goods and Merchandize, as well as Provisions, might be safely exported thither, freighted the Ships Martha and Sir William Erskine, beitrg well armed, and having

and that the Petitioners, by the strict legal Interpretation of the said Act, notwithstanding the Protection and Encouragement thus held out by the said Proclamation, and the Sanction and Usage at the Custom Houses in Great Britain, having incurred and sustained heavy Losses and great Expences, cannot obtain any Aid or Relief but from this House, and they know of no other Persons suffering under the Operation of the Prohibitory Act, whose Cases are similar to those of the Petitioneis; and that the Petitioners are ready to give satisfactory Proofs of their Loyalty to His Majesty, and Attachment to the British Government: And therefore praying, That their Case may be taken into Consideration, and that the House will grant them such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seein meet.

A Petition of the American Loyalists, Sufferers by having furnished Provisions and dther Articles for public Use during the late War, and by having their Property taken and destroyed by the British Army and Navy, for which no Payment hath been made, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are of that Class of Subjects whose Persons were attainted, and Estates confiscated, in consequence of their Loyalty to His Majesty, and Attachment to the British Government; and that, during the War in America, the Petitioners, on many Occasions, furnished Provisions and other Articles for public Use, and at other Times their Effects were taken by His Majesty’s Army and Navy, their Houses and Estates occupied and demolished, and their Property destroyed, by Order, lest it should fall into the Hands of the Enemy, whereby the Re-volters were often prevented from advancing and attacking His Majesty’s Troops, and in other Instances they suffered in their Property and Individual Rights, for which' Supplies, Seizures, and Devastations, no Payment or Recompence hath as yet been made; relying, however, on the Justice of their Pretensions to Retribution, inasmuch as the chief End of Civil Society is to protect, and not to distress, the faithful Subject, and conceiving that whatever he is thus deprived of by the Servants of the Empire, for the Benefit of the Whole, ought to be paid for out of the Public Treasury, they, when Peace took place, preferred their separate Memorials to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, praying to be redressed, convinced that, as their Demands were undeniably well-founded, they would be attended to and satisfied; and that, in these reasonable Expectations, the Petitioners were so far gratified, that their Lordships, in their Desire to do Justice, promised that the said Claims should be referred for Liquidation to the Commissioners then about to be appointed to enquire into the Losses of the Loyalists in general, and, in consequence thereof, the said Claims were presented to the said Commissioners, but they conceiving that the Act of Parliament from which they derived their Authority did not enable them to take Cognizance of such Claims, they consequently declined the Business; and that the Petitioners then repeated their Application to the Lords of the Treasury, and their Memorials were afterwards referred to the Auditors of Public Accounts, where they remained near Twelve Months, and the Petitioners are now told, that the said Auditors decline liquidating the said Demands, alledging, that they cannot, without neglecting the other important Business of the Public; and that so great a Length of Time having thus elapsed since the public Exigencies made it necessary to deprive them of their Property, they trust that the House will see the Justice and Propriety of affording immediate and effectual Relief to Claimants whose other Sacrifices and Losses in America have reduced many of them from a State of Affluence to that of Indigence, little removed from Want: And therefore praying. That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and devise a proper Mode whereby their Demands may be speedily liquidated and paid.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.'

A Petition of the Right honourable Anthony James F.arl of Earl of Newburgh, Viscount Kinnaird and Baron Le- Newburgh’s vingston, of Flacring, in the Kingdom of being Petition*

offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His.

Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That of all the Estates which were forfeited to the Crown by the Adherents to the Cause of the Family of Stuart, either in the Year 1715 or 1745, the Derwentwater Estates alone remain still vested in the Trustees of the Public; and that Parliament still retains the same Power and Controul over the Dencentwater Estates, which it had over all the Scotch Estates, which have been so lately restored to the Families of the forfeiting Persons, and which were, by the Twenty-fifth of his late Majesty, annexed to the Imperial Crow-n of this Realm, to remain for ever unalienable from the same, for the Purposes in the said Act mentioned, and, the Petitioner is confident, that if he asks a less Favour, and sheas equal, if not further Pretensions, than the Persons who have experienced such Favour of the Legislature, his Application will not be rejected; and that the Petitioner trusts that he will be found to have at least equal Pretensions with the other Sufferers for the same Cause, to apply for the Restoration of all those Parts of his Family Estates which were actually forfeited by his Ancestors, yet lie does not presume to petition Parliament to be re-admitted to any Part of those Estates, although the Public will for ever continue to receive considerably more from them than from such to which the Petitioner applies to the Humanity of Parliament to be restored; and that the Petitioner submits, that One Part of the Derwent-water Estates was settled, previous to the Attainder of the Petitioner’s Ancestors, in such Manner that it could not be forfeited for any longer Time than during the Life of the forfeiting Person, in case such forfeiting Person should have Issue Male; and that the last Earl of Derwentwater accordingly forfeited an Estate, which he took under a Settlement made in the Year 1712, during his own Life, which Estate, after his Death, was enjoyed, under the Limitations thereof, by Mr. John Radclyffe, his only Son, from the Year 1716 till the Year 1731, when he died under Age and unmarried; and that Mr. Charles Radclyffe, the younger Brother of the said Earl, and Grandfather of the Petitioner, had, under the same Settlement, an Estate for Life, equally limited, after his Death, unto his First and other Sons, in the same Manner as it had been limited to the First and other Sons of the said Earl of Dencentwater, and the Petitioner’s late Father wras such first Son, law fully begotten, of the said Charles Radclyffe; as therefore Mr. John Radclyffe was not deprived of his Estate on Account of the Attainder of his Father, it is evident that the late Earl of Newburgh was not deprived of that Estate on Account of the Attainder of his Father, for by one and the same Settlement each Father had a Life Estate, which he forfeited to the Crown, and each Son had an Estate Tail, vested in him as a Purchaser, precisely in the same Manner; and that the Petitioner is confident that it will appear to every Member of the House, who considers the Circumstances of his Case, that if it were thought proper to restore all the Estates which had been unquestionably forfeited by the other forfeiting Persons, to whose Families the same have been restored, it will be found still more reasonable to restore that Part of the Petitioner’s Family Patrimony which was divested out of his Father, not by virtue of the Attainder

Annuities, Part of the said Omnium, and that the Three first Payments upon the said £. 2,000 Three per Cent. Annuities, amounting to £.522, were duly made by the Petitioner, but he being confined with Sickness to his Vo I.. 42.

Bed, and afterwards becoming delirious, the Fourth Payment due thereon of £. 232, upon the 27th. Day of October 1784, was therefore omitted to be made, the Circumstance of the Petitioner having any such Stock, not being known by any of the Petitioner’s Family or Friends; and that shortly afterwards the Petitioner’s Son received Intelligence from the Cashiers at the Bank of England, that the said £. 2,000 Three per Cent. Annuities (as appeared to them from the Third Payment thereon having been made by the Petitioner) was in the Petitioner’s Possession, and that the Fourth Payment had not been made thereon and that, as soon as the Petitioner was somewhat recovered, the Petitioner’s Son mentioned the Circumstances to him, who could not recollect that he then had any such Stock, but his Illness having much impaired his Memory, and not having any Memorandum of the said Stock, he concluded he had disposed thereof; and that, when the Petitioner was perfectly recovered, lie did not conceive that he had such Stock, until the Receipts for the Three Payments made thereon were accidentally found, but the Times for the further Payments thereon being then elapsed, and the Accounts at the Bank closed, the Petitioner could not be permitted to make the said Payments; and that the Petitioner presented a Memorial to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, for Relief in the Premises, which was referred by their Lordships to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, who reported thereon, that Three Payments, amounting to £. 522, had been duly made upon the said £. 2,000 Three per Cent. Annuities, as hereinbefore stated, but their Lordships were pleased to reject the said Memorial, forasmuch as the Statute in respect of the said Loan of the Year 1784 (i. e.) 24 Geo. III. Cap. to.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Charles Marion Welstead informed your Committee, That the Duke of Mancheste, as Lord of the Manor of Saint Ives, in the County of Huntingdon, is Proprietor of a Stone Bridge over the River Ouse, at the down of Saint Ives aforesaid, and of a Causew ay extending about 600 Yards from the said Bridge, and also of a small Wooden Bridge upon the said Causew ay, and is entitled to a Toll for certain Carriages and Cattle passing over tire same.

That the said Bridges. and Causeway have been repaired till of late at a small Expence, but that since Several Turnpike Roads have been made to communicate with the said Town, great Number of Carriages and Travellers pass over the said Bridges and Causeway, by reason whereof the said Bridges are become greatly decayed, and in Danger of falling, and require to be immediately repaired; and the said Causeway is frequently impassable in Times of Flood, and it is necessary, in order to render the Passage over the said Causeway at all Times safe, that the same should be considerably raised. — And the Witness added, That the said Bridges and Causeway are also narrow and incommodious for Carriages and Travellers; and the same cannot be made safe and commodious without a considerable Expence; and that the Revenue arising from the Tolls now received is inadequate to defray that Expence.

And the Witness further said, That Application hath been made to the Duke of Manchester, by several Gentlemen of the County of Huntingdon, requesting him to cause the said Bridges and Causeway to be repaired, and rendered safe and commodious for Carriages and Passengers at all Seasons of the Year. — And the said Duke, being present, acquainted your Committee, That he is willing to undertake to cause the several Works aforesaid to be executed and done in a proper and substantial Manner, in case he shall be authorized to collect such additional Tolls, over and above his present Tolls, as shall be sufficient to defray the Expence that will attend such Undertaking.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Bridge over the River Ouse, at the Town of Saint Ives, in the County of Huntingdon, and for rendering the Passage from the said Bridge, over certain Low Grounds adjoining thereto, safe and commodious for Travellers: And that the Earl Ludlow and the Lord Ilinchingbrookdo prepare, and bring in, the same.

" including all the external and internal Walls, and " so much of the Party Walls, if any, as belong to " such Stack of Warehouses; and no Enlargement " shall be at any Time thereafter made to any Stack of Warehouses already built or begun, so as to increase the same beyond the said Thirty-five Squares " on the Ground Plan, including such Walls as aforesaid, except such Stack of Warehouses be separated " and divided by one or more Party Wall or Party " Walls, built in every Respect according to the Dircctions hereinbefore contained concerning Party " Walls, into Divisions of not more than Thirty-five " Squares each, including such Walls as aforesaid,

" on the Ground Plan ol such Warehouses; and that " no Stack of Warehouses shall communicate with any " other Warehouse or Building through a Party Wall,

" unless the Door Case and Sill of every such Communication be of Stone, and unless there shall be " to every such Communication a Door of wrought " Iron, of the Thickness of a Quarter of an Inch at least in the Pannels thereof; and no Timber " Band or Lintel shall be laid into the Brick Work " of any Wall, in any such Stack of Warehouses,

" nearer than Eighteen Inches to the Opening of such " Communication." Then

Richard Jupp, Esquire, Surveyor of Buildings to the East India Company, being examined, said, That the Company are possessed and in the Use of Warehouses heretofore erected, and which, on the Ground Plan thereof, exceed Thirty-five Squares without any Division; and their present Trade requiring a very considerable Addition of Warehouse Room, they are now building new Warehouses upon the Ground where His Majesty's Navy Office lately stood — That it is necessary to the Company’s Trade, that their Warehouses should be of greater Dimensions than Thirty-five Squares without any Division. — And the Witness further said, That if the Company shall be obliged to conform in that respect to the Regulations and Directions in the said Act contained, the same will be attended with the utmost Inconvenience to the Company in the conducting their Business, and will besides occasion a very heavy Expence; and that the Company’s Warehouses are built with every possible Precaution against Fire, cither within the same, or from surrounding Buildings, and in a Manner which makes it w holly unnecessary, with regard to the Public Safety, to confine such Buildings to the Dimensions, Regulations, and Directions prescribed by the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the East India Company to continue their Warehouses already built, and to build new Warehouses, exceeding certain Dimensions, freed and discharged from the Regulations and Directions contained in an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the lteign of His Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for the further and better Regulation " of Buildings and Party Walls, and for the more " effectually preventing Mischiefs by Fire, within the " Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties " thereof, and other the Parishes, Precincts, and Places " within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, the Parishes " of Saint Mary-le-Bon, Paddington, Saint Pancras,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Whitworth, an Engineer, being examined, said. That there are several extensive Manufactures carried on in the Burgh of Paisley, to the great Advantage of Persons engaged therein, and of the Public — That 4he River Cart, which runs 'through the said Burgh, and falls into the River Clyde about Two Miles therefrom, is at present only "navigable for small Boats in Floods or Spring Tides,'and even then with much Difficulty and Hazard — That from a Survey, which <the Witness, has lately made, he is of Opinion, that if the said River was properly deepened, from the Sneddon Bridge, at or near the said Burgh, to its Junction with toe River Clyde, and a Canal or Cut made Vol. 42.

past the East End of Inshinnan Bridge, end across the Turnpike Road leading from CKasgow to Greenock, with a Draw-bridge over the same, the Navigation of the said River would become safe and easy, from which great Advantage would be derived, not only to the Trade and Manufactures of Paisley, but to the Country in general.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Magistrates and Town Council, of Paisley to improve the Navigation of the River Cart, and to make a Navigable Cut or Canal across the Turnpike Road leading from Glasgow to Greenock:

And that Mr. Shaw Stewart, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, and Mr. John James Hamilton, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

towlAMtnt A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Petition from A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are the Attorn its thereunto subscribed, being Attornies and Solicitors, of \ orkshire. in jiie Courts of Law and Equity, and re-

sident within the County of York, the City of York, and County of the same City, and the Town of Kingston-upon Hull, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, before they can be admitted to practise in any of His Majesty’s Courts of Law or Equity, are compelled to serve a regular Clerkship, and to undergo an Examination touching their Capacity for the Conduct of Business in those Courts, and are also subject to many other Regulations established by various Acts of Parliament, which have proved highly beneficial to the Profession at large, and calculated to bind the Petitioners to the due and punctual Performance of their Duty to their respective Clients; and that a Branch of the Profession of the Law, which the Petitioners also carry on jointly with the proper Business of an Attorney and Solicitor in the said Courts, and which consists in preparing and writing Deeds, and other solemn Contracts, for passing and assuring Real and Personal Estates, and Rights and Interests therein, is wholly excluded from the Benefit of the aforesaid Regulations, and may be carried on and practised by Persons of every Description, without any previous Admission or Qualification required by Law, which, in the Apprehension of the Petitioners, is attended with Inconvenience and Prejudice, as well to the Parties concerned, as to the Public in general, inasmuch as Persons of mean Fortune, Character, and Education, are thereby permitted , to intrude themselves into that Branch of the Profession; and that the Petitioners contribute to Government by various Taxes imposed by Parliament on the Petitioners in respect of their Admission and Inrolment, as Attornies and Solicitors, in the several Courts above-mentioned, and of their Employment in the ' same, all of which the Persons practising only as Conveyancers are wholly exempt from, whereby the Feta and Profits of Business, to which the Petitioners would be entitled, are diminished, whilst others are admitted to a Participation with them, of a very lucrative Branch of die Profession, without incurring the same Expences, Disabilities, or Burthens; and the Petitioners also apprehend, that the Laws now in Force, for the Regulation of Attornies and Solicitors, may be beneficially amended by the Imposition of an addi-donal Duty on Articles of Clerkship, and by a reasonable Regulation limiting the Time for the Taxation, and securing the Payment of their Bills of Fees and Disbursements: And therefore praying, That the

House will take the Articles above stated, and the Laws* now in Force for the Regulation of Attornies and Solicitors, into Consideration, and that such Regulations may be made for Remedy of the *same as the House shall find proper; and that Leave may be given to bring in One or more Bill, or Bills, for that Purpose, or that such other Relief may be given as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of those whose Names are thereunder Petition written, being Justices of the Peace for the County againstCam-and Town of Cambridge, was presented to the House, I11 and read; Setting forth, That, at a Quarter Sessions held for the said County at Cambridge last,

a Bill for the Recovery of Small Debts in the County and Town of Cambridge was submitted to the Consideration of a very full Bench of Justices, who were of Opinion that such a Bill vvas unnecessary and inexpedient; and the Petitioners finding a Bill for that Purpose is now brought into Parliament, and not having an Opportunity allowed them of reconsidering at their Quarter Sessions the Tendency of such a Bill, are compelled thus to appeal to the House, and request they would not suffer it to pass into a Law, as they are well convinced it will have a very bad Effect, and prove highly injurious to every Rank and Order of Society in the said County and Town.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House being informed that One of the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door;. he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of and under divers Charters, recognized and confirmed by several Acts of Parliament, the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London have had and exercised, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and exercise, the Office of Bailiff and Conservator of the Water of Thames, to be exercised and occupied by the May6r of the same City for the Time being, during the Time . of his Mayoralty, or by his sufficient Deputies, in, upon, and about, the Water of Thames, that is to say, from the Bridge of the Town of Staines, in the County of Middlesex, and towards the East unto London Bridge, and from thence to a certain Place called otherwise Yendland, otherwise towards the Sea,

and East, and in Medway, and in the Port of the City of London aforesaid; and upon whatsoever Bank, and upon every Shore, and upon every Wharf of the same Water of Thames, within the Limits and Bounds aforesaid, and in, upon, and about, all and every of them, and also, for all the Time aforesaid, have had and taken, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and take, to their own proper Use, by the Mayor of the same City for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or his sufficient Deputies, all Wages, Rewards, Fees, and Profits, belonging to the said Office; and that, by reason of the increased Navigation on the River Thames, and the Want of proper Regulations in the mooring and stationing of Ships and Vessels in the Port of London, great Inconveniencies and Loss of Property are sustained by the Merchants and Owners of Ships, and Robberies are frequently committed in the Night Time within the said Port, to the great Prejudice of the Trade and Commerce of the City of London, and the Kingdom in general; and that the Petitioners are advised, and believe, that Regulations are proper and necessary to be made, to remedy those Inconveniencies, and, in order to carry the same into Execution with full Effect, it will be necessary to purchase the Chains for mooring Ships and Vessels in and upon the said River, and to establish a Nightly Watch for the Protection of the Lives and Properties of all Persons concerned in Navigation within certain Parts of the Port of London, and the Petitioners conceive the present Conservatorial Powers are not sufficient effectually to remedy the several Inconveniencies aforesaid; and that a Plan for effecting the before-mentioned Purposes hath been some Time under the Consideration of the Petitioners, and a Treaty for the Purchase of the present Rights of fixing and using Mooring Chains hath been com-

o o o

menced, but such Treaty being unavoidably delayed, the Petitioners were thereby prevented applying to Parliament for an Act to enable them to carry the said Plan and Purposes into Execution, till after the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills was elapsed: And therefore praying, That Leave may lie given to exhibit a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the Purchase of the said Mooring Chains, for regulating the lying and mooring of Ships and Vessels, for the Safety and Improvement of the Navigation of the said River, and for providing and establishing a Nightly Watch for the Protection of Persons and Property, in such Manner, and within such Limits, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Free Burgesses of the Town of Plymouth was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Plymouth, was prepared to be presented to the House, stating, that the Isthmus which joins Mount Batten to the Land on the Eastern Shore of Plymouth Sound, has, from the Incroachment of the Sea on the South Side, been considerably reduced, and also from a Sand Bank formed off Mount

Batten, the Harbour of Cat is become in a very ruinous Condition, and that Sutton Pool, which was formerly protected by a Building erected on the Rocks, has, from the uncommon Gales of Wind, been Washed away, and the Shipping and Wharfs have received considerable Damage, and expressing the Hopes of the Petitioners, that Parliament would grant them some pecuniary Aid for securing the said Harbours, but the said Petition could not be presented to the House within the Time limited for receiving Petitions for private Bills, because it was not at that Time ascertained that His Majesty’s Consent would be obtained, which Consent is required, by a Standing Order of the House, previous to the receiving any Petition for any Sum of Money relating to public Service: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to present the said Petition, notwithstanding the Time limited for receiving Petitions for private Bills is elapsed.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said several Free Burgesses of the Town of Plymouth.

Then a Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Plymouth, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners think it unnecessary to represent to the House the very great Importance of the Port of Plymouth to the Commerce of this Country, it being obvious to every One, from its Western Situation, that it must, from the Change of Wind or Accidents, be frequently the Rendezvous of Ships of all Descriptions, coming into, or going out of, the Channel; and that the Sound, where Vessels usually Anchor, to be in readiness to put to Sea, from its open and exposed Situation, and the heavy Sea which falls in with Southerly and South West Winds, is by no Means a safe Situation for Ships or Vessels, particularly those of a small Size, and in order to prevent their going on Shore, they are often obliged to take Shelter in Catwater or Sutton Pool, small Harbours lying directly within the Sound; and the Petitioners, seeing the Necessity of preserving those Harbours, exceedingly lament that they are driven to the Necessity of stating to the House, that they and their Countrymen will be shortly deprived of further Benefit from them, unless they are aided by the Public — That the Isthmus which joins Mount Batten to the Land on the Eastern Shore of the Sound, and which separates the latter from Cutwater, has, from the Incroachments of the Sea on the South Side, been reduced to about Eighty Yards wide, and is every Year considerably decreasing, so that in Time the Sea must certainly make its Way into Catwater, and if ever that should happen, the Harbour would entirely be destroyed; and that in order to secure the Isthmus from the Incroachments above stated, Walls were formerly built opposite to the Sound and Catwater, but from the constant beating of the Sea for a long Series of Years, it has been entirely demolished; and that there is another Impediment, which is a Bank of Sand off Mount Batten, the Southern Part of Catwater, great Part of which it will be absolutely necessary to remote, if not the Whole, in order to deepen the Water that Ships may get in with greater Safety at Low Water, the Bank at present not admitting of their near Approach to it, and at such Times Ships have been driven on Shore in Deadman's Bay, before their Anchors could bring them up; and with regard to (i Sutton

37 Geo. III.

Sutton Pool, which may in Fact be called the Northern Arm of Cutwater, and is a Part of the Property of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Petitioners beg Leave to state that it was formerly secured by a Building erected on the Rocks on the East Side of the Entrance, and which entirely secured the Shipping within from the Inclemency of the Weather, but from the uncommon Gales of Wind which have of late Years prevailed, that Building has been entirely destroyed, and the Shipping, as well as the Wharfs, have received considerable Injury, and have been often totally destroyed; and that, in order to remedy Evils so much to be dreaded by the Commercial Part of this Country, as well as the Inhabitants of the Town of Plymouth, the Petitioners hope that the House will grant them such pecuniary Aid as will enable them to secure the Two Harbours above-men*

575

tioned from the further Incroachments of the Sea, and to remove the Bank of Sand off of Mount Batten, which if not soon executed wiH not only be the Loss of immense Property, but of the Lives of many of His Majesty’s Subjects.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That William M Esquire, do, upon Friday Morning next, attend the Committee of the whole House to whom it is referred to consider further of the several Articles of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal.

Ordered, That David Anderson, Esquire, do attend the said Committee, at the same Time.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take into further Consideration so much of His Majesty’s Most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 23d Day of January last, as relates to simplifying the Public Accounts in the various Branches of the Revenue.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Steele took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Steele reported from the Committee, That they

had made a further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and that he wns directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take into further Consideration so much of His Majesty’s Most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 23d Day of January last, as relates to simplifying the Public Accounts in the various Branches of the Revenue.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for repealing the several Duties of Customs and Excise, and granting other Duties in lieu thereof, and for applying the said Duties, together with the other Duties composing the Public Revenue; and for permitting the Importation of certain Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, into this Kingdom;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The House being informed, That Major General Charles Ross, who has petitioned this House, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the District of Boroughs of Kirkwall, Wick, Domock, Tain, and Dingwall, desires to withdraw his said Petition.

The House being also informed, That the Magistrates and Council of the Town or Borough of Dingwall, who have petitioned this House, likewise complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said District of Boroughs, desire to withdraw their said Petition.

And a Motion being made, That the said Petitioners have Leave to withdraw their said several Petitions;

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Motion be adjourned till Friday Morning next.

The House was moved, That the Entry in the Journal of the House of the 11th Day of May, in the last Session of Parliament, of the Address agreed to by this House to be presented to His Majesty, for Pensions to certain Captains in the Navy, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, That the Entry in the Journal of the House of the 5th Day of March 1773, of the Address agreed to by this House to be presented to His Majesty, for an Addition to the Allowance to several of the Junior Captains and Com-

Vol. 42.

manders in His Majesty’s Navy, for their Support when out of Employment, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Supply Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the deferred, whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Ways and Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the de" whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. tFilliam Kilburne being examined, said, That he is a Callicoe Printer, at WalUngton, in Surrey; that he designs his own Patterns, and that, out of a Number of Patterns which he has produced for the Approbation of the Public, many have not met the Taste, by which he sustains a considerable Loss; of those which are

that had a rapid Sale? he replied, He could not then recollect an Instance. — And being asked, Whether he could recollect how many of Mr. Kilburne % Patterns he at different Times has copied ? he answered, He could not — supposes Ten may have been copied — does not think Fifty. — And being asked,

approved, he is entirely cut off from any Share of Whether it was the Practice of the Trade to copy ori Prpfit, owing to such Patterns being immediately ginal Patterns as soon as they came out, if they are copied upon coarser Cloth and bad Colours — That good Patterns ? he said, It was; and has been a

general Practice. — And being asked, Whether it has come to his Knowledge, in the Course of his Business, that the Patterns drawn in the Country have been copied by the Printers in and about London? he replied, That he did not recollect any Instance of it.- — And being asked. Whether the Price for cutting Patterns is higher in Town or in the Country ? he said, Certainly higher in Town. — And being asked, Whether the Patterns cut in London are not, in general, superior to those cut in the Country ? he said, It was so in some Instances: Then

Mr. Kilbume being again called, was asked, What is meant by an original Pattern? he replied, That it is an Assemblage of Flowers or Fruits placed in a Variety of Colours, so that they shall strike the Trade as something new, and not seen before: It never occurred to the Witness, in the Course of his Business, that Two Draftsmen, or Men of Genius, ever by Chance produced any Thing to prevent the Sale of each other’s Patterns. — And being asked, Whether the Draftsmen do not sometimes sell the same Patterns to Manufacturers in different Parts of the Kingdom? he said, Not to his Knowledge; that if they did, it would ruin them as Draftsmen, and no One would afterwards so employ them. — And being asked, Whether he has not sometimes taken Patterns from Foreign Manufactures? he said, He has frequently taken Hints from them to improve his own Manufacture; that he never considered such Patterns as original. — And being asked, How many of the original Pattern produced to the Committee have been sold? he said, About Twenty; he speaks from Information received from Mr. Browne. — And being asked, If there was not a considerable Expence in cutting the Pattern? he said, A very considerable One; in the Manner we do it, we pay from £.10 to £. 20 in cutting a Pattern. — And being asked, If the Pattern was to be equally well executed, would not the Expence be as great, of getting it executed, in the Country ? he said, It would not be so great, because in the Country nothing is paid for the Design. — And being asked, How low the lowest Pattern costs him in cutting? he said, About Fifty Shillings. — And being asked, Whether all the Colours he makes use of will stand the Wash? he said, That when a Copy is made from a Foreign Design, some of the Colours will, and some will not, stand the Wash. — And being asked, How many Draftsmen there are in London who draw original Patterns? he said, He did not know. — Then the Witness was asked. How many Master Printers in London draw their own Patterns ? he said, About Five or Six; and that Three of the Petitioners draw their own Patterns.

Petition respecting Insolvent

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, for themselves, and others under the like Situation and Circumstances, was presented to Debtors Bill. t|ie House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been arrested for Debts, which they were unable to pay, and committed to Prison, many of them having suffered Six, and others Twelve Months Imprisonment, or more, and afterwards obtained their Liberty on Account of their Plaintiffs either not declaring against them in due Time, or of Delay or Error in the Course of the Proceedings, by obtaining a Supersedeas of such Actions; and that such Discharge by a Supersedeas is only a temporary Relief, for, by Law and Practice, the Petitioners, and all others under the like Circumstances, are still liable to be proceeded against to an Execution for Payment of such Debts, and if the Insolvent Bill now depending in the House should pass into a Law, without including the Petitioners, they will then be at the Mercy of their Creditors, without any future Prospect of Relief, and, to avoid the fatal Consequences of Executions against them, must necessarily be obliged to leave the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and admit them to the Benefit of the said Insolvent Act, under such Conditions as may be deemed necessary, or to grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into Committee a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for on Insolvent the Relief of Insolvent Debtors, and for the Relief of Debtors Bankrupts in certain Cases.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Robert Smyth took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Robert Smyth reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Vol. 42. 7 Q Port

Hull Docks.

610 28° Martii. A. 1787.

Port of Kingston upon Hull, in the Manner directed by the said Act, and the Company therein described were im powered to make a Bason or Dock, to extend from the River Hull to a Place in the said Town, called Beverley Gates, or as near thereto as conveniently might be, and to make the same in all Parts equal in Depth to the Bed of the River, or at least within Fifteen Inches of the same, for the Admission of loaded Ships, and of such Width at least as the Ground granted by the said Act would admit, and such Reservoirs, Sluices, Bridges, Roads, and other Works, as should be judged necessary, and also a Quay or Wharf of a sufficient Length for the Trade of the said Town and Port, to range along the Side of the said Dock next the Town; and the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Town of Kingston upon Hullthe Guild or Brotherhood of Masters and Pilots, Seamen of the Trinity House of Kingston upon Hull, and the several Persons whose Names are therein for that Purpose expressed, and all others who should become Subscribers towards the Expence of carrying on the said Works, their Successors, Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, together with such other Persons as they or the major Part of them should at any Meeting appoint, were united into a Company for the Purposes of the said Act, and were declared to be a Body Politic and Corporate by the Name of " The Dock Company at " Kingston upon Hull;" and certain Parts of His Majesty’s Military Works at Kingston upon Hull were thereby granted and appropriated for the Purposes before mentioned, and no other; and the said Company were thereby required at all Times sufficiently to repair, support, and cleanse the said Dock and Quay, and all other the Works to be made by them, by virtue of the said Act; and in order to facilitate the Execution of the said Works the Sam of £. 15,000 was directed to be paid out of His Majesty’s Customs at the said Port of Kingston upon Hull, at the Times and in the Manner therein mentioned; and the said Company were authorized to raise among themselves a Sum of Money not exceeding £. 80,000, to be divided into Shares of £.500 each; and the several Subscribers were to receive after the Works were completed, a proportionable Part of the Profits arising from the Money to be raised by the Authority of the said Act, and to bear an adequate Proportion of the said Money towards carrying on the stud Undertaking; and if the said Sum of £. 80,000 should not be raised, or should be insufficient for making the said Dock and other Works, the said Company were thereby authorized to borrow at Interest, on the Credit of the Rates and Duties granted by the said Act, so much Money as might make up the said Sum of £. 80,000, and such further Sums of Money, not exceeding £ 20,000, for completing the said Works; and certain Rates and Duties, particularly expressed in the said Act, were thereby granted to the said Company, and made payable from the 31st Day of December 1774, and the said Company were thereby impowered to lessen the Duties of Tonnage granted by the said Act, and to raise the same again, as to them should seem meet, so as the Duties, when advanced, should not exceed the Duties thereby granted; and certain Commissioners were by the said Act authorized to appoint Officers, make Bye Laws and Contracts, but subject to the Controul of the said Company, and also to purchase Lands for the Purposes of the Act; and if any of the Lands so to be purchased should not be used or wanted for those Purposes, the Commissioners were directed to sell (he same, and apply the Money arising from such Sale to the Use of the Company.

Then Mr. Thomas Westerdcll, thte Dock and Harbour Master, being examined, said, That the Dock Company have made a Dock from the River Hull to near Beverley Gates, and also a Quay or Wharf to the same, as directed by the Act; that he was appointed

by the Trinity House, and has been in Office since the Year 1774. — Being asked. If he understands the Powers vested in him by the Act ? he said, He hopes he does; that those Powers are the birthing and regulating the Ships in the Harbour and Dock. — And being asked, If he does not look upon the Haven or old Harbour, according to the Powers of the Act, to be, along with the Dock, the Port of Kingston upon Hull ? he said, He does in Part. — Being asked, In what Part? he said, When the Dock is so full that there is no Room within it, he has a Right to stop such Ships as have not Occasion to go to the Quays for the Revenue, and to order them into the old Harbour; that he conceives he has a Right to remove from the Dock into the Harbour old "Ships, such as are rendered useless for Sea Service, and no others, according to the Act.

Being asked, Whether the Act does not direct Ships to be moored near to the Banks of the Humber? he said, Only Ships rendered unfit for Sea Service, that he knows of; that it is only in that Sense that he means he has Powers to remove. — Being asked, Whether he has not received Orders and Directions from the Trinity House, and even Counsel’s Opinion, for that Purpose? he said, He received a Letter from the Trinity House, with a Copy of Counsel's Opinion, which he said he had in his Pocket; but that it contained no Directions as he conceives.

The Letter then being produced and read, he was asked, Whether he did not say, that, notwithstanding the Opinion of Counsel, he had his own Opinion, and should follow his own Judgment? he said. He had Occasion for that; he could receive no Orders from the Trinity House after he had sent them a Letter with the State of the Dock, though he had received-several Letters before to follow their Orders. — Being asked, Whether he has, since the Dock was opened in 1778, given Directions for a proper Number of Ships to be laid up in the old Harbour in the Winter Moriths, by which Means both Dock and Harbour might accommodate each other? he said, He never looked upon it that he had it in his Power to refuse any Ships coming into the Dock, until the same was full; if he had ever received Orders from the Trinity House to stop the Ships coming into the Dock, he should have done it. — Being asked, How many Ships of moderate Size, such as usually trade to Hull, the old Harbour would contain under the Regulations of the Dock Act? he said, He thinks about Sixty, but it would stop in a great Measure the Merchants Business. — Being asked, If he has not seen more tfian Three in a Tier ? he said, He has seen Six, but that was before the Dock was opened.

And Mr. Westerdellbeing further examined, said,

That the Trade at the Port of Hull has increased within these Ten Years last past — that the Ships which frequent that Port are become more numerous and of larger Dimensions — that proper Accommodation cannot be obtained for the Shipping in the present State of the Dock; and that it is not practicable to cleanse the Dock, whilst the Shipping continues so crowded, with the present Machine used for that Purpose. — That Vessels have been prevented from entering the Dock, owing to the Want of a sufficient Depth Of Water, occasioned by Mud Banks and other Obstructions; and that others have been detained within the DoCk owing to similar Causes, and retarded from prosecuting their Voyages. — And being asked, If he could mention any particular Vessels that have been prevented from entering into or going out of the Dock, within Twelve Months last past? he said, Yes, a Brig belonging to Mr. John Huntington, and another Vessel Whose Name he could not recollect; the first in going out, the other in coming in — The Vessel was prevented by the Mud from going out, and the other prevented from coming in by a Mud Bank, near the Entrance

7 Geo. III. a8° Martii 611

Entrance — That several Vessels have been refused Admittance into the Dock this Winter, for Want of sufficient Room to do Business — That alarming and dangerous Consequences are to be apprehended, in case of Fire, to the whole Shipping in the Dock, and to the Town; and that in case the present Bason and Dock should be enlarged and extended, such Losses, Damages, and Inconveniencies would in a great Measure be prevented, and a more safe and commodious Station be provided for the receiving, harbouring, lading, and unlading Ships and Vessels resorting to, and trading with, the Port of Hull — That he conceives the 98th Clause of the Act ought to have been Part of the Case submitted to Counsel for his Opinion, relative to the Power of removing Ships or Vessels out of the Dock; and that he conceives it was more material for that Purpose, than the other Three Clauses put together — That he did not know of Counsel’s Opinion being taken on that Subject previous to the 16th of January 1787 — That he never received any Directions from the Trinity House, authorizing or enjoining him to remove any Ships (not old ones) out of the Dock; nor did he ever remove any Ships by Compulsion, except old ones, out of the Dock; that he does not know that the Dock Company, at any Time prior to the 16th of January 1787, called upon him so to do. — And being asked, Whether he was not made acquainted with a Vote and Order of the Trinity House, of the 7th of September 1785? he said, He had an Order from the Trinity House, to do his Duty in the old Harbour and the Dock, according to the Act — Being asked, Whether, supposing Thirty or Forty Ships were laid up in the Winter Months in the Old Harbour, there would not be every Convenience wanted ? he said, No. — And being asked, What Time of the Spring Tide the Ship was prevented going into the Harbour P he said, It was the 20th of November 1786, about the Height of the Springs; but that they had dien very poor Tides.

Then Mr. James Green, Secretary to the Trinity House of Hull, was asked, Whether the whole Money actually advanced by the Subscribers in the Purchase of Lands for making the Dock, Erection of Buildings, and other the Purposes of the Undertaking, exceeded the Sum of £. 30,000, or £. 250 a Share? he said, It did not.

Then Mr. Josiah Pricket being examined, said, That the Company have purchased several Parcels of Land, and in particular One Parcel, amounting to Ten Acres and upwards, and which, from its Vicinity to the Dock,' is of great Value, and in his Judgment it is worth, to be sold, Ten Shillings a Square Yard and upwards; for that he has known several Parcels that have been sold at Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, and at One Pound and upwards, a Square Yard; that he prepared the Conveyances of them himself — That he ascertains the Purchases made by the Dock Company, by Extracts made from the Books of the Register’s Office kept for the East Riding of the County of York — That of some of the Purchases he

knows the exact Purchase Money, it being expressed in the Purchase Deeds inrolled in the Register’s Office; and of One of die Purchases, the Tide Deed to which is not inrolled, he learnt the Price by a Letter from Mr. G rims tons Steward; the Purchase Money given by the Dock Company to Mr. for the Purchase of the Ground bought of him, was about £. 200 an Acre, as he learnt by a Letter he received from Mr. Graves, Mr. Grimston's Steward; the Purchase Money given by the Dock Company to the Mayor and Burgesses, for Property the Dock Company purchased of them, appears to be expressed in the inrolment of the Purchase Deeds thereof, and to amount to the Sum of £. 6,575; the Property purchased of Mr. Krmdton, as expressed in the Inrolment of the Purchase Deed, amounts to £, 1.100 — That

Vo L. 42.

he believes there are upwards of Ten Acres of Land Hull Docks, purchased by the Dock Company, exclusive of Roads, that are now unappropriated to the Purposes of the Act, and that he thinks the Value of those Ten Acres of Land to be £. 24,200, which is at the Rate of Ten Shillings per Square Yard — That a considerable Part of those Ten Acres lie at present useless — That he conceives nearly the whole erf that Land to be unnecessary for the Purposes of the Act. — Being asked,

Whedier lie knows what the Company paid for those Ten Acres ? he said, It was comprehended in different Purchases. — And being asked, How he accounts for this great Price being given for Land in that Spot? he said, Partly from the great Increase of Trade and Commerce in the Place, and the Influx of Inhabitants; and notwithstanding the Buildings that have been al- . ready erected, he does not know a House that remains uninhabited; and he further believes, that was this very Piece of Ground now at Market, it would produce the Sum he has estimated it at — That he attributes the Increase of Inhabitants, and the Increase of Trade, to the Situation the Dock is now put in —

Being asked. Whether he understands that this Land, which he has told the Value of, is any Part of the Ground directed by the Act to be applied to the Purpose of making the Dock, or whether it was a voluntary Purchase by the Dock Company ? he said, lie never conceived that the Dock Act authorized the Company to purchase Grounds for the Purposes of Speculation, but for the express Purposes of the Act, and no other — That he conceives the Dock Company were prevented by the Act from making any Purchases, but for the Purposes of the Act — That he does not know whether the Value of this Land was settled . by a Jury under the Act of Parliament, or whether it was a Purchase, as between One Individual and another — That the Dock Company had a Power by the Act to call for the Intervention of a Jury, in any Purchases they made, in case the Parties should not render that unnecessary by agreeing without — That he believes the Purchases were all made in the Year 1775 — That he does not know whether it was previous to the Payment of the £. 15,000 allowed by Government — Being asked, If he knows whether this Ground has been applied by the Dock Company to any Use, and what? be said, He has seen Piles of Deals delivered from Vessels there — That there are Gentlemen present who have paid a Consideration for the Privilege of laying Deals there — That he has , been resident at Hull Eighteen Years. — Being asked,

Whether he does or does not know that the Company have used the Whole of this Ground, or Part of it, for the Purpose of depositing the Soil taken out of the Dock? he said. During the Time of making the Dock, they made Use of it for that Purpose, but it is his Opinion that One Half of the Quantity would have answered the Purpose; that he means to speak to the whole Quantity purchased — That they now make use of some Part of it for Purposes of that Kind.

Mr. James Green being then further examined, said,

That the Profits to which each Subscriber is entitled produced on an Average, for the Years 1783, 1784, and 1785, a clear Annual Income of £.29. 15 s. 4$ for each Share. — That the whole Average of the -Profits of the Undertaking exceeded those Three Years considerably. — Being asked, Whether he means the Dues received by the Dock Company, exclusive of any Ground which might have been sold? he said, He means the Whole of the Dock Company’s Receipts —

That he cannot ascertain, from the Inspection of the Books, what has been the Profits of the Company, exclusive of the Sale of Lands. — And being asked, If he knows of any Period in which the Company have sold any Part of the Laud that belonged to them, and at what Period it was? he said. Mr. Speaker,

The Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of thU Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several public and private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: And that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Privy Seal, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March Omr thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-seven; for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants, ana Officers of the Militia, who have neglected to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace; within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for that Purpose:

An Act for granting Rates of Postage for the Conveyance of Letters and Packets between Great Britain and the Port of Waterford, in the Kingdom of Ireland, by Way of Milford Haven:

An Act to continue the Laws now in Force for regulating the Trade between the Subjects oPHis Majesty’s Dominions and the Inhabitants of the Territories belonging to the United States of America, and to render the Provisions thereof more effectual:

An Act for building a Bridge at or near the Ferry over the River Trent, from Gainsborough, in the County of Lincoln, to the opposite Shore in the Parish of Saundby, in the County of Nottingham:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for lighting and " watching the Villages of Camberwell and Peckham,

" in the County of Surrey, and certain Roads therein " mentioned, leading thereto; and for establishing a " Foot Patrole between Peckham and Blackman Street,

" in the Borough of Sowas read. And,; Claud Champion Crespigny, Esquire, being examined,

said, That the said Act has in some Respects been found defective, particularly from the Want of a separate Set of Trustees for each Village, which, on Account of the length of Road directed to be lighted and watched,

I has been attended with great Inconvenience to the In-

habitants of Camberwell-, and that the Purposes of the said Act, so far as relates to Camberwell, might be better executed, and at less Expence, if separate Trustees were appointed, and separate Rates collected for that Village, and the Roads and other Places belonging thereto.

James Mill, Esquire, confirmed the above Evidence.

Mr. Gilbeit, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eighteen thousand..Five hundred Seventy-four Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Ten Pence Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency, on the 5th Day of July 1786, of the Fund established for paying Annuities, granted by an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1758.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Twenty-seven thousand Seven hundred Ninety-six Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Three Pence Half-penny, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency, on the 10th Day of October 1786, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1778.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-five thousand and Thirty-nine Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Five Pence Half-penny, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency, on the 5 th Day of July 1786, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign erf His present Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1779.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Eighty-four thousand Two hundred Thirty-four Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence Half-penny, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency, on the 10th Day of October 1786, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1780.

Inverness Then a Petition of the Freeholders of the County Court House, of Inverness, and of the Magistrates and Council of *c. Petition. Town of Inverness, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s

627

Circumstances, the Funds of the Town have been so reduced, that the small Remnant has only enabled them to give the Bridge a temporary Repair, which accommodates Foot Passengers, and, to accomplish a thorough Repair of the said Bridge, would require no less than £. 900; and that, in more opulent and populous Parts of the Kingdom, an Exigence of this Kind might be supplied by establishing a Toll by Act of Parliament, but here the Corporation are unable to defray even the Expence of the Act, and the Country being thinly inhabited, the Passengers are mostly Military, who are exempted from Tolls, so that it would be utterly impossible to provide for the Repair in that Way, and that Country in general are so much behind their Neighbours in most of the Arts, and in Improvements of every Kind, that they may be considered yet in a State of Infancy; they require the fostering Hand of Government to rear them to that Maturity, which, it is to be hoped, will in Time greatly strengthen and enrich the United Kingdom, and Government indeed are so sensible thereof, that they have for many Years past liberally granted several Sums for Roads and Communications; and that this Petition was ready to be presented to the House on the last Day limited for receiving Petitions for private Bills, but from not having been properly signed, the same could not be presented that Day: And therefore praying, That they may have Leave to present their said Petition, notwithstanding that the Day limited by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills has elapsed.

Leave given. Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Freeholders of the County of Nairn, and Magistrates and Town Council of the Borough of Nairn.

Home reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Freeholders, Justices of the Peace, and Heritors, of the County erf Berwick, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of thp House, of the 25th of April 1774) relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the Rime, as it appeared to them, to the House; and be read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in sit the Clerk’6 Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Fordyce, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Great Post Road between London and Edinburgh, leading from the Extremity of the Liberties of the Borough of Berwick upon Tweed, by Ayion Bridge, and the new Bridge over the Pees or Pass of Cockburnspath, to Dunglas Bridge, on the Coniines of East Lothian, and also the Branches leading from Billie Causeway and Preston Bridge, to join the said Post Road at or near Cockburnspath Tower, are in many Places so deep and ruinous, that Travellers cannot pass without great Inconvenience, and are in Danger of becoming altogether impassable; and that the Aids which already have been obtained from public Bounty, and from private Contributions, have been found insufficient for the Purpose of making the said Road, which cannot be effectually amended and kept, in Re-ipair by the Funds arising from the Laws now in Force.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and widening the Road leading from the Borough of Berwick upon Tweed, by Ayton Bridge, and the new Bridgeover the Pees or Pass of Cockburnspath, to Dunglas Bridge, and also the Roads leading from Billie Causeway and Preston Bridge, to join the said Road at or near Cockburnspath in the County of Berwick: And that Mr. Home, Mr. Archibald Doug-<las, and Mr. John Hamilton, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Bill for the better repairing, paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Highways, Streets, and Lanes of and in the Town of Sandwich, in the County of Kent, and in the several Parishes of Saint Peter the -Apostle, Saint Mary the Virgin, and Saint Clement, in the said Town and County, and for removing and preventing Incroachments, Nuisances, Obstructions, and Annoyances in the said Highways, Streets, and Lanes, and on the Common Quay belonging to the said Town and Port, and in the Haven adjoining to the said Quay, and the Bridge built over the said Haven, and to regulate the Births and Mooring Places of Vessels at the said Quay, and the proper Times for Vessels to pass through the said Bridge, was read a Second Time.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The Bill, now ingrossed, for repealing the several Consolida-Duties of Customs and Excise, and granting other t,on Bill Duties in lieu thereof, and for applying the said Du- passe ties, together with the other Duties composing the Public Revenue; and for permitting the Importation of certain Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, into this Kingdom, was read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, directing that distinct Accounts be kept erf the Produce of the Revenues, and be laid Annually before both Houses of Parliament.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks, which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part <rf the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, directing that all Sums which shall remain in the Exchequer on the 5th Day of July 1787, <tf the Duties repealed, and the Deficiencies repaid to the Sinking Fund, be carried to the Consolidated Fund.

And the said Clause was Thrice readand, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 105. 1. 5. To leave out from " notwithstanding " to the End of Line 33.

Pr. 125. 1. 29. To leave out " Three Pence," and insert " One Twentieth " Part of a Penny" instead thereof.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put.

That the Bill do pass;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

So it was resolved in the Affirmative: And that the Title be, An Act for repealing the several Duties of Customs and Excise, and granting other Duties in lieu thereof, and for applying the said Duties, together with the other Duties composing the Public Revenue; for permitting the Importation of certain Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French King, -into this Kingdom; and for applying certain unclaimed Monies remaining in the Exchequer, for the Payment of Annuities on Lives, to the Reduction of the National Debt.
