63^ 5 Apr ilis1787.

County of the same City, in the room of Sir Harbord Harbord, Baronet, created a Peer of Great Britain (which Election was held on the 15th Day of September 1786) Sir Thomas , Baronet, the Honourable Henry Hobart, and Robert John Buxton, Esquire, were Candidates, and, at the said Election, the said Henry Hobart, having a Majority on the Poll, was returned by the Sheriffs as a Member to serve in Parliament for the said City and County; and that certain Persons, being Electors of the said City, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Electors, and also the said Sir Thomas Beevor, on or about the 16th Day of February last, presented their Petitions to the House, complaining of the said Election and Return, on the following, among other Grounds; viz. " That " after the Vacancy happened, and previous to, and " during the Time of the said Election, the said " Henry Hobart, by himself, his Agents, Friends, and " Managers, was guilty of many notorious and fla-t grant Acts of Bribery and Corruption, by giving " divers large Sums of Money to the Electors of the " said City and County, and by corruptly promising " to the said Electors, or some of them, large Presents, Gifts, Advantages, and Rewards, in order " to procure him, the said Henry Hobart, to be elected " to serve in Parliament for the said City and County; " and that the said Henry Hobart, by himself, his " Agents, Friends, and Managers, did, after the " said Vacancy happened as aforesaid, and before and " during the said Election, give, present, and allow " to divers Persons, having Voice or Vote in the said " Election, Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, " and Provision, and made Presents, Gifts, Rewards, " and Entertainments, and made Promises, Agreements, Obligations, and Engagements, to give or " allow Money, Meat, Drink, Provisions, Presents, " Rewards, Advantages, and Entertainments, to and " for several Persons so having or claiming Right to " vote in the said Election, and to and for the Use, " Advantage, Benefit, Profit, and Preferment of such " Persons, so having or claiming Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure him the said " Henry Hobart to be elected to serve in Parliament " for the said City and County; and that the Committee chosen to try the Merits of the said Election and Return, having heard the Evidence on the Part of the Petitioners (which was confined to the Allegations before stated, relative to the bribing and entertaining the Electors as aforesaid) and having also heard the Evidence on the Part of the said Henry Hobart, and having met on the 9th Day of March, to deliberate thereon, came to the following Resolutions; viz. "That the Honourable Henry Hobart is not duly " elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament " for the City of Norwichand also, " That Sir " Thomas Beevor, Baronet, is not duly elected a " Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the " said City of Norwichand also, " That the last " Election of Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the said City of Norwich, was a void " Election and that the said Resolutions being reported to the House, a new Writ was ordered to be issued, and was accordingly issued on the said 9th Day of March, directed to the Sheriffs of the said City of Norwich, whereby, after stating that the Election of the said Henry Hobart was adjudged to be void, the said Sheriffs were commanded, that, in the Place of the said Henry Hobart, they should cause to be elected one other fit Person; and that, in pursuance of the said Writ, the said Sheriffs proceeded to a new Election on the 15th Day of March 1787, when the said Sir Thomas Beevor and Henry Hobart were again Candidates, and, upon the final Close of the Poll, taken at the said Election, the Sheriffs declared the Numbers

Jo be as follows — for tire said Henry Hobart 1,393, and or the said Sir Thomas Beevor 1,313; and, the said

Hemy Hobart, having the Majority, has since been returned to serve in Parliament for the said City of Norwich, and County of the same City; and that the Petitioners conceive that the Election of the said Henry Hobart having been declared ‘void on the Ground of his having violated the Acts of Parliament against Bribing and Entertaining the Electors, he was thereby, and by the true Construction of such Acts of Parliament, and according to the Law and Custom of Parliament, rendered incapable to represent the City of Norwich in Parliament at any Election to fill the said Vacancy, and therefore that he was not eligible, and ought not to have been returned at the said late Election, but that the said Sir Thomas Beevor was duly elected, and ought to have been returned, as being the only Person who offered himself in the Place of the said Henry Hobart; and that this appears by the Writ before stated, which expressly commands that some other Person shall be elected in the Place of the said Henry Hobart, and by which the said Henry Hobart himself is therefore excluded: And therefore praying, That the said Henry Hobart may be declared not duly elected, and that the said Sir Thomas Beevor may be declared duly elected to serve in Parliament for the City of Norwich, and County of the same City, or otherwise that the said late Election for the City of Norwich, and County of the same City, may be declared a void Election, and that the Petitioners may have such further and other Relief as the Nature of their Case may require, and the House shall think reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 1st Day of May next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum: '

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of Controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

petition A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers in the Town against the of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, whose Shop 'lax. Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the

House, and read; Complaining of the Acts of the Twenty-fifth and Twenty-sixth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for laying a Duty on Retail Vot- 42.

A Petition of the several Persons whore Names are Petition thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Estates, House- against St. holders, and Inhabitants, of and within the Parish of George, Ha-Saint George, Hanover Square, within the Liberty of the workhouw City of Westminster, was presented to the House, and Bill, read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for confirming the Purchase of a House and Premises at Little Chelsea, to be used as an additional Workhouse for the Poor of the said Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, and for authorizing the Select Vestry to expend unlimited Sums of Money, as they may think proper, in Buildings and Alterations at Little Chelsea, and to charge such Expenditures to the Account of the Poor of the said Parish; and that the Petitioners are advised, that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will frustrate an Enquiry, instituted by the Petitioners in an inferior Court, as to the Necessity of the said Purchase, and thereby operate as an ex post facto Law; and that the Petitioners are well assured that the Purchase of an additional Workhouse is quite unnecessary, and that the Appointment of One so remote from the Parish will, unavoidably, prove greatly expensive, burthensome, oppressive, and injurious to the Petitioners, and the Parishioners in general, as a new Household, with additional Masters, Servants, and Agents, of every Denomination, at an immense Expence, must be appointed, which will of course very much increase the Rates assessed on the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and that very dangerous Consequences may arise from the unlimited Power given by the said Act to the Select Vestry, for expending any Sums of Money in Buildings, and Alterations of Buildings, at Little Chelsea; and, the Petitioners conceive, there are other substantial Objections to the said Bill being passed into a Law: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, inasmuch as it tends to stay the Proceedings of an inferior Court, and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for confirming the Purchase of a

Articles of Impeachment against Mr.tlastiogs

25* Aprilis. 1787.

Articles of Impeachment of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal.

Whereas the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies had, for a long Time past, carried on an extensive Trade, obtained great Territorial Possessions and Revenues, entered into various Alliances and Connections, and waged frequent Wars with the native Powers in India: And whereas it became necessary that the said U nited Company, in pursuance of and by the Authority in them vested by Act of Parliament, and Charter under the Great Seal, should create certain great Officers for the Management of these important Affairs, and for the more perfect conducting and directing of the various Concerns from them resulting: And whereas, among others, the Office, created and known by the Name and Designation of President of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal, was an Office of high Trust, Power, and Dignity; on -the due and incorrupt Execution of which, the Welfare of the said United Company, the Happiness of the native Inhabitants of India, the Honour of the Crown of these Kingdoms, and the Character of the British Nation, did most materially depend: And whereas Wah'en Hastings, Esquire, was, by legal Authority, constituted and appointed to succeed to the Situation and Office of President of the Presidency of Fort William, in Bengal, by an Appointment bearing Date the Twenty-tilth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one: That the said Warren Hastings did, on or about the Month of April, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two, succeed to the said Office; by which said Appointment and Succession, all the Power, Authority, and Dignity, which ever had been, or could by Law be granted, were conveyed to the said Warren Hastings, in the most ample Form and Manner possible: And whereas the great and growing National Importance of the Affairs of the East India Company had made them peculiarly the Object of Public and Parliamentary Consideration: And whereas, in consequence thereof, an Act passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the establishing certain Regulations for the " better Management of the Affairs of the East India " Company, as well in India as in Europe:" And whereas by the said Act it was, among other Things, enacted, that a Governor General, instead of a President as aforesaid, should be appointed to preside over the Affairs of the said East India Company: And whereas, still greater Power, Authority, Dignity, Trust, and Responsibility, were by the said Act annexed to the Office of Governor General, than had belonged to the Office of President of the Presidency aforesaid; on the due and uncorrupt Execution of which said last mentioned Office, the before-recited important Interests, relative to the native Subjects and protected Princes in as

well as to the said East India Company and the British Nation, did likewise in a most especial Manner depend: And wherea's the said Warren Hastings was

appointed, by the Act of Parliament aforesaid, to the Office of Governor General, by which Act the Power and Authority thereof were conveyed to the said Warren Hastings, in the most full and ample Manner possible: And whereas, by virtue of several subsequent Acts of Parliament, he the said Warren Hastings has been frequently re-appointed to the said Office of Governor General, with all the Power, Authority, Dignity, Trust, *and Responsibility, originally annexed to the same: — That, in fact, the said Warren Hastings did accept of these great Offices of President and Governor General of the Presidency of Fort William, in Bengal, so bestowed on him as aforesaid, and did continue to act therein, without any Suspension or Intermission whatever, from the Period herein first mentioned, until the Month of February, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five: That the said Warren Hastings did solemnly swear faithfully to discharge his Duty therein; by all which he became bound, by the most solemn Obligations, to the Company, the Crown, and the Nation, faithfully to discharge the Duty of the Trust reposed in him, during all the Time aforesaid: Yet the said Warren Hastings, not regarding the sacred Obligation of his Oath, nor the important Duties of the high Offices to which he was appointed, but entertaining base and corrupt Views of procuring for himself and his Dependants exorbitant Wealth, and arbitrary Designs of raising himself, by Means of the undue Influence so acquired, to excessive Power, as well to gratify his inordinate Ambition, as to secure himself from Punishment for the many unjustifiable Acts by him done and committed in the Exercise of his Office, did, whilst he was President and Governor General as aforesaid, by the various unwarrantable and criminal Practices herein after set forth, faithlessly, illegally, and tyrannically violate the Duties of his Station: By each and all of which Practices the Welfare of the East India Company has materially suffered, the Happiness of the native Inhabitants of India been deeply affected, their Confidence in English Faith and Lenity shaken and impaired, and the Honour of the Crown, and Character of this Nation, as far as in him lay, wantonly and wickedly degraded.

ARTICLE FIRST.

That Rajah Bulxcant Sing, Prince or Zemindar of certain Provinces or Districts in India, called Benares, and Gazepoor, dependant upon the Mogul Empire, through Sujah ul Dmvlah, Nabob of Oude, and Vizier of the Empire, did, in the Commencement of the English Power in India, in or about the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-four, attach himself to the British Nation, and was, in the Opinion of the Directors of the East India Company, of signal Service to the Affairs and Interests of this Kingdom.

That, in Consideration of those Services, the said Bulxcant Sing was, by the Treaty of Peace concluded at Allahabad, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five, between Siyah ul Dawlah and the British Nation, fully secured in the Possession of his Territories, which Possession he retained till his Death.

That by the Influence of the British Bengal Government, and in Consideration of a large Sum of Money, and a considerable Increase of Tribute paid to the Vizier, his Son Rajah Cheit Sing did, on the Death of his Father, the said Bulxcant Sing, succeed to the said Territories; and on or about the Month of October, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy, was fully invested with the Government thereof.

That in the Month of June, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-three, Warren Hastings, Esquire, (being then President of the Presidency of Fort William, in Bengal) was empowered by the President and Council (that is by himself and Council) to renew, on Behalf of Rajah Cheit Sing, the Stipulations which had been formerly made with the Vizier in Favour of his Father Rajah Bulxcant Sing, in Consideration of his Services in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-four.

That in consequence of these Powers, the said Wivr-> ren Hastings did, by various Treaties and Agreements, renew and secure to Rajah Cheit Sing and his Posterity the Inheritance of the above-mentioned Tdritories (which said Territories had been already conveyed to him by Acts of the Vizier in his Favour) upon the 4 . same

37 Geo. III. 25° v

same Terms as they had been granted to his Father Buiwant Sing, excepting only the Increase of Tribute heretofore mentioned; and the said Treaties or Agreements did expressly provide, that no Increase of the same should ever be demanded from him; and the same were fully guaranteed by the East India Company, and their Faith pledged that they should remain inviolable, and that there should never be any Deviation from them.

That the said Warren Hastings was bound, as well by the Ties of Justice as by the Obligations of public Faith, to afford the Protection of the East India Company to the said Rajah, more particularly as the Inheritance, and even the Life of the said Rajah, was no longer safe, than whilst he enjoyed such Protection.

That he the said Wart'en Hastings did think himself bound by the said Treaties and Agreements in Favour of Rajah Cheit Sing, to afford him Protection, and to prevent the Vizier from breaking through or deviating from the said Treaties, and did accordingly, some Time in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, interfere and prevent, or did approve of the Interference of the Resident at the Court of Oude for the Purpose of preventing the said Vizier from levying a Sum of Five Lacks of Rupees in Advance from the said Cheit Sing, under Pretence of his the said Vizier’s urgent Necessities, by declaring that his Excellency (viz1 the Vizier) could not on his Part demand either an Increase of Rent or Sums in Advance from the said Rajah; and that the Demand of Five Lacks would, if complied with, establish a Precedent against the said Cheit Sing, contrary to the Letter of the Treaty with him; and that the Honourable Board, viz' the Council of Fort William, of which Warren Hastings, Esquire, was then Governor General, would not see the Rights of their Dependants infringed upon; and that Rajah Cheit Sing was to be considered in that Light; and that the said Vizier must expect to see him protected, for he was not. to be put upon a Footing with his the said Vizier’s other Zemindars.

That the above, and all other Stipulations in Favour of the said Rajah, were fully known to, and approved of, and confirmed and ratified by. the said Warren Hastings.

That the said Warren Hastings did, some Time in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, propose and carry in Council a Resolution, that it should be made a Condition of the Treaty then negociating with the Vizier, that Rajah Cheit Sing should exercise a free and independant Authority tin his Dominions, subject only to the Payment of his Tribute.

That an Assignment was afterwards obtained from the Vizier, by the Company, of the Tribute payable by the said Rajah, whereby the Rights of Superiority which the said Vizier was entitled to hold and to bestow were transferred, yet the Tenure and Condition of the Rajah continued the same as before; the said Assignment being, as the said Warren Hastings has himself declared, without any Encroachment on the just Rights of the Rajah, or the Engagements actually subsisting with him; the Nature and Extent of which had lieen fully known to, and often recognized by, the said Warren Hastings, and which never were, by any subsequent Agreement, Treaty, or otherwise, done away or superseded.

That the said Warren Hastings did, some Time in the Month of June, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, lay before the Council at Fort William, in Bengal, several Propositions, for the Purpose of carrying into Effect the Intentions of the Board to render the said Rajah more independant, to prevent him from being reduced to what he calls the 'Vo 1.. 42.

{prills. 7

mean and depraved State of a mere Zemindar, and to raise him to a Situation of Power and Dignity unknown to any of his Ancestors: That in order to carry the said Intentions into Execution, the said Warren Hastings did inter alia specially propose, and with the Approbation of his Council did actually convey to Cheit Sing the Power of executing criminal Justice and of coining Money within his Dominions, which Powers, in that Country, have always been considered as Marks of Sovereignty: And did further propose, that whilst the Rajah should continue faithful to his Engagements, and punctual in his Payments, and should pay due Obedience to the British Government, no more Demands should be made upon him by the East India Company, of any Kind; or on any Pretence whatsoever should any Pa-son be allowed to interfere with his Authority, or disturb the Peace of his Country: Which Proposition was agreed to by the Council, and was ordered to be communicated to the said Rajah Cheit Sing by Francis Fouice, Esquire, the then Resident at Benares;which voluntary Restraint was proposed by the said Warren Hastings, and laid by the Government upon its own Actions, in order, among other Purposes, to inspire the Rajah with the greatest Confidence, without which he the said Rajah would expect from every Change of Government additional Demands to be made upon him, and would of course descend to all the Arts of Intrigue and Concealment practised by other dependant Rajahs; and because, by proper Encouragement, he would prove a powerful Ally, and a useful Barrier to the East India Company; but that he would be neither the one nor the other, if the Conditions of his Connection with the Company were left open to future Variations.

ARTICLE SECOND.

That the Mother and Grandmother of the present Vizier Asoph ul Dowla, Nabob of are amongst

the Women of the highest Rank, Family, and Distine* tion in Asia, the former being the Wife of the late Sujah ul Dowlah, and the latter W idow of Sufder Jung and Daughter of Sadit, the Predecessor of the said Sufder Jung in the Government of Oude, which said Suf der Jung, Father of Sujah ul Dowlah, and Grandfather

of the present Nabob of Oude, first obtained his Rank among the Princes of India through the Means of the said Alliance.

That the said Mother and Gr&ndmothef of the said Asoph ul Dowla were in Possession of certain Landed Estates, called Jaghires, and certain valuable Move* ables, for the Purpose as well of maintaining their own Rank and Dignity, as for the Maintenance of their numerous Family and Dependants.

That on or about the Months of September or October One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, John Bristoru>, Esquire, the then Resident at the Court of Oude, was requested by Asoph ul Dowla, Nabob of Oude and Vizier of the Empire, to use his Endeavours to persuade his said Mother, commonly called the Bow Begum, to assist him with a Sum of Money, under a Pretence of his great Distress and urgent Necessities, which were principally occasioned by the heavy Debt which he had incurred to the Hast India Company.

That the said Bow Begum did positively refuse to ad* vance or pay to the Nabob any Sum or Sums of Money whatsoever, unless for the Sake, and under the Guarantee of the English.

That in consequence thereof a solemn Treaty was finally concluded between the said Vizier and the said Begums, by which she the said Begum consented to pay to the Vizier the Sum of Thirty Lacks of Rupees in Money and Goods, and granted to him a Release for a Sum of Twenty-six Lacks, which she had formerly advanced to him the said Vizier; which said Sum of Money was paid and released under the express Condition that no farther Sum of Money should ever be demanded from her by the said Vizier, upon any Occasion, or upon any Pretence whatsoever, and under the farther express Condition, that the Jaghires, Lands, Money, Goods, and Property of every Kind, then in her Possession, should be firmly secured and guaranteed to her, under the Protection and Guarantee of the English Nation; and that no further Loan, Claim, or Demand of any Sort should ever be required from her.

That the said Agreement or Treaty was confirmed by the most sacred Forms of the Mahomedan Religion by the said Vizier, and was fully guaranteed by the said Bristow upon the Part of the East India Company-

That the said Guarantee was afterwards, vizi, in or about the Month of November of the Year last aforesaid, fully approved of, and so securely confirmed by the Governor General and Council, JVarren Hastings being then Governor General as aforesaid.

That in consequence of such Proposal, John Willes, Esquire, was appointed to the Office of Resident at the City of Farruckabad, and did proceed to the said City in Execution of his Duty, in which however he was much impeded by the Neglect and by the Orders of the said Warren Hastings; by which Treaty aforesaid, entered into at Chunar, the implied Consent given by the same to the Appointment of a Native Sizwall, and subsequent Breach of Faith to the Vizier by ordering his Jlecall; the Delivery over of Jung to the

Corruption of his Servants; Re-delivery of him to the Rapacity of the Viziers Servants; Re-appoint-' ment of a British Resident, in direct Contradiction to the said Chunar Treaty; and by all the other Acts and Deeds before mentioned, done and omitted to be done by him the said Warren Hastingshe has been guilty of great Neglect of Duty, Usurpation of Authority, complicated Breach of Treaty, and Duplicity, towards both the said Vizier and the said Muzuffer Jung, to the great Disgrace of the British Name, and the Discredit of the British Government in India; having reduced himself to the Situation that he could neither deliver Muzuffer Jung from Oppression, without a Breach of Faith to the Nabob Vizier, nor suffer him to remain under the said Oppression, without violating all Faith, and all Justice, and Regard to him.

And by all and every one of the aforesaid Acts, done, perpetrated, and committed by him the said Warren Hastings, he was, and is, guilty of High Crimes and Misdemeanors.

ARTICLE FOURTH.

That it was the Duty of Warren Hastings, Esquire, while Governor General of Bengal, strictly to attend to the Expenditure of Public Money; and more particularly, in a Time of War and public Distress, to be careful that those Revenues upon which the Welfare and Safety of the Empire did necessarily depend, should not be diminished or ruined by Dissipation and Prodigality, and should not be diverted from the Public Service, and squandered, for the Purpose of increasing his own personal Influence, and providing for his Dependants.

That it was the Duty of Warren Hastings, Esquire, in every Instance in his Power, to pay due Obedience to the Orders of the Court of Directors, his lawful Superiors.

That it was a fundamental Regulation of the East India Company, that all Contracts should be put up to Public Auction, and disposed of to the best Bidder — And it was, by the Thirty-sixth Paragraph of the Instructions given by the Court of Directors of Vor. 42.

ifrilis. 6 75

the East India Company, to the Governor General Articles of and Council, dated some Day in March, in the Year Impeach-One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-four, spe- ment against dally directed, That all Contracts, with the Conditions, Mr, Hast, D68-should be publicly advertised, and sealed Proposals delivered in for the same; and that every Proposal should be opened in Council, and the Preference given to the lowest, provided sufficient Security should be offered for the Performance of the same; and that all such Proposals, with all Proceedings thereupon, should be entered in a Book, and be regularly transmitted to the Court of Directors.

That it was the express Order of the Court of 'Directors of the East India Company, that their Servants in Bengal should Advertise for, and should receive every Year, such Proposals as might be offered for supplying the Troops with Provisions, and for furnishing Draft and Carriage Bullocks to be employed with the Army; and that they should in all Cases accept the Proposals which might appear most reasonable in Point of Charge; and that they should take Care, that in all their Advertisements a sufficient Time should be allowed, before the Expiration of the Contract which might then subsist, or the Time which they might limit for receiving Proposals, for such Persons who might become Candidates for the Con-tractorship to prepare their Proposals for such Contract.

That divers other Orders and Commands, to the same Purpose and Effect, have been issued by the said Court of Directors, at different Times, to their Servants in India.

That the Opium produced in Bengal and Bahar is a very considerable and lucrative Article in the Export Trade of those Provinces; and has of late Years been under a Monopoly for the Advantage of the East India Company, and has been provided by a Contractor; previous to the making a Contract with whom, and in the Contract made, all the Rules and Regulations prescribed by the Directors of the East India Company ought to have been substantially observed and followed.

That it was particularly directed and ordered, that the said Opium, when so provided, should be consigned to the Board of Trade, who were directed to dispose of the same by public Auction.

That it was further the Duty of the said Warren Hastings, not only to be careful in the Expenditure of the Public Money, in the making of Contracts, and in providing for Services; but it was also his Duty to be particularly careful not to lavish the Money of his Employers in excessive Salaries and Emoluments to favoured Individuals, contrary not only to the general Principles of his Duty, but to the positive Orders of his Masters.

That the Court of Directors did especially order and direct that the Sum of Six thousand Pounds per Annum, or some other such Sum, should be paid to the Commander in Chief, in full for his Services, as Commander in Chief, in lieu of Travelling Charges, and of all other Emoluments whatsoever.

That it was particularly the Duty of the said Warren Hastings, not to create, by his Prodigality, that Public Distress, which he has since offered as the principal, if not the only Excuse, for many of his violent and oppressive Acts; and it was particularly his Duty not to rob, by enormous and extravagant Pensions to his Friends and Favourites, that Prince, whose Subsidy to the Company was among its best Resources, but whose Wants and Necessities had forced him to incur an enormous Debt to the Company, to the Ruin of his Country, and the great Distress of the East India Company.

That the said Warren Hasting?,without Regard to his Duty, or the Trust reposed in him, the Distress of the Company, or the Orders of the Court of

Philip TVyatt Cr&wtker, Esquire, Solicitor to the City, being then examined, said. That the Right of placing, removing, and using Mooring Chains within the Port of London, between London Bridge and Bugby's Hole, is at present vested in Sir Peter Burrell, Baronet, by virtue of a Grant from the Crown, for a Term of Years — That the City of London are advised nd understand, and that he believes it to be so, that in order to give full Effect to the Regulations necessary to remedy the Evils before stated respecting the lying And Mooring of Ships, it is essentially necessary that they should be possessed of the Rights and Privileges now held by the said Sir Peter Burrell, Baronet, by virtue of the said Grant — That the Lord Mayor of London being as such Conservator of the River, the vesting the City with the above-mentioned Rights find Privileges, will tend to completely enable them to effect every Purpose that can be requisite for the Security and Accommodation of the Navigation within the Port of London; that, therefore, it is highly requisite that the whole Right of placing and using the Mooring Chains should be obtained and vested in the City of London, for the Use and Advantage of the Public. — And he also said, That he was of Opinion that the Conservatorial Powers now vested in the City are not sufficiently effectual to remedy the Inconveniences Complained of.

Joseph Bushnan, Esquire, Comptroller of the Chamber of the City of London, being examined, said. That he apprehended a very considerable Sum of Money would be required to effect and carry into Execution the several Objects and Purposes enumerated in the Petition; and that he apprehends, and is of Opinion, that a small Tax or Tonnage on the Ships and Vessels, or their Freight, or both, entering the Port of Lcmdort, will produce the Fund required, in the most equitable fend proper Wav.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Margate and Parish of Saint John the Baptist, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Petition hath been presented to die House, for a Bill for better paving, cleansing, lighting, watching, and preserving the Streets, Highways, Lanes, and Passages of the said Town, and for other Purposes, and Leave hath been given to bring in the same; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the extending the Provisions of the said Bill to the Streets, Highways, Lanes, and Passages of and throughout the Whole of the said Parish of Saint John the Baptist, instead of confining the same to the Town of Margate only, Mould be more convenient and advantageous to the Parish in general; and that. Complaints having been made of the Extortions and Impositions of Chairmen, Porters, Carters, Carmen, and other Persons working for Hire as such, within the said Town and Harbour of Margate, and Parish of Saint John the Baptist, the Petitioners conceive that it would tend to prevent in future the Evils complained of, if proper Powers were given to the Commissioners, to be named in the intended Bill, for regulating such Chairmen, Porters, Carters, Carmen, and other Persons, and the Rates and Fares to lie paid to them respectively: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be allowed to extend the Provisions of the said intended Bill, so as to include the Streets, Highways, Lanes, anil Passages of the Whole of the said Parish of Saint John the Baptist, within which Parish the said Town of Margate lies, and also to include such Powers and Regulations as to the House shall seem expedient, re-

lative to such Chairmen, Porters, Carters, Carmen, and other Persons, and their respective Rates and Fares.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Exeter Gaol Mr. Bastard reported from the Committee, to whom wted>n rC' t*le ^et, tion of Denys of Hudscott, in the County

1,or ' of Devon, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Charles IVade being examined, said, that Denys Rolle, Esquire, the Petitioner, and his Ancestors, have been for a great Number of Years past possessed of the Office of Keeper of the Gaol of Exeter, in the County of Devon, by virtue of some Estate situate in that County, or otherwise: And

A Member present informed your Committee, That the present Gaol at Exeter is in a very improper State for the Purposes of a Gaol for the said County, and that it would be much to the Advantage of the said County that the said Gaol should in future be in the Keeping of the Sheriff of the County, and be on the same Footing as other Gaols of this Kingdom — That Mr. Rolle, the Petitioner, had agreed with many of the Magistrates and principal Gentlemen of the said County to give the Sum of One thousand Pounds to be employed in the immediate Improvement and Repair of the said Gaol, in Consideration that the same should in future be in the Keeping of the Sheriff of the said County, and Mr. Rolle and his Estates be discharged from all Offices or Duties respecting the same, other than as the Proprietors of other Estates may be liable in respect thereof.

Vol. 42.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of African Merchants trading to Africa, together with several Company’* Accounts thereunto annexed, being offered to be pre- Petition' sented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House an Account of the Money granted in the Year 1785, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to " Africa," and that they have invested the Money, granted in 1786, for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts having been originally ill-constructed, and composed of the very worst Materials, were delivered to the Petitioners in a very ruinous Condition by the Royal African Company, and the Sums Annually granted by Parliament for their Support

8 O and

694

2 7 — 3 o* .

1787.

and Maintenance being nearly expended in the Civil and Military.Establishments, and in the necessary-contingent Charges, there remained very little for the Purpose of Repairs, inso much that most of them had fallen into Decay, yet the Petitioners, by enforcing the most strict and parsimonious Oeconomy throughout their Service, are now endeavouring to make such Savings as will enable them to put the said ports in as good Repair as they are capable of, and have already given the necessary Orders to that Effect; and that sundry Abuses having been alledged to exist in the Conduct of the Officers employed by the Petitioners on the Coast of Africa, and more particularly in the Management of the Public Money committed to their Care, the Petitioners thought proper, in the Year 1779, to suspend their Governor in Chief, and the Council, at Cape Coast Castle, and to appoint certain Commissioners to examine, in Africa, into the Conduct and Accounts of their Officers, from the Beginning of the Year 1770, and the said Commissioners, or their Successors, having reported fully to the Petitioners upon the different Objects referred to them, and in particular upon the Accounts of their Officers in Africa, and the Petitioners having carefully examined and confirmed the said Reports, it appears by the same, that, at the End of the Year 1776, the Petitioners were indebted to sundry of their said Officers, as specified in the said Reports, to the Amount of £. 24,694. 145. 11 Id. Company’s Pay, but the Account of Richard Miles, Esquire, One of the said Officers, to whom the Sum of £.6,704. 13$. lift/, appeared to be then due, having been afterwards made up by the Petitioners to the End of the Year 1779; the Balance then due to him being £. 5,544. 95. 5d. and the said Richard Miles having been employed since then by the Petitioners, as their Governor in Chief in Africa, and it appearing by the Accounts to the End of his Government, that the Balance of his Account was then reduced to £300. 15 s. 2 d.so that out of the £.6,704. 135. 11 the Sum of £.6,403. 185. 9 appears to have been paid off, which, deducted from the above Sum of £. 24,694. 145. 11 Id.there will remain a Balance of £. 18,290. i6«. 2d. due by the Petitioners to their said Servants, which they are not in a Condition to pay, without the Assistance of the House*; and that the Petitioners having represented, in their Petition to the House, in the last Session of Parliament, that they had been put to sundry extraordinary Expences in assisting the Operations of His Majesty’s Arms in Africa, in the Course of the last War, in Maintenance of Convicts, and other Contingencies, amounting in the Whole to £.7,762. 18& 10 iCompany’s Pay, for Payment of which the House had made no Provision, they now take the Liberty to annex the particular Accounts of the said extra Charges, humbly submitting that the same cannot be defrayed out of the usual Grants from Parliament, without great and manifest Injury to the several Settlements under their Management; and that, by an Act of the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty, the River Gambia, and its Dependencies, were vested in the Petitioners, but the old Fort having been destroyed in the late War, and having no Fund, either to erect or to maintain a Fort for Defence of that River, they have hitherto been unable to take Possession of it, so that it still remains exposed to the Intrusion of Strangers, and more particularly of the French, who, in Violation of the late Treaty of Peace, have made a Settlement therein, and carry on a considerable Trade, to the very great Injury of the British Merchants; and that, however the Grants from Parliament might, at the Commencement of the present African Establishment, have been sufficient to maintain the Forts in some tolerable State of Defence, and to afford such Gratifications to the Natives as would preserve their Friendship and Affection, the same Grants at present are by no Means equal to those necessary

Objects, the Prices of the different Products of,

more particularly of Ncgroe Slaves, having, of late Years, very considerably increased, the Merchandize from Europe, employed in their Purchase, have suffered a proportionate Depreciation, inso much that Presents, which were formerly sufficient to secure the Interests and Confidence of the Chiefs of the Country, are now scarce worth their Acceptance, and the Petitioners being unable, out of the usual Supplies, to satisfy their Desires, they conceive themselves at full Liberty to receive from Strangers those Advantages which the Poverty of the British Forts cannot afford them, of which Disposition the Fren, in particular, have availed themselves, and, in Breach of the last Treaty of Peace, have lately effected a Settlement in the very Heart of the British Possessions upon the Gold Coast, to the infinite Detriment of the said Possessions, and of the British African Trade; and that the British Forts in Africa having thus, through their Poverty, lost the Affection of the Natives, and having no Garrisons to preserve them in any Degree of Respect, are fallen into such a State of Contempt as exposes them to continual Insults, which have increased to such a Height, that a Chief of one of them has been lately dragged out of his Fort, and treated with every Species of Indignity by the Natives; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the Preservation, Improvement, and Extension of the Trade to Africa, and for the Defence and Maintenance of the British Forts and Settlements absolutely necessary thereto, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum as may be sufficient for the effectual Support and Maintenance of the said Forts, for such Presents as may be proper to secure the Friendship of the Natives of the Country, for Discharge of the sundry Debts and Expences upon their Establishment not provided for, and such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Charles Robinson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Margate, and Parish of Saint John the Baptist, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of , whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; anil had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared to your Committee, by the Votes of the House, That Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill to amend and render more effectual an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty King George the First, for the Support and Maintenance of the Pier of Margate, in the County of Kent, for building a new Stone Pier, and for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the said Town, and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein. Ami

Mr. Robert Shelton Cotell being examined, said, That

if the Provisions of the said Bill were extended to the Streets, Highways, Lanes, and Passages, of and throughout the Whole of the said Parish of Saint John the Baptist, instead of confining the same to the Town of Margate only, it would he more convenient and advantageous to the Petitioners, and the Parish in general.

And the Witness further said, That Complaints having been made, of the Extortions and Impositions of Chairmen, Porters, Carters, Carmen, and other Persons plying and working for Hire as such, within the said Town and Harbour of Margate, and Parish of Saint John the Baptist, it would tend to prevent in

future the Evils complained of, if proper Powers were given to the Commissioners to be named in the said Bill, for regulating such Chairmen, Porters, Carters, Carmen, and other Persons, and the Rates and Pares to be paid to them respectively.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considera- Norwich tion the Petition of the several Persons whose Election Names are thereunto subscribed, Freemen of the City Petition con* of Norwich, and County of the same City, on Behalf sid6red-of themselves and the rest of the Electors of the same City and County, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said City, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and One Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Thirteen Members then present, were drawn, who wrere not objected to.

Letters Patent, bearing Date the 14th of March 1778, for authorizing a Scheme for granting Annuities ts the Widows and Children of the Members of the College of Surgeons at Edinburgh, were produced and read.

And,

Mr. Thomas Hay being examined, said, That certain Alterations which have been proposed to be made to the said Scheme would be greatly for the Improvement thereof, and that it would be of Advantage to the Scheme, if the stud Letters Patent were to be confirmed by Act of Parliament, together with the Proceedings had in consequence of the Letters Patent, so far as the same have been agreeable to the Terms thereof, subject to certain Alterations and Additions, and if the Corporation, and the Trustees and Officers elected by them for managing the Scheme, were more effectually impowered to carry the same into Execution. — And he further said, That the Alterations proposed to be made were founded on Calculations which had been well considered by the College; and that the present Amount of the Capital raised by the Corporation is £.3,165, which exceeds the original Calculation by £. 1,200. — And being further examined, he said, That there are now Thirty-seven Members who are Contributors to the Scheme; and that there is an Error in the original Scheme in making the Corporation I;und contribute only £.25 a Year, whereas it was meant that there should be One Pound for every Contributor; and that, by the Calculations now made, it appears that the Annuities may be encreased with Safety to the Scheme.

Petition A Petition of John Sime, of North Leith, Ship-builder, against Leith was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice Harbour Bill. of gj|j for eniarging and improving the , Harbour of Leith, for erecting Docks and other Buildings, for ' widening and making Roads to the said Harbour, for widening and enlarging certain Streets in the City of Edinburgh, and the Avenues leading to the same, and for increasing the Number of the City Guard; and Setting forth, That upon the Suggestion of its being necessary not only to deepen, scour, and enlarge the said Harbour, and the Quays, Piers, Docks, and Warehouses, already constructed, and to widen the Streets, Lanes, and Passages leading to and from the same, but also to construct new Quays, Piers, Docks, and Warehouses, for building, repairing, laying up, lading, and unlading, Ships and Vessels, and for con-

taining Goods and Merchandize, and to make new Streets, Lanes, and passages tp and frpnj foe said Harbour, it is proposed by foe said Bill, that the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council of Edinburgh, and foeir Successors in Office, shall be authorized and Empowered to agree, with foe Owners apd Occupiers of all the Houses, Grounds, and Areas, in North Leith (excepting, the Church and Church Yard) for ..foe Purchase thereof, in order to the said Houses befog pulled down, and the Grounds and Ari^s madp u?e of by the said Lord Provost, Magistrate?, and Council, and their Successors, as they shall think proper, for the Purposes before mentioned, and, . in case of the Owners and Occupiers of the said Houses, Grounds, and Areas, hot agreeing yoliintarily to surrender foeir Properties and Possessions, it is proposed that, they shall be compelled so to do, upon receiving such..a Value as shall be put on the same by a Jury; and, that foe Petitioner is Proprietor of various Houses, a large Dry Dock, a Quay, a Building Yard, Two Smithies for the Manufacture of Anchors, Bolts, Nails, &c. some Areas of Ground, and other valuable Premisses, all situated in the Town of North Leith, and comprehended in the Boundaries described in the said Bill, and is also Lessee of another Dry Dock, Two Smithies,' Three Building Yards or Slips, and Two Houses, sundry Cellars, and other Accommodations contiguous thereto, which likewise fall under the Description of the said Bill, and, was the same to be passed into a Law, not only the Petitioner would be stripped of a valuable Property, and of a Trade still more so, but above Two hundred Persons, dependant on his Business, would be deprived of Bread, by which the Public at large, as well as the Petitioner, and those employed by him, behoved to be very great Sufferers; and that the Petitioner apprehends not only that there is no Necessity for this Attack on his Property, but that to take the Property belonging to or possessed by him, is not requisite for the Enlargement of the Harbour, because it is demonstrable that to widen it at the Place where foe said Property is situated would destroy the Harbour itself; and that the said Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, have not yet, so far as the Petitioner can learn, fixed ori any certain Plan for the Accomplishment of the Objects which they have in View, but, be their Plan what it may, the Petitioner is confident that it is not in their Power to accommodate him with Premisses equal to those which he now possesses, should the latter be demolished, and if they are not to be demolished for the Purpose of Public Utility, he humbly confides in the Justice of the House, that they will not suffer him wantonly to be stripped of his whole Fortune, which is here at Stake; and that the Petitioner conceives, that the said Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, are not aware of the Value of the Property and Trade which they are proposing either to annihilate, or to take into their own Hands, and, if the former is their Object, the Petitioner trusts he will be able to shew not only that an adequate Recompence to him would load the Community with an enormous Expence, but that the Public at large would be essentially injured in all the various Branches of Trade and Manufactures, connected with the important Business of Ship-building, and, if foe latter is the Object of the Bill, the Petitioner throws himself on the Protection of the House, in perfect Confidence that nothing short of absolute Necessity, and evident Public Utility, will be deemed sufficient to authorize such a Violation of the sacred Right of Property, which the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, have not pretended to shew, and cannot shew in this Case: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by himself or his Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law, so far a# his Property and Trade are concerned.

Docks, &c. requisite for the proposed Improvements upon the said Harbour, and the Magistrates and Town Council, are by the said Bill proposed to be empowered, besides the Ground necessary for the said Quay, Piers, Docks, &c. to employ certain Parts of the said Grounds for erecting Warehouses, and also to sell such Parts of the said Grounds, as may not be necessary for the Purposes of the said Act, whereby immense Sums of Money will be levied by the Magistrates and Town Council, to the Prejudice of the present Proprietors, who, by the Operation of the said proposed Act, will be obliged either to yield up their Property and Interests in the Whole of those Grounds, whether truly necessary for the proposed Improvements or not, on such Terms as the Lord Provost and Magistrates of Edinburgh shall propose, or to have it brought into Contest before a Jury of Citizens, many of whom are incapable of judging of the true Value of such Subjects which are mostly rural; and that the Petitioners, who are Proprietors of very considerable Parts of the Property by the said Bill proposed to be taken away, are so sincerely desirous of contributing, as far as they can with Justice to themselves, to the Success of a Scheme which, if confined within proper Bounds, and regulated upon Principles of private Justice, may prove highly beneficial to the Public, without injuring any Individual, that they are willing to part with as much of their respective Properties as shall be absolutely necessary for the Construction of the intended Addition to the Harbour, and the Quays and Piers necessary for the Purposes of Navigation, and are content to accept of such Price for the said Grounds as shall be fixed in their Option, either by Commissioners to be named and appointed, or by a Jury of Landed Gentlemen of a certain Extent of Yearly valued Rent, and real Property, who alone are fit to judge of the Value of the Tenements in Question, but the Petitioners cannot consent to be compelled to give up Part of their Property on any Terms whatever, to be turned to Purposes not necessary for the Improvement proposed by the said Bill, and tending only to raise Money for the Purpose of defraying the Expence of Works in which they are not more interested than the Public in general, and for procuring over and above large Sums to the Corporation of Edinburgh, for the Application of which no Provision is made in the said Bill, and which may be applied to Uses, with which the Petitioners have not the most remote Connection, and from which they can

derive no Benefit; and that the Petitioners hold their Property free from any Restraint, and liable to no Challenge whatever, and they conceive, that taking from them, without their Consent, such Part of it as is not necessary for carrying into Execution the Object of the said Bill, cannot be vindicated upon any Principle of Expedience, and far less of public and absolute Necessity, neither of which require that the Petitioners should be deprived of their Property, even at an adequate Price, for the Purpose of defraying the Expence of a public Work, which, if it cannot be executed from the Profits derived from the Improvements itself, ought to be made a Burden, either upon the Public at large, or upon those for whose particular Advantage it is calculated; and that, as the Petitioners oppose this Part of the Bill upon solid Principles, which regulate private Property, and which the House will never violate, they think it unnecessary to say any Thing further in Vindication of their Opposition to a Measure of which, in its general Object and Tendency, they approve, but which they can never allow to be carried into Execution, at the Expence of material Justice, and to their own extreme Hurt and Prejudice: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, in so, far as is here complained of, may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the same.

Mr. James Brewster, a Master Builder and Mason, being examined, said. That there is a Guildhall in die Borough of Grantham, where the Alderman and Burgesses hold their Session — That in the Guildhall there is a Court House, and Rooms for the Alderman and Burgesses, and Junes, and also Apartments for a Gaoler, and a Gaol for Prisoners — That the Whole of the Building is very ancient, and the Room where the Sessions are held, and the Gaol, are in such a State of Decay, and so incapable of being repaired, that he is of Opinion it will be absolutely necessary to re-build the same.

Mr. John Langwith confirmed the foregoing Evidence; and being examined, said, That the Gaoler’s Apartments are in such a State, that they may be repaired. — And he produced to your Committee a Plan and Estimate of the Expence of taking down the present Guildhall and Gaol, and of re-building the same, and of repairing the Gaoler’s Apartments. — And he added, That the Expence thereof will amount to the Sum of f. 1,000, and upwards.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for talcing down the Guildhall in the Borough of Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, and re-building the same: And that Mr. Cuand Me. George Sutton do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Jobling being examined, said, That the said Town of Neuxastle is very large and populous; that a great Number of People of Fortune and Consequence reside therein and in the Neighbourhood, the Principal of whom have by voluntary Subscriptions erected Buildings within the said Town, properly situated for the Purpose of a Playhouse; for which Subscribers the Gentlemen who have signed the Petition are Tiustees; that it would be the Means of providing a rational and desirable Amusement for the Inhabitants of the said Town and Neighbourhood, if a Patent or Licence were obtained for the Represen* tation of Theatrical Entertainments within the said Buildings.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to enable His Majesty to license a Playhouse in the Town and County of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne: And that Mr. Brandling and Sir Matthew White Ridley do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Richard Tod and Thomas Stoddart, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, it is intended by the said Bill to remove Leith Mills, the Property of the Petitioner Richard Tod, and occupied by him, and the other Petitioner, Thomas Stoddart, which Mills are of great public Utility, and consist of a Com Mill, Saw Mill, and Barley Mill, with some Fields, Houses, and Islands adjoining; and that upon the Possession of those Mills the Petitioners Trade and Business depends, and if taken from them, no possible Retribution can be made to them; and the Magistrates and Town Council of Edinburgh, who are by the Bill impowered to remove the same, will have it in their Power likewise to give the Petitioners Property and Business to any Person they shall please to favour: .' nd therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of John Scougall, Assistant Master, and Andrew Cossets, Depute Master of the Incorporation

of Ship Masters in Leith, was likewise presented to the House, and read; also taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, that certain Tolls and Duties in Name of Anchorage, Beaconage, Pilotage, and certain Fees to the Shore Master of Leith, and his Deputy, are to be levied by the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council of Edinburgh, which the Petitioners conceive they have no Right to by any Grant or Charter, and those Exactions are now under Challenge, and the Subject of a Suit in the Court of Session in Scotland; and that the Petitioners conceive there are other substantial Objections to the said Bill in its present Form, particularly in the proposed Mode of levying the Prime Gilt belonging Jo the said Incorporation: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Gaborien, a Lieutenant in the Navy, being examined, said, That Plymouth Sound is an open Road, and unsafe for Merchant Ships and small Ships of War to ride with Safety in — That in Gales of Wind tb the Southward Catuater and Sutton Pool are the only Places of Safety to which they can resort — That the Prevalence of those Winds occasions the Harbours of Cutwater and Sutton Pool to fill up, and greatly diminishes the Depth of Water.

Ntition for A Petition of Henry Heath, and others, whose Names Leave to are thereto subscribed, being Owners and Part Own-

Petition for ers Ships and Vessels, employed in the Coal Trade

regulating from the River Tyne, on Behalf of themselves and all

the Coal other the Owners and Part Owners of Ships in the said

Trade at Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Setting ^ewcaate, That on the 26th Day of February 1729, several

Petitions were presented to the House from the Owners and Masters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, belonging to the Towns of Newcastle,

Whitby, and Scarborough, stating, " That the Petitioners were greatly fallen to Decay by the many " Difficulties they had lain under for many Years, 44 and unless they were relieved by Parliament, would " inevitably be reduced, and that Branch of the Na-uvigation, which had always been esteemed the principal Nursery for Seamen, be exposed to certain " Ruin, and the Petitioners conceived that many of their Difficulties had arisen, and were occasioned, " by the Corporation of the Lightermen of London: " And praying That the Coal Trade might be laid 41 open, and such other Encouragements given thereto, " as the House should think proper;" and that on the 13th Day of February 1760, Petitions were presented to the House by several Owners or Masters of Ships, belonging to the Ports of Whitby and -borough, on Behalf of themselves and several others, stating, "That the Petitioners and others were very " largely concerned in Shipping, employed chiefly in the Coal Trade at Newcastle, Shields, and -41 fond, which Business the Petitioners presumed had,

41 by long Experience, been found of the greatest " Advantage to this Nation, by raising and continU-" ing very great Numbers of Seamen (who, upon all " Exigencies and Emergencies, had been incorporated into the Royal Navy, and otherwise employed, to " the Safety and Honour of this Kingdom and its " Colonies) and by otherwise employing many Thousands of the industrious Poor, and, that the Peti-

" tioners apprehended it very essential to the Manufacturers and Poor of this Country, to be supplied " with Fuel on easy Terms, and that all Proceedings " tending to a Monopoly must of course be very prejudicial; and representing to the House, that, of " late Years, the Persons employed as Fitters in the " Coal Trade at the Ports of Newcastle and -

" land had become Owners of 5hips to a very great Extent, and, in order to ingross and keep the " Trade in their own Hands, had made it a Practice " to refuse a Loading of Coals, except it was an inferior Sort, to the Petitioners, unless taken upon Freight, at a very considerable under Value, and " at other Times obliging them to wait with their " Ships Eight or Ten Weeks for a Loading, and at " the same Time loading such Ships as they were " themselves most interested in immediately on their " Arrival, by which Means such Ships frequently " made Two or Three Voyages to London before the " Petitioners could get One Loading to sail with, " whereby great Numbers of the Petitioners Ships, " which used to make Eight or Ten Voyages in the " Summer Season, could not then make above Five " or Six in the whole Year, to the great Loss of the " Petitioners in their Fortunes, and to the very great " Prejudice of the Consumers of Coals at London and " other Places, because the Petitioners were obliged " to keep up the Price of their Coals, in order to " make themselves some Amends for their extraordi- nary Expences and Loss of Time, by which Method " of monopolizing, the Fitters, whose Ships made so " many more Voyages in a Year than the Petitioners, " of course had immense Profits upon their Coals, " and were getting Fortunes upon the Wreck of the " Petitioners, and at the Expence of the Public, and " would in a short Time become Masters of the whole " Coal Trade, and have it in their Power to prescribe " such Rules, and set such Prices, as they should " think proper for further aggrandising their own " Fortunes; and that upon Account of the great " Check the Petitioners had met with in their Trade, " they were greatly discouraged from, and found themselves incapable of, taking Apprentices, which " the Petitioners represented would, if not timely " prevented, have very dreadful and fatal Effects " upon the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, " by destroying that great Nursery for Seamen; and that, by an Act made in the Sixth and Seventh " Years of the Reign of King William, Provision was " made for regulating the Weight of every Chaldron of Coals, but their being no Power to punish Persons not complying with the Directions of the said " Act, the same had proved ineffectual, to the further " great Prejudice of the Consumers of Coals, and the Petitioners apprehended, that if the Persons employed as Fitters at Newcastle, Sunderland, and the adjacent Ports, were obliged, as formerly, to keep " public Lists in their Offices of such Ships as applied. " for a Loading, and likewise were obliged to load all Ships as they were entered in their Course, and " also, if proper Power was given for ascertaining " the Weight of every Chaldron of Coals at the several Ports aforesaid, it would be a great Means " of preventing the Evils and Disadvantages above " complained of, and be of'great public Utility: " And therefore prayed the House to take the Pre- raises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief " therein as to the House should seem meet" — And that in consequence of the first-mentioned Petitions an Act was passed in the Third Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for the better " Regulation of the Coal Trade;" and, in consequence of the last mentioned Petitions, an Act was passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Loading " of Ship# with Coals, in the Ports of Newcastle and

" /

Sunderland," and that the Provisions made by the said Two Acts have been found inadequate to remedy the Frauds and Abuses in the Coal Trade in the River Thames, and the Inconveniences and Evils existing in the Loading of Ships with Coals in the River Tyne, by Turn and Rotation, as therein mentioned, and the Petitioners conceive, unless some speedy Regulations are adopted in the Method of ascertaining the Turn or Rotation in which Ships are to be laden with Coals, and for removing many Impositions and Frauds existing in the said Trade, the Shipping in that Trade must greatly decrease, and consequently that grand Nursery for Seamen Ire much impaired; and that a Plan for removing the said several Inconveniences and Evils, and to prevent other Impositions in the Coal Trade, has for some Time been under the Consideration of the Petitioners, which hath not succeeded, but the Petitioners were thereby unavoidably prevented from applying to Parliament for an Act to enable them to carry the said Plan into Execution till after the Term limited by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Rills was elapsed: And, as the Petitioners apprehend a delay in obtaining the necessary Parliamentary Aid will be highly prejudicial to the said Trade, and of great Detriment to the general Interests of this Kingdom, therefore praying. Grounds, and Areas, agreeing voluntarily to sur* render their Properties and Possessions, it is proposed that they shall be compelled so to do, upon receiving such a Value as shall' be put on the same by a Jury; and that the Petitioners, being either Proprietors or Occupiers of almost the whole Town of North Leith (excepting (lie Property and Possessions of Mr. John $ime, Ship-builder) apprehend that they must be greatly injured, should the said Bill be passed into a Law, but as they conceive that they can easily shew, to the Satisfaction of the House, that neither absolute Necessity, nor public Utility, requires their being stripped of their Properties and Possessions, as proposed by the said Bill, so they trust that the Justice of the House will protect them in the Enjoyment of their respective Rights; and that the Petitioners have been rather taken by Surprize in this Attack on the sacred Right of Property, which has for its Object no less than the Demolition of a whole Town, consisting of about Two thousand Inhabitants, all essentially necessary, in their various Professions and Occupations, to the Prosperity of the Port, whose Improvement is the ostensible Purpose of the said Bill: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law, so far as their Properties, Trades, and Possessions are concerned.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, up, on their Petition, if they think fit

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Petition A Petition of John Reid, Gardener, at Reidhall, near against Leith Leith, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Harbour Bill. of the Bill for enlarging and improving the

Harbour of Leith, for erecting Docks and other Buildings, for widening and making Roads to the said Harbour, for widening and enlarging certain Streets in the City of Edinburgh, and the Avenues leading to the same) and for increasing the Number of the City Guard; and Setting forth, That in order to the Accomplishment of those Objects, it is proposed to be enacted, that the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council of Edinburgh, and their Successors in Office; shall have full Power and Authority to agree with the Owners and Occupiers of certain Houses, Grounds, and Areas in the said Bill mentioned, and in case the Parties do not agree, Power shall be given to the Magistrates and Town Council to take from the different Proprietors, without their Consent, and against their Will, their Properties and Estates, lying within the Boundaries therein described, and to pay them only such value for the same as shall be fixed thereon by a Jury, composed of Persons therein described; and that the Grounds proposed to be thus taken from private Individuals are of much greater Extent than is necessary for enlarging the Harbour, and constructing the necessary Quays, Piers, Docks, &e. requisite for the proposed Improvements upon the said Harbour; and the Magistrates and Town Council are by the said Bill proposed to be empowered, besides the Ground necessary for the said Quays, Piers, Docks, &c. to employ certain Parts of the said Grounds for erecting Warehouses, and also to sell such Parts of the said Grounds as may not be necessary for the Purposes of the said Act, whereby immense Sums of Money will be levied by the Magistrates and Town Council, to the Prejudice of the present Proprietors, who by the Operation of the said proposed Act will be obliged either to yield up their Property and Interests in the Whole of those Grounds, whether truly necessary for the proposed Improvements or not, on such Terms as the Lord Provost and Magistrates of Edinburgh shall propose, or to have it brought into Contest before a Jury of Citizens, many of whom are incapable of judging of the true Value of such Subjects, which are mostly rural; and that the Petitioner, who is Proprietor of a consi-

derable Part of the Property "by the said Bill proposed to be taken away, is so sincerely desirous of contributing, as far as he - can with Justice -to himself, to a Scheme, which if confined within proper Bounds, and regulated upon Principles of private Justice, may prove highly beneficial to the Public, without injuring any Individual; that he is willing to part with as much of his Property as shall be absolutely necessary for the Construction of the intended Addition to the Harbour, and the Quays and Piers necessary for the Purposes of Navigation, and he is content to accept of such Price for the said Grounds as shall be fixed in their Option, either by Commissioners to be named and appointed, or by a Jury of Landed Gentlemen of a certain Extent of Yearly valued Rent and real Property, who alone are fit to judge of the Value of the Tenements in Question; but the Petitioner cannot consent to be compelled to give up any Part of his Property on any Terms whatever, to be turned to Purposes not necessary for the Improvements proposed by the said Bill, and tending only to raise Money for the Purpose of defraying the Expence of Works in which he is not more interested than the Public in general, and for procuring over and above large Sums to tine Corporation of the City of Edinburgh, for the Application of which no Provision is made in the said Bill, and which may be applied to Uses with which the Petitioner has not the most remote Connection, and from which he can derive no Benefit; and that the Petitioner holds his Property free from any Restraint, and liable to no Challenge whatever, ana conceives that taking from him, without his Consent, such Part of it as is not necessary for carrying into Execution the Object of the said Bill, cannot be vindicated upon any Principle of Expedience, and far less of public and absolute Necessity, neither of which require that the Petitioner should be deprived of his Property, even at an adequate Price, for the Purpose of defraying the Expence of a public Work, which, if it cannot be executed from, the Profits derived from the Improvement itself, ought to be made a Burthen, either upon the Public at large, or upon those for whose particular Advantage it i% calculated: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, in so far as is here complained of, may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioner may be heard, by himself or by his Counsel, against the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by himself or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.
